- The corner fence (Flats). The generalist who'll take almost anything for pennies on its worth, no
questions, fast — the crew's default for offloading small hot goods and the first fence a green crew
meets. High convenience, terrible rate, and a memory the crew hopes is short.
- The specialist fence. The chop-shop that only moves vehicles and drones; the ripperdoc (Ch. 21) who
buys and re-installs salvaged chrome; the data-broker who deals only in paydata (the digital score —
stolen files, access codes, corp secrets, the highest-margin and most dangerous merchandise in the
sprawl); the talismonger who trades foci and forbidden components. Better rates, real discretion, but
each is a relationship you have to earn.
- The quartermaster (the buy side). The same web that fences your loot sells you your kit, and here the
hard gate is Availability — the shadow market's measure of how hard a thing is to get and how much
heat comes with it. Street goods move freely; military-grade weapons, high-end cyberdecks, restricted
chrome, and true paydata are high-Availability — you need the right fixer, the right Renown, and the
willingness to be remembered asking. The higher up the Availability ladder you reach, the fewer people
can sell it and the more each of them owns a piece of you for having asked.
- Provenance is peril. The corps mark their property (Ch. 8/21) — tagged chrome, watermarked paydata,
SIN-locked gear — so a fence isn't just paying for the item, they're pricing the risk that it's traceable.
The best fences launder provenance; the cheap ones just gamble that the heat lands on you, not them.
A fence's real product is deniability, same as a runner's.

chunks.heading: The Shadow Economy
chunks.text:
Favors, debt, and Renown — the currency under the currency
Beneath the credsticks runs the shadow economy's older, harder currency: what people believe you're
worth and what you owe. Nuyen buys the job; this is what gets you the next one.
- The favor economy. Half the shadow economy never touches a credstick. A fixer floats you a meet; a
gang (Ch. 18) grants safe passage; a ripperdoc patches you off-books — and now you owe. Favors are
the connective tissue that money can't buy and can't fully repay, and a crew's web of who-owes-whom
is as real an asset (and liability) as its gear.
- Debt is the Machine's favorite leash — and the shadow's, too. The bright ledger enslaves through
Lifestyle and financed chrome (Ch. 21); the shadow ledger enslaves through the favor you can't return,
the fixer you burned, the Johnson you crossed. The most dangerous position in the sprawl isn't broke
— it's owing the wrong person.
- Renown is the crew's credit rating. Down here, reputation is literally bankable: a crew's Renown (the
setting's single reputation track, scaling by tier) determines which fixers take their calls, which
Johnsons trust them with the big score, what Availability the market will extend them, and how far a
favor will stretch. Renown is earned by delivering and keeping quiet; it's spent by cashing in the web
you built; and it's lost in an instant by burning a client, a crew, or a fixer. A runner's name is their true net
worth, and the whole shadow economy is, finally, a machine for pricing trust in a world the Machine built
to make trust impossible.
The wider economies — what the street opens onto
The inner-sprawl run economy is the entry tier; sketched here for later passes are the larger markets a
proven crew reaches:
- The wasteland economy — salvage, water, reclaimed-land rights, and the frontier barter of Cinderhold
and the settlements (Ch. 6): higher-Availability, higher-risk, thinner on credsticks and heavier on trade,
and shadowed by what the reclaimed ground is really doing (Ch. 3).
- The syndicate economy — Nyx's Undermarket "the Churn" and the hive-spanning criminal wholesale
above the street's retail (Ch. 8/18): where the gangs' goods and the crew's biggest scores ultimately
flow.
- The off-world economy — the void black market and the colony scrip where you rent your air (Ch.
10/21): the space race's shadow ledger, the highest tier of all.

chunks.heading: Technology & Everyday Life
chunks.text:
deliberately built as a hinge (Ch. 6): from Cinderhold's gate a crew can turn outward into the wastes (the
high-tier, high-lethality wasteland and wild-zone runs — thinner law, thinner Signal, the Incursion in the open)
or inward into the hive itself (the street-level megaplex run — the extraction, the data-steal,
the wetwork, the heist, the milk-run-gone-wrong). Street level is the default starting tier; the wilds are the
escalation. So this chapter's job is texture — the tech, chrome, drones, transit, and media a low-Lifestyle
crew touches every day in the Grid and the Flats — the lived-in surface that makes an inner-sprawl run feel
like one. Wasteland tech (survival rigs, off-grid power, salvage) is sketched here but belongs to the
Hostile-Environments material; the weight of this chapter is the inner megaplex.
The texture of the lit world
Everything in the hive is networked, metered, and owned (Ch. 6, Ch. 8). Tech is not a gadget you buy once;
it is a subscription you live inside. The Wired (Ch. 9) is not a place you go — it is the air the sprawl breathes:
every door, drone, cred-transfer, ad-panel, transit gate, and cortex-jack is a node on it. The dominant
sensory fact of daily life is the overlay: nearly everyone runs a cheap ocular or cortex link that paints the
world with corp-served AR — wayfinding, ads, SIN-status badges floating over strangers, hazard tags, the
ever-present soft glow of a reality that has been edited for you by whoever owns your feed. To move
through the Grid is to see the version of the hive your Lifestyle tier is licensed to see. To run the shadows is,
first, to learn what the overlay is hiding.
- The SIN is the master key. Your System Identification Number (Ch. 6) is your existence: it pays, it opens,
it is scanned a thousand times a day by gates and drones and shop-panels that simply will not transact
with a blank. This is the everyday engine of the whole game — a ghost (no SIN) is locked out of the lit
world's every convenience, which is exactly why they're free of its every leash. Fake SINs, burner SINs,
and SIN-spoofing are the street-level crew's most constant tool and most constant risk; a run often lives
or dies on whether your borrowed identity survives one more scan.
Cyberware culture — chrome is class, chrome is confession
Caduceus and the flesh-corps (Ch. 8) made the body a product, and the street made it an identity.
Cyberware is everywhere and it is legible — the hive reads your chrome the way it reads your altitude:
- In the Crown/Spires, cyberware is invisible: seamless, medical-grade, ruinously expensive
augmentation you're not supposed to be able to see. The elite are heavily augmented and would be
insulted if you noticed. Clean, warranted, Caduceus-serviced, on the ledger.

chunks.heading: Technology & Everyday Life
chunks.text:
- In the Grid, chrome is aspirational and financed: the wage-worker's dental-plan augment, the
corp-issued skillwire that ties you to your job, the augment you're still paying off and that stops working
if you miss a payment. Your body, rented back to you.
- In the Flats/Sinks, chrome is scarred, mismatched, and proud: back-alley 'ware, salvaged mil-surplus
arms (Ironclad castoffs), obvious cyberlimbs and visible optics worn like tattoos. Street chrome says I
chose this and I own it outright — the opposite of the financed Grid augment. The ripperdoc (the
unlicensed street surgeon; cf. Caduceus's Grafthouse and Cinderhold's own) is a pillar of low-Lifestyle
life: cheaper, deniable, no records, and no guarantees.
- The cost that isn't nuyen. Grounding this in the master rules and Ch. 5: heavy augmentation trades flesh
for capability, and the setting quietly frames too much chrome as a spiritual thinning — a body more
owned, more made, more distant from the un-augmented soul the Word first spoke. The Crown's
seamless augmentation and the Sink-rat's junk arm are the same bargain at different prices. Chrome is
never just gear here; it is a small, daily choice about how much of yourself you'll sell to keep up.
Drones, security, and the watched street
The sprawl is saturated with drones and sensors, and this is the single most important everyday fact for a
street-level crew. The lit hive is watched: fixed cams, sensor-arachnids in the corridor ceilings,
corp-security response drones, delivery and maintenance drones threading every level, and — increasingly
— Kestrel Dynamics' autonomous couriers (Ch. 8) gliding through the Grid on their clean, cheap, ubiquitous
routes. Surveillance density is the zone-security gradient made physical:
- The Grid is a panopticon of convenience — order is real but rented, and the price is that you are seen. A
drawn weapon here summons a response in seconds.
- The Flats are where the cameras thin, the drones patrol in packs instead of blankets, and local power
(gangs, level-bosses, Mama Cassavir's web, Ch. 8) fills the gap the corps left. This is the edgerunner's
natural country — watched enough to be dangerous, dark enough to work in.
- The Sinks are near-blind: dead cams, no Signal, no maintenance — which is its own danger (Ch. 3, Ch.
6).
- The runner's craft is therefore, at street level, largely a craft of the watched street: spoofing a SIN past a
gate-scanner, blinding or hijacking a cam-net, slipping a Kestrel courier's route, knowing which corridor
the security drones sweep and when. The Hacker, the Wrench/Rigger (who can turn the drones), and
the Scout live here.
Transit and the shape of a run
Movement in the hive is vertical first, horizontal second, and it is gated by Lifestyle at every step. The great
transit spines — corp-run lift-stacks, maglev arteries, and cargo conveyors — move the wage-body up and

chunks.heading: Technology & Everyday Life
chunks.text:
down the strata, but every tier-boundary is a checkpoint: to ride from the Flats up into the Grid, or from the
Grid into the Upper Tiers, is to pass a SIN-scan and a security posture-check that gets harder the higher
you climb. This is a gift to street-level play: the vertical is the obstacle. A run is often shaped like a climb —
get a Flats crew, with the wrong SINs and visible chrome, up into a Grid or Spire target and back down
again without tripping the boundary between them. Below the licensed transit runs the grey transit of the
Flats and Sinks: unlicensed lifts, smuggler's shafts, the maintenance ways and dead conveyors that fixers
and runners use precisely because they don't scan you — Mama Cassavir (Ch. 8) knows every one of
them. And at the very bottom of the map, the hive opens outward at the gate (Cinderhold, Ch. 6) onto the
wastes — the seam where the inner game hands off to the wasteland game.
Media, ads, and the manufactured calm
The hive is narrated to itself, constantly. Every surface is a screen, every overlay carries a feed, and the
content is the same at every level: reassurance. Obsidian (Ch. 8) pipes simsense and entertainment; the
corp news-feeds report a world that is safe, growing, and fine; the Radiant Concord's luminous liturgy (Ch.
8) broadcasts comfort across the Wired; and the ads never, ever stop. This is not neutral texture — per Ch.
1 and Ch. 5 it is the manufactured calm that keeps the wage-billions from noticing the drift: a media
environment engineered so no one has to feel the war, or the debt, or the dark under the floor. For a runner,
the media layer is both cover and enemy: the same feeds that drown out the Incursion also drown out a
firefight three corridors over, and a crew that knows how to feed the narrative (a staged distraction, a
planted story, a doctored overlay) can move through the sprawl on the hive's own willful blindness. The
truth, when a crew finds it, travels badly — nobody wants the feed interrupted.
The two doors from the Reach
Everything above resolves into the campaign's core promise: from the Reach, a crew chooses its door.
- Inward — the street-level megaplex run (the default, entry tier). The extraction, the data-heist, the
escort, the wetwork, the sabotage, the milk-run gone wrong — fought in the watched corridors of the
Grid and Flats against corp security, rival crews, gangs, and the vertical itself. Lower lethality, denser
social and stealth play, the shadow economy at arm's reach, home base a lift-ride away. This is where a
crew starts, learns the sprawl, and builds Renown.
- Outward — the wasteland / wild-zone run (the escalation, higher tier). The salvage expedition, the
frontier defense, the dead-zone recovery, the Incursion in the open (Ch. 3, Ch. 6) — thinner law, thinner
Signal, hostile environments, and stakes that touch the cosmic war directly. Higher lethality, higher
reward, and a one-way pressure toward the setting's deepest truths. This is where a proven crew goes.
- The design guidance for later stubs (Factions, Shadow Economy, Timeline, Campaign Present) is to
honor this gradient: seed a rich bench of street-level, inner-sprawl content first — fixers, gangs, corp

chunks.heading: Technology & Everyday Life
chunks.text:
targets, level-bosses, the run economy of the Grid and Flats — so the entry tier is deep and playable,
and treat wasteland/wild-zone material as the higher-tier layer a crew earns its way out to.

chunks.heading: The Hive as a Vertical Timeline
chunks.text:
Deep time, one calendar, two silences. Veyra keeps a single continuous civil calendar, inherited unbroken from the dead nations across more than a thousand years; the campaign present is simply the year 2050. What the calendar does not say aloud are two things: the corps treat everything before the Charter (~120 years ago) as prehistory — a thousand years of history quietly uncounted, because to the Ten the world began with the boardroom — and no one at all is permitted to date the Incursion, because the corps do not admit it exists. History runs deep here on purpose: the Founding of the peoples (Ch. 1) sits a full thousand years behind the present, long enough that the how of it is forgotten, and the recent corporate age is only the thin bright skin on top.

Everyone agrees what year it is. What they don't agree on is how old the world is — the corps act like it began with them — and no one at all is allowed to say how long the war has been climbing. One calendar, two things you don't say out loud. A note on the dates. Deep-past dates are deliberately soft ("~1,000 years ago," "the mid-1000s") — the vagueness is canon, not laziness: a thousand years is long enough to forget. Only the recent Charter-era dates are meant to be firm. The Five Ages All dates on the one civil calendar; the present is 2050, the Founding a full millennium behind it. AGE

chunks.heading: The Word & the First
chunks.text:
People before counting Cosmology. Creation spoken; the base human stock seeded; the Dark loosed (Ch. 1). The Founding & the High-Corporate Age ~1050 to 1450 Mortals engineer the breeds; the ancestor-corporations rise; the castes bred true into peoples. The Old World & its Fall ~1450 to 1930 The age of nations; the poisoning of Veyra; the Collapse into arcologies. The Charter Age ~1930 to 2050 The Ten, the Congress, the hives, the Wired — the world the Machine advertises. The Quiet War ~1990 to now, denied The Incursion climbing under the Charter's comfort. Officially, it isn't happening. I. The Word and the First People — before counting Cosmology, not chronology (Ch. 1–3); the floor under everything. The Word is spoken — the Light speaks creation, and Veyra, the Spoken World, is set as the willed proving-ground of free choice, still being spoken. The Dark One turns — the Adversary, who cannot create but only deface, is in the present age loose and ascendant (Ch. 1, 3), the oldest fact behind every later one. The First People — the Light seeds a single willed stock, baseline humanity (Homo sapiens basalis); everything else that walks the Ground, mortals made later. II. The Founding & the High-Corporate Age — ~the year 1050 to ~1450 The setting's founding act of mortal hubris (Ch. 1, the Founding) — the deep spine the recent Charter sits a thousand years on top of.
- ~1050 (a thousand years ago) — The Founding. The mortal powers of a lost high-corporate age — the ancestor-corporations, forerunners of today's Ten — learn to rewrite the seeded human stock and make of it a catalogue of castes: the Elvani (the aesthetic caste, an aristocracy the wealthy could commission), the Corran (the labor caste for the deep mines), the Goliar (the heavy caste for hazardous industry), and others. Engineering a people is not the Dark's work — it is artistry and pride (Ch. 1) — but

chunks.heading: The Word & the First
chunks.text:
the class system of the modern hive is the fossil of this genetic caste design: the strata were drawn in flesh a thousand years before they were built in steel.
- ~1100–1350 — The castes breed true. Over centuries the engineered lines become genuine peoples — Elvani salons and patron-houses, Corran guild-clans and long memory, Goliar kinship-crews — each married within itself (cross-lines cannot interbreed), each grown into a culture with its own dialects, codes, and grievances. The mutual contempt (Elvani over Corran, and back again) is this old.
- ~1250 — The discarded lines. Not every experiment bred true. Failed, abandoned, and broken branches of the Founding are cast out — the deep ancestry of some Mutant lines, the wreckage of the Founding no house wants to admit authorship of (Ch. 5). The first cast-out underclass predates the hives by centuries.
- ~1350–1450 — The high-corporate age fades. The ancestor-corporations decline and are half-forgotten; their science passes into myth, their names into ruins. What survives them is the catalogue they made — the peoples, now walking free of their makers, and the idea, never quite lost, that some were built better than others.
- The forgetting. A thousand years is long enough that the how is gone. Everyone knows the ancestries were made in the Founding, the way we know about fallen empires — settled, ancient, unremarkable. Almost no one can say how it was done, and no one alive can do it again. The knowledge of remaking a people is one of the great lost arts the deep past swallowed. They were commissioned like furniture, a thousand years ago, by companies whose names are weathered off the ruins. Then they went and became people anyway — which was never in the specification, and is the most stubbornly human thing about them. III. The Old World & its Fall — ~1450 to ~1930 The age of nations and its ruin (Ch. 6) — the corpse that became the wastes. The age of nations (~1450–1900) — long after the Founding, Veyra is ruled by states, governments, borders, armies, now more than a century past living memory; this is the world the civil calendar was built to count, and the churches never stopped counting it. The long poisoning — centuries of war, extraction, and hubris scar Veyra into the wastelands and wild zones (Ch. 6): the toxic frontier, the dead cities, the ground where the Veil first tore in the open; the wastes are not wilderness but a graveyard the size of a world. The Collapse (~1900–1930) — the nations do not survive their own poison; in the ruin, survivors do not rebuild states but build arcologies, sealed and vertical and corporate-owned. Ferrum Dynastic, oldest of the coming Ten, is already here pouring the first foundations. The old civil order dies; the corporate one is not yet born. The nations spent the world and called it growth. When the bill came due there was no country left to pay it — only companies, and a poisoned frontier full of the things the countries left behind. IV. The Charter Age — the world as it looks — ~1930 to 2050 The rise of the Machine (Ch. 6–9) — recent history, the only firmly dated stretch, the order the wage-billions believe is permanent and think is the whole story.

chunks.heading: The Word & the First
chunks.text:
- ~1930 (~120 years ago) — The Charter. The ten strongest arcology-corporations stop competing to mutual destruction and sign the founding accords of the Corporate Congress. A cartel wearing a parliament's robes becomes the planetary government; the Extraterritoriality Accords make each seated corp a sovereign country and forbid open war between the Ten while sanctioning the deniable kind — the clause that quietly births the entire runner economy. The corps will come to treat this year as the true beginning of the world.
- ~1930–1970 — The raising of the hives. Under Ferrum's hand the arcologies grow into true hives — continent-anchored vertical megastructures built level on ruined level. Ossian Reach rises as the crown-jewel, the one hive where all Ten keep a tower and the Congress convenes. The vertical ladder — Halo, Spires, Grid, Flats, Warrens, Sinks — sets like concrete: altitude becomes wealth. The great foundation-pumps are sunk in this era; some have now been beating like cathedral-sized hearts for the better part of a century.
- ~1950–1980 — HALO takes the sky. HALO Ascendant's orbital solar arrays and life-support spine make the hives livable and everyone beneath them a tenant of light and air; HALO rises to the First Chair, the denier seated at the head of the table.
- ~1960–2000 — The Wired is woven. Meridian Signal threads the Wired through every level — net, feeds, simsense, the manufactured consensus reality of the wage-billions. Meridian becomes not just the network but the narrative: the conglomerate that decides what the world is allowed to believe. Unknown to anyone, the Wired is a planet-wide thin place that echoes the Signal — the corps have wired the whole world close to the Veil (Ch. 3, 9).
- ~1970–2010 — The Machine closes around the person. The SIN becomes the master key to every convenience (a person with none is a ghost); Argent makes nuyen and debt the universal medium; Caduceus makes the body a rented thing. Life becomes wholly mediated — a world engineered so no one need ever choose, which (Ch. 1) is a world drifting Null-ward. The Radiant Concord, the corporate false-church of the Light, rises in this comfort as its beloved, institutional, secretly-inverted mirror.
- The megacity comes fully alive (~1990 → now). By the late Charter Age the Reach is what the crew steps out into today: thirty million lives stacked kilometers deep, the sky replaced by a hundred thousand signs, and traffic as a second weather — the ground gridlocked, the air lanes stacked, the drones swarming every gap (see the texture panel below). A megacorp is a nation that fired its citizens and kept its customers. The Charter is only about a hundred and twenty years old — a baby, next to the breeds it rules — but it has convinced almost everyone it is the shape the world has always had. The Reach in Motion — the living megacity Woven into the Charter Age so the timeline reinforces the setting, not just the plot; all drawn from the lore bible's street-level canon.
- A city with no sky and no floor. Come up out of a transit tube onto the Flats and the first thing that hits you is the weight of the light — no sky, just a hundred thousand signs stacked forty stories deep, noodle-stall holos and blessing-tier ads and simsense come-ons in six languages, all bleeding pink and cyan and sodium-gold into the standing rain. The rain never stops on the Flats; it falls from the

chunks.heading: The Word & the First
chunks.text:
condensation of a million air-scrubbers on the levels above, warm and faintly chemical, and drags the neon down the girders in smeared ribbons until the whole street looks like it's melting.
- Traffic as a second weather — three tiers at once. The Reach moves on three stacked circulations that never stop. Ground: the Flats and Grid choke on foot-millions, cargo-crawlers, rickshaw-haulers, and armored corp transit nosing through crowds that part for nothing smaller than an Aureole convoy — gridlock is permanent; the street is a river you swim, not cross. Air: above the rooflines, stacked flight lanes run kilometers up the hive face — corp VTOLs and executive shuttles in the high clean lanes, cargo lifters and transit gondolas in the middle, everything sequenced by HALO traffic-control and Meridian's grid; to look up from the Flats is to see not stars but a ceiling of moving running-lights, layer over layer, all the way to where the Halo burns. Drone: the constant swarm in every gap the big traffic leaves — delivery quads, Sanctum surveillance eyes, ad-drones, repair-skitters on the girders, Nyx's black-market couriers running dark between the lanes; the air at street level is never empty and never quiet.
- The heartbeat under everything. Somewhere below your feet a foundation-pump the size of a cathedral has been beating like a heart for a thousand years — the deep pulse of the hive, older than the Charter, older than anyone's grandparents, that you stop hearing until the night it skips.
- The Halo you'll never reach. Past the Grid, past the Spires, past where anyone you know will ever stand, HALO's ring of orbital-fed daylight crowns the top of the hive like a second sun — so bright and so far that from the Flats it reads as a rumor of morning that will never actually arrive. The whole vertical is visible and none of it is reachable: the city is a mountain you live inside. V. The Quiet War — the hidden thread — ~the last 60 years, and no feed will run it The Incursion (Ch. 3), climbing under the Charter's comfort. This is the timeline's secret history. Every entry below is real — and every entry exists in the official record under a mundane name. Nowhere in corp media is the word "demon," "angel," or "the war" permitted; there is only structural, technical, criminal, and market language for it. Meridian owns the narrative, Sanctum owns the records, and both are certain the truth would break the world faster than the thing itself. The rule of the age: you cannot report what you are not allowed to name. The Incursion is not hidden by a single conspiracy — it is hidden by the whole architecture of the Charter, which has no category for it. A dead-air zone is a "decompression hazard." A hollowed outpost is a "loss of contact." A Wired-demon is a "rogue AI." A corrupted zone is a "structural condemnation." A person erased from the inside is a "cognitive-decline case." The cover stories are not even always lies — they are the only words the Machine has, and it prefers them.
- ~1990 (~60 yrs ago) — The first quiet floors. As the hives dig deeper, the first dead-air zones surface in the oldest Sinks. Filed as structural condemnations and walled off. No one connects them; a thousand years of forgetting means no one has the frame to. (This is where "a generation ago" begins — really two generations of small, denied incidents.)
- ~2005 — The first "rogue AI." As the Wired matures, the first Edge-demons wearing the net appear in the logs — indistinguishable from an emergent Null-ward program (Ch. 3, 9). Meridian coins the permanent euphemism — "anomaly" — and begins the practice that defines the age: the analysts who ask what it really is have accidents.

chunks.heading: The Word & the First
chunks.text:
- ~2020–2040 — Blacklight opens the door wider (the "why-now"). Meridian's classified deep-net arm, Blacklight Systems, pushes intrusion deeper than anyone ever has, chasing bandwidth and prediction, and wears the thinnest membrane in creation through. This is the leading answer to why the Dark got loose now — not a cosmic event but a corporate R&D program, run for quarterly advantage, that mistook a doorway for a data-pipe. In the record it is a series of "containment incidents." In truth it is the moment the Quiet War stops being background and starts climbing.
- ~2025 — Deadfall Nine goes quiet. A decommissioned Ferrum foundation-stratum in the Reach's Sinks
— Sublevel 9 — falls silent and is walled off rather than explained. Official cause: structural condemnation. Runners will come to call it the Quiet Floor — the Incursion's first surfaced wound in the home hive, dead-air climbing, and the closest thing the setting has to a ticking clock. Ferrum's Deepworks maintains the seal and the story both.
- ~2025–2045 — The Warrens are written off. Over the same span the corps quietly stop mapping and maintaining the deep underlevels between Flats and Sinks — the Warrens — filed as "deprecated infrastructure." The map of the hive shrinks while the feeds insist it doesn't. It is easier to forget a level than to explain what's on it.
- ~2040–2050 — The truth reaches the systems that were never supposed to fail, and is renamed on arrival. Dead-light climbs HALO's power-spine toward the Halo itself, filed as "array volatility" (HALO's The Dimming). Nyx outposts in the deep Sinks are found hollowed, filed as "loss of contact" (Nyx's The Tithe). The deep net starts answering back, filed as a "persistent intrusion signature" (Meridian's The Static Sermon). The seal on the Nine leaks and the levels above go quiet, filed as "foundation subsidence" (Ferrum's The Foundation Fault). Four corners of the Ten, four surfacing wounds of one war, four mundane cover stories — and four runs, because the only people who can be sent to a thing that officially isn't happening are people who officially don't exist.
- ~2046–2050 — The truce goes brittle (the coming Resource War). No open war between the Ten in a generation, but many feel one coming: resource hunger (the hives built out, the new Space Race devouring capital), the slipping First Chair (Vaine of HALO vs. Solenne of Meridian), and a buried cause almost no one connects — the Incursion is quietly scrambling the resource map, turning wasteland claims barren and lethal. The corps prepare to fight over ground whose real problem is the un-making, and they will call that a market dispute too.
- 2050 — the campaign present (Ch. 24).
Nobody decided to hide the war. It's worse than that. The Machine has no word for it — so a demon in the wires is a rogue AI, a hollowed floor is a subsidence, a man unmade from the inside is early-onset dementia, and the apocalypse goes out on the evening feed as a run of bad luck in the industrial sector. You can't panic a city about a thing it isn't permitted to name. That's the corps' whole plan, and so far it's working.

chunks.heading: The Campaign Present
chunks.text:
The now the game assumes. It is 2050 in Ossian Reach, the political heart of Veyra, where all Ten are present and the Congress convenes. To the thirty million on the Grid this is an ordinary, comfortable, over-surveilled year: the arrays hold, the feeds are bright, the SIN opens every door, the traffic never stops, and the war is not even a rumor — because there is no permitted word for it. To a crew of ghosts working the Flats, it is the year the cover stories stopped adding up. The state of the war — the doom-clock The Dark One is loose and ascendant; the Incursion is actively worsening — the world is losing but not lost. The Unmaker — the Last Word — reaches through aspects, heralds, and hollowings: dead-air zones, hollowed outposts, stretches of the Wired collapsing into Nullspace-static. Its leading edge in the home hive is Deadfall Nine, and the Nine is climbing. None of this is on any feed. The crew's peril is double: the thing itself, and the far larger force of everyone who cannot afford to let it be named. Open threats, live on turn one
- The First-Chair fight. Vaine (HALO) vs. Solenne (Meridian) — a succession struggle at the top of the world, fought in votes, feeds, and deniable runs.
- The brewing Resource War. The generation-long truce fraying over wasteland claims that are quietly going barren; the crew's early jobs are the sparks.
- The Space Race. Each conglomerate pouring capital into nearby worlds for resource — starving the old frontier and raising the stakes of the Chair.
- The surfacing Incursion. The Dimming, the Tithe, the Static Sermon, the Foundation Fault — one rising dark seen from four corners of the Ten, each a run that hands the crew proof the deniers have no word for and can't allow to exist.
- Cinderhold's clock. At the gate to the wastes, Kestrel's "Clean Route" creeps toward buying the last free settlement onto the ledger, while the dead-air spreads in the ground it wants to pave. The three fixtures, ready now The crew's on-ramp is Mama Cassavir, "the Switchboard," in the upper Flats — the seam between clean contracts above and dirty ones below. The place they should not go is Deadfall Nine, the Quiet Floor. The way out of the box is Cinderhold, at the gate to the poisoned wastes, held by Ranger-Captain Cael Marrow, "the Gate." Why the crew matters You are ghosts — unregistered, deniable, choosing — in a world engineered so no one need ever choose, and in an age that has forgotten how to name its own crisis. That makes you the two things the Machine cannot manufacture: people who act off the ledger, and people who can say the true word for what's happening. The faithful and the crew do not win this war; they hold it back — seal a tear, banish a herald,

chunks.heading: The Campaign Present
chunks.text: deny the Unmaker one more stretch of ground — and keep the Word being spoken one more day. It is 2050, and by the count no one is allowed to keep, it is very late. The lights are on, the traffic roars in three tiers, the feeds are bright, and everyone who matters says the world is fine. Down on the Flats, where the rain never stops and a cathedral-sized heart has been beating under the street for a thousand years, a crew that was never recorded is about to learn the true name of a thing the whole world has agreed not to say.

chunks.heading: Themes & Tone
chunks.text:
- Chrome, magic, horror pressure, and urban survival in a world where the spiritual war is real. (From baseline.)
- Bodily cost, corruption, and augmentation matter.

chunks.heading: Peoples & World
chunks.text:
**Source:** *GHOSTWIRE — Lore Source (V1 rules stripped)* → Book One Part III (Peoples) + Founding (Part I); aligned with *GHOSTWIRE-Lore-Book-V2-FINAL* peoples plates (`docs/masters/_lore_extract/GHOSTWIRE-Lore-Book-V2-FINAL_hits.txt`).  
**Harvested:** 2026-09-18 (ET) · fiction / world color only. Mechanical ancestry packages remain in `docs/raw/05-ancestries.md`. Images not embedded this pass.

Eight kindreds, engineered or made, each a people with memory, pride, and contempt.

chunks.heading: The Founding — the Making of the Peoples
chunks.text:
The Word made one people; mortals made the rest. When The Light seeded the prime world (Ch. 1), it set upon it a single willed people — call them the base stock, the first humanity. The many species that fill the world today — the slender and beautiful, the towering and tireless, the compact and unbreakable — are not separate creations of the Word. They are engineered: designed roughly a thousand years ago (or more) by the mortal powers of a lost high-corporate age — the ancestor-corporations, the forerunners of today's Ten — who learned to rewrite the seeded stock and made of it a catalogue of castes. This is the setting's founding act of mortal hubris, and it rhymes forward through everything: the peoples remade themselves by artifice long before anyone bolted chrome to a spine or opened a channel in the Wired.
- Engineered as castes, not as gifts. Each species was built for a purpose the ancestor-corps wanted filled, most of the eight playable species are engineered Homo sapiens subspecies (Homo sapiens gracilis, fossor, giganticus, and so on), a detail corp geneticists still record in the Linnaean binomial. The three clearest cases:
- The Elvani (“elves,” Homo sapiens gracilis) — the aesthetic caste, designed as an upper-class distinction: slender, striking, unnervingly graceful, slow to age, engineered to be seen in the boardroom, the media suite, and the pleasure-tiers. A bespoke aristocracy the old wealthy could literally commission. Their beauty and poise are engineered traits, not magic — a fact they are content to let others forget.
- The Corran (“squats,” Homo sapiens fossor) — the labor caste, built compact, immensely strong, and hardy to work the deep mines and the cramped service crawls no baseline human could survive. The corps still read them as “just labor.”
- The Goliar (“ogres,” Homo sapiens giganticus) — the heavy caste, towering muscle engineered for hazardous industry, demolition, and enforcement — still deployed as breachers and riot-line and still underestimated as “just grunts.”

chunks.heading: The Founding — the Making of the Peoples
chunks.text:
The class system of the modern hive (Ch. 6) is the fossil of this genetic caste system: the strata were literally designed before they were ever built in steel. (Pure Humans — Homo sapiens basalis — remain the base stock the Word seeded; Changers, Mutants, Revenants, and Cyborgs are made, not bred — see below.)
- Castes became peoples. Over a thousand years the engineered lines bred true — and, by design or accident, cannot interbreed with one another (the universal genetic-incompatibility rule: cross-species unions are common and socially normal but never produce children, so there are no born half-species). Each line scattered, married within itself, and grew into a genuine culture — the Elvani with their salons, patron-houses, and exacting social codes; the Corran with their guild-clans, dialects, and long memory; the Goliar with their kinship-crews and plain-spoken loyalty. A person today is not a product; they are the descendant of one, which is a very different and much more human thing. The vanity caste became a nation, the labor castes became nations, and none of them asked to be born to the role their makers intended. The mutual contempt is already canon: the Elvani look down on the Corran as brute labor, and the Corran return it with interest.
- The made, not the bred. Four of the eight are not engineered breeds at all but conditions laid over a living person: Changers (metamorphic strains), Mutant Humans (mutagenic corruption), Revenants (embodied undead), and Cyborgs (Machina sapiens — machine-first beings no longer legally or biologically “human”). They are made within a single lifetime, not descended from the Founding — the Founding explains the bred peoples; these are what the world does to individuals now.
- Known, but normalized. This is not a hidden truth waiting to be uncovered. Every educated person knows the ancestries were made in the Founding, the way we know about fallen empires — it is ancient, settled history, not a corporate secret. What is live is what it means now: who is “refined” and who is “stock,” who deserves the Crown and who was built for the Sinks, whose ancestors commissioned and whose were commissioned. The prejudice is the more insidious for being dressed as heritage rather than hatred.
- Reconciled with the cosmology. The Founding does not violate Ch. 1. The Dark One cannot create, only deface — but mortals, made in a creating world, can shape what the Word already spoke. Engineering a people is not damnation and not the Dark's work; it is artistry and pride, morally neutral in itself, exactly like chrome (Ch. 5). It becomes the Dark's road only where it reaches toward domination and un-speaking — which is precisely the shadow lying over the elven aristocracy and the corps that still trade in “who was built better.”
- The Mutants, re-read. This casts Ch. 5's Mutants in a colder light: some Mutant lines are not only taint bred true but failed, abandoned, or corrupted branches of the same old engineering — castes that broke, experiments the ancestor-corps discarded, or lines the Incursion (Ch. 3) later got into. The hive's tainted underclass is, in part, the wreckage of the Founding no one wants to admit authorship of.

chunks.heading: Peoples Of The World
chunks.text: Eight kindreds, engineered or made, each a people with memory, pride, and contempt.

chunks.heading: Pure Humans — The Base Stock
chunks.text: Names: Homo sapiens basalis · Baseline Human · Norms, Naturals, Purebloods, flatlines. Kind: bred (the seeded stock — the one people the Word actually made; Ch. 1). Origin & nature. Pure Humans are the original people — the single willed stock The Light seeded on the prime world before any mortal hand rewrote it (Ch. 1, the Founding). Every other bred species is a variation the ancestor-corps cut from this cloth; every made condition is most often laid over a human body. They carry no engineered caste-purpose, no undead grave-pull, no mutagenic taint, no machine chassis — which is precisely their identity: the unmodified default, the widest-open build, the point of comparison for everyone else. Their gift is adaptability (the Adaptive Edge): no single thing they do best, and nothing they cannot learn.

chunks.heading: Pure Humans — The Base Stock
chunks.text: Culture & place in the world. Humans remain the demographic majority and the assumed "standard citizen" around whom the megacities, their products, their SINs, and their laws are all designed — the default the corporate world quietly builds for. This is both privilege and trap: a human is normal and therefore invisible, neither prized like an Elvan nor feared like a Goliar nor owned outright like a Cyborg, free to disappear into the crowd of a hundred million. That very ordinariness makes them the setting's great swing vote in the Cosmic War. The least visibly altered by the war, they make the ideal vessel, agent, convert, or victim — the Light recruits them, the Dark tempts them, and the corps spend them. Most runners are human for the simplest reason: humans are who the world overlooks.

chunks.heading: Cyborgs — The Machine-First
chunks.text: Names: Machina sapiens (deliberately outside genus Homo — machine-first, no longer legally or biologically "human") · Full-Conversion Cyborg · Borgs, Chrome, Tin-men, Husks. Kind: made (a total conversion of a once-living person; not a bred people). Origin & nature. A Cyborg is the far end of the chrome road. A cyber-augmented human bolts implants onto a living human chassis and stays human (Ch. 12); a Cyborg has spent all of their Body Integrity — the artificial chassis no longer overlays the person, it replaces them. Whether by catastrophic injury salvaged into a frame, corporate conversion of an asset, or a soul's own hunger for the machine, the result is a being that runs on modules and mag-servos, healed by medtech and Technomancer resonance rather than rest or medicine. They do not scale by growing flesh; they scale by slotting hardware.

chunks.heading: Cyborgs — The Machine-First
chunks.text: The severed thing. Full conversion cuts the Cyborg off from the one source. They can never touch magic — arcane, divine, elemental, resonant, infernal, holy — because in the locked cosmology all magic is a mortal reaching for the Word (Ch. 2, the one-source rule), and a machine-first being has no living aperture left to reach with. This is the setting's starkest statement that the soul is not in the parts: you can rebuild the body to the last gram and still sever it from the Signal. It is also why the Cyborg is existentially unstable — emotionally damped, capped in Presence, and prone at zero Stamina to System Crisis, a psychosis-rage the Director drives until it burns out or the frame is destroyed. Culture & place in the world. Cyborgs are feared as inhuman, prized as assets, claimed as property, and — by a growing few — revered as the next stage of the species. They live the setting's central question of whether soul, machine identity, and divine or infernal influence can share one body. Frames give them their working castes: the Warframe (heavy combat chassis), the Infiltrator (stealth/insertion), and the Medtech (field repair and surgery); two further frames are held in reserve. A Cyborg on a crew is muscle and hardware that magic cannot mend — and a soul the war is fighting over from a strange, cold distance.

chunks.heading: Changers — The Skin-Turners
chunks.text: Names: Homo sapiens versipellis ("skin-turner") · Metamorphic Type · Changers, Shifters, skins, weres. Kind: made (a metamorphic strain, not a Founding caste — one species with internal lines). Origin & nature. Changers are one species braided from three possible roots: engineered animal hybridization (corp bio-labs splicing beast into human), occult shapeshifting strains (old were-lineages the war stirred back to life), and dimensional morphic contamination (flesh that touched a thinning membrane and learned to run). Whatever the root, every Changer shares the Alternate Form birthright — a human-passing form, an overtly bestial hybrid combat form, and a full beast form — and a Feral Tell, some animal marker (eyes, gait, teeth, scent) that the passing form can minimize but never fully erase. They cannot be surprised while aware; they are also baited through that Tell.

chunks.heading: Changers — The Skin-Turners
chunks.text: The lines. Changers run in subtype families, each a different animal instinct made flesh: the Wolf (pack hunter — strength and the hunt), the Rat (survivor and infiltrator — the gutter's own), the Feline (ambush predator — the pounce from the dark), the Reptile (cold endurance — the patient coil), and the Avian (scout and skirmisher — the eye from on high). Two more families are held in reserve. Culture & place in the world. Changers do not have one culture; they have as many as they have lines and origins, bound by a shared experience of not quite passing. In the megacities a Changer is a walking contradiction — human enough to hold a SIN, beast enough to be hunted when the Tell shows — so many run in tight kin-packs that blur the line between family, gang, and hunting party. Some corps prize engineered Changers as living infiltration and tracking assets; the occult and dimensional strains are more often feared as monsters or courted as recruits by both sides of the war. On a crew a Changer is versatility incarnate: the face who becomes the scout who becomes the beast that ends the fight.

chunks.heading: Revenants — The Undying
chunks.text: Names: Homo mortuus redivivus · Reanimate / Post-Mortem Type · Revs, Deaders, Rotters, Ghosts (late-stage). Kind: made (no one is born a Revenant — they are the returned dead). Origin & nature. No one starts life as a Revenant. They are made in the moment of death: a person who died with a purpose too fierce to release — vengeance, an oath, a debt, a flat refusal — and rose again, sustained by will rather than blood, keeping the memories and personality of the life they left. In this setting the Cosmic War supercharges that return: the Light may send a soul back to finish holy work, the Dark One may deny a soul its rest out of spite, or a corp's resurrection-tech may fail in a way that is really something older reaching through the tear. A Revenant begins as embodied undead and only slowly loses the flesh.

chunks.heading: Revenants — The Undying
chunks.text: The Decay and the dread. A Revenant's body is a countdown. Over a career they walk a Decay ladder — from Fleshbound (a rotting, cold-fleshed corpse that walks) to Withered/Skeletal (dried toward hardened bone) to Spectral (translucent, phasing, ghostlike) — trading a little humanity at each rung for a little more of the grave's power, until the late-stage Revenant is nearly a wraith. Their Undying Return means a felled Revenant does not die but drops inert and rises again after a respite — which makes them relentless, and terrifying to fight. But it is not true immortality: fire taken while inert, consecrated or annihilating force meant to lay the dead to rest, or the deliberate destruction of the inert body ends them for good. This is why fire is a Revenant's oldest fear, and why an enemy who knows what they are facing brings a torch. Culture & place in the world. Revenants have no homeland and no bloodline — they are recruited from every other people by death itself — so their "culture" is one of purpose and unfinished business. They are walking proof that in this war death is not final, which makes them holy to some Light-orders (a soul granted a second chance) and abominations to others (a thing that should be laid to rest); the Dark One's cults covet them as recruits already halfway across. Corps that dabble in resurrection-tech both create them and hunt them. Every Revenant is a story with its last chapter unwritten — the ideal crew member with a reason, and the ideal antagonist who will not stop coming.

chunks.heading: Mutants — The Marked
chunks.text: Names: Homo sapiens aberrans · Aberrant / Mutagenic Type · Muties, Tainted, Wrongborn. Kind: made or born-marked — but never a clean bred people; always carries the taint. (See also Ch. 5, corruption, and the Founding note that some Mutant lines are failed or discarded engineered stock.) Origin & nature. A Mutant is human clay the world has rewritten — by inherited taint, by a birth in a corrupted zone, by a magical accident, an infernal bargain, or deliberate corp gene-forging. Born or made, there is no difference: every mutation is, at root, a wound the world left in a body that the body turned into a weapon. Some Mutant strains are older than any individual — the Founding note is explicit that a fraction of Mutant-kind are failed, discarded, or corrupted lines of the same thousand-year-old engineering that made the Elvani beautiful and the Corran strong: castes that came out wrong, and were culled or cast into the

chunks.heading: Mutants — The Marked
chunks.text: Sinks to breed among themselves. Others are freshly touched last week. All of them share one thing. The Corruptive Flaw. Every Mutant carries a permanent Corruptive Flaw — the price of their power, and the setting's clearest fingerprint of the Dark One on ordinary flesh. The Flaw deepens as the Mutant leans into their gifts (a hidden Corruption Load that rises with every serious mutation), scaling from a Latent quirk, to a Manifest visible burden, to an Ascendant danger where the Dark's hand shows openly and control itself must be rolled for. This is the tragic engine of the species: power and corruption are the same current, and the more a Mutant reaches for one the more they drink of the other. A Mutant is never just a monster — most are victims of a war fought across generations, bearing a stain they never chose. Culture & place in the world. Mutants are feared as monsters, hunted as threats, hidden by their own kind in undercity enclaves, or forged on purpose by corps as expendable bio-assets — and where they stand in society tracks almost exactly with how visible and how deep their taint runs. Loose strains (Brute, Aberrant, Tainted, Latent) give them concept-families rather than true castes, because mutation is chaotic by nature and refuses to be sorted. The Dark One's cults revere powerful Mutants as chosen vessels; Light-orders meet them with pity, suspicion, or crusading steel. On a crew a Mutant is raw, escalating power with a cost the whole table can see coming — the friend who is always one bargain away from becoming the thing they fight.

chunks.heading: Elvani — The Aesthetic Caste
chunks.text: Names: Homo sapiens gracilis ("slender/graceful") · Aesthetic-Class Engineered Type · Elves, corp-dolls, Prettyboys, Pointers, Highborn. Kind: bred (a Founding caste; breeds true, cannot interbreed). Origin & nature. The ancestor-corps engineered the Elvani to be seen: the faces of the boardroom, the media suite, the diplomatic table, and the pleasure-tiers — a bespoke aristocracy the old wealthy could literally commission. Slender, striking, unnervingly graceful, quick, commanding, and slow to age, they were the vanity caste made flesh. A thousand years on they are a fully distinct people with their own high culture — salons, patron-houses, exacting social codes — and one crucial, deliberate truth: their beauty and charm are engineered, not magical. An Elvan's "glamor" is poise and pheromone and perfect bearing, not sorcery; they cast no better than anyone, and they are happy to let others forget the difference. Their

chunks.heading: Elvani — The Aesthetic Caste
chunks.text: signature is Ephemeral Grace — the twinned gift of a charm that lands like truth and a body that nothing quite catches. Long-lived, not deathless. The Elvani are Ageless in the engineered sense: their physiology resists aging and preserves youth for centuries. They are not immortal — violence, disease, drain, and eventually extreme old age still take them, and they die like anyone else; they simply take a very long time to do it (contrast the Revenant's made undeath, Ch. 15, which is the only true "deathlessness," and even that ends in fire). A several-hundred-year lifespan is advantage enough: an Elvan can outwait a rival's whole career, and — because they breed true and forget nothing — an Elvani grudge or debt can outlast the humans who first incurred it. Culture & place in the world. The Elvani sit at the top of the corporate social ladder and are never quite allowed to forget who put them there: adored and objectified, elevated and owned, a status symbol before a person. That gilded cage breeds patron intrigue, blackmail-webs dressed as salons, and the occasional beautiful runner who walks away from everything the world told them they were for. Their contempt for the Corran as "brute labor" is canon and mutual — the two engineered castes, cut from the same act a thousand years apart in station, despise each other on sight. The overtly Elvani conglomerate is Argent Exchange (Ch. 8), where this whole caste-legacy becomes present-day corporate power. A disgraced or discarded Elvan is fertile ground for the Dark One's whisper that real freedom is power, not patronage.

chunks.heading: Corran — The Labor Caste
chunks.text: Names: Homo sapiens fossor ("delver/digger") · Corran / Labor-Class Engineered Type · Squats, Deepers, dust-eaters. Kind: bred (a Founding caste; breeds true, cannot interbreed). Origin & nature. The ancestor-corps engineered the Corran as the laborer breed — compact, immensely strong and hardy, built to work the deep mines, the cramped service crawls, the high-pressure and low-clearance spaces machines couldn't reach and baseline humans couldn't survive. They read as dwarves in build and constitution but stripped of the old fantasy trappings: no universal beards, no rune-magic birthright — just Corran men and women, proud and practical, engineered to endure and not go down. Their signature is Unyielding: the immovable laborer who refuses to be pushed, pulled, knocked down, or budged.

chunks.heading: Corran — The Labor Caste
chunks.text: Culture & place in the world. A thousand years on the Corran are a fully distinct people with their own communities, dialects, and above all guild-clans — the tight, loyal work-crew-families that double as information networks and safehouse chains a crew ignores at its peril. The megacorps still read them as low-class — "just labor" — and the Corran repay it with deep solidarity, a very long memory, and a chip on the shoulder the size of a mine cart. Because they breed true and forget nothing, a Corran feud or debt runs for generations. They sit at the bottom of the corp class ladder and know it, which makes them natural runners, union agitators, undercity power-brokers, and reluctant heroes with real grievances — and fertile recruiting ground for both a Light-faith that prizes endurance and loyalty, and a Dark One who offers power to the perpetually overlooked. Their mutual contempt with the Elvani (Ch. 17) is a ready-made table tension.

chunks.heading: Goliar — The Heavy Caste
chunks.text: Names: Homo sapiens giganticus ("giant") · Goliar / Heavy-Class Engineered Type · Ogres, slabs, Wallbreakers, Big-uns, Grunts. Kind: bred (a Founding caste; breeds true, cannot interbreed). Origin & nature. The ancestor-corps engineered the Goliar as the heavy breed — towering slabs of muscle built for hazardous heavy industry, demolition, load-bearing, and security/enforcement work no baseline human could survive and no Corran was big enough to do. Where the Corran are compact and unbreakable, the Goliar are enormous and overpowering — the most physically front-loaded people in the world. Their signature is Towering Menace: large size and long reach, crushing might, and a bulk so intimidating it turns their blunt manner into fear-based social power.

chunks.heading: Goliar — The Heavy Caste
chunks.text: Culture & place in the world. A thousand years on the Goliar are a fully distinct people with their own communities, kinship-crews, and a hard-won culture of loyalty, plain speech, and slow-burning pride. The corps still deploy them as muscle — bouncers, breachers, bodyguards, riot-line — and still underestimate them as "just grunts," mistaking a slow tongue for a slow mind, which is a mistake made exactly once. Their loyalty runs deep and their memory of who treated them like people and who treated them like equipment runs deeper — fertile ground for both the Light's message of dignity and the Dark One's promise of power to the used-up. A Goliar crew-boss commands a respect no corp badge can buy, and their plain-spoken honesty in a world of liars makes them either the most trusted member of a crew or the one who never sees the double-cross coming. The sight of an angry Goliar coming through the wall ends most negotiations early.

chunks.heading: Ossian Reach — Street Color
chunks.text:
**Source:** *GHOSTWIRE — Lore Source (V1 rules stripped)* → Ossian Reach fixtures (Part II Ch. 6) + street factions (Part IV Ch. 20); Flats primer color from in-repo *Ossian Reach Handbook* extracts (`docs/setting/reach-handbook/01–02`); Ashenreach from `docs/setting/ashenreach.md`. Hit-index: `docs/masters/_lore_extract/`.  
**Harvested:** 2026-09-18 (ET) · optional print color only — **not** a gazetteer reprint of Reach Handbook journals. Print Ch. 27 stays a thin pointer. Gang signs (B91) inject after the L3 headings below.

> Street color and hive fixtures for the booklet. District dossiers, NPC stat blocks, and critter sheets stay in setting / Foundry packs.

chunks.heading: The Default Home Hive
chunks.text:
The campaign's default sprawl is Ossian Reach — the continent-anchored crown-jewel hive where the core campaign is assumed to run unless a table says otherwise. It is one of the great vertical hives of Veyra (Ch. 6): kilometers up into real sky, kilometers down into dead-level dark, built layer on ruined layer until no one alive remembers its ground floor.
- The name. Ossian is a founding-era name — the hive is raised on the fossilized bones of everything it was built over (os, bone; the hive is a reef of its own dead levels), and Reach is what the founders called the impossible thing they built: a structure that reaches from the Sinks to the Crown, from the buried dark toward the sunlit sky. Ossian Reach: the bone-tower that reaches for the light. Locals just say "the Reach," and to live in it is to spend your life somewhere on the climb between the two.
- Why it's the default. Ossian Reach is a HALO-dominant hive — fitting, since HALO Ascendant holds the sky, the power, and now the First Chair (Ch. 8). Its Crown is a HALO arcology-halo of orbital-fed light; every other conglomerate keeps a tower here because this is where the Congress convenes. That makes the Reach the political heart of Veyra — the one hive where all Ten are present, the Sunlit Chair

chunks.heading: The Default Home Hive
chunks.text:
sits, and Vera Solenne wages her campaign for it. A crew working the Reach is working the center of the board.
- The vertical, named in the Reach. The strata (Ch. 6) get local names here: the Halo (the Crown — HALO's orbital-lit apex), the Spires (upper corp towers), the Grid (the vast wage-body), the Flats (the semi-lawless underlevels where most runs begin), the Warrens (the written-off deep-underlevel warren-country beneath the Flats — the Reach's own name for the Low↔Squatter seam where corp maps end, salvage and off-grid holdouts live, and the descent toward the Sinks truly begins), and the Churn's country — the Sinks, the sunless dead-level dark where Nyx's moving Undermarket ("the Churn," Ch. 8) drifts and the buried past stirs. The way down is the campaign's descent-engine; the way out is the gate to the wastes (Ch. 6).
- What makes it runnable. Ossian Reach gives a table everything at arm's reach: all Ten conglomerates present, the Congress and the First-Chair fight live overhead, Nyx's Undermarket as the crew's supply chain and job board in the Sinks, at least one known thin place (a Blacklight-tainted deep-net node under a Meridian tower, Ch. 8–9) and one corrupted zone bleeding up from a dead level, and a clear vertical spine — Halo to Sinks — that is the Lifestyle ladder made walkable.

chunks.heading: The three fixtures of the Reach
chunks.text:
Every campaign hive needs three things a GM can grab on turn one: someone who hands out the work, somewhere the players should not go, and a way out of the box. Ossian Reach has all three, named and ready. The signature fixer — Mama Cassavir, “the Switchboard.” The Reach's default job-giver works out of a shuttered transit exchange on the upper Flats, a dead switching-station she's wired back to life and named herself after — an old woman (or so she appears) who sits at the junction of everything that moves through the middle of the hive. Soft chrome and a good cosmetician sell the grandmother; underneath she is a datajacked cyborg Controller with a Switchboard Deck and a private overlay-cell. Cassavir is the seam between up and down: she takes clean-branded contracts down from the Spires and corp cut-outs above, and dirty ones up from Nyx's Churn (Ch. 8) below, and she connects the crew to whichever end pays. She is not street muscle and not a mage — she is the phone, the one node everyone in the Flats routes through, and her power is that severing her would cut a hundred quiet deals at once, so no one does.
- Her code. Cassavir sells introductions, not people. She will burn a client to protect a crew's anonymity but never the reverse, because her whole franchise is being the fixer runners trust when every corp would sell them out — and she guards that reputation like the asset it is. Cross her once and you don't get killed; you get disconnected, which in the Reach is worse..), and a relationship to spend and endanger.

chunks.heading: The worst corrupted zone — Deadfall Nine
chunks.text: (“the Quiet Floor”). The Reach's known corrupted zone is a sealed dead level deep in the Sinks: officially Sublevel 9, a decommissioned Ferrum foundation-stratum (Ch. 8) that went dark a generation ago and was walled off rather than explained. Runners call it Deadfall

chunks.heading: The worst corrupted zone — Deadfall Nine
chunks.text:
Nine, or just the Quiet Floor — because the defining symptom of the corruption here is the Unmaker's dead-air (Ch. 3): sound thins, then signal, then thought. Deep in the Nine the Wired doesn't reach, a scream carries no distance, and people who linger come back emptied — or don't come back at all. It is the closest surfaced wound of the Incursion in the whole hive, and it is climbing: the seal leaks, and the levels just above the Nine are slowly going quiet too.
- Why it's the worst. It is not monsters — it is un-making. The zone attacks the things a crew relies on to survive: comms, coordination, courage, memory. It's a place that punishes exactly the corporate certainty the Crown is built on (nothing is wrong) by being living, spreading proof that something is. Ferrum's Deepworks (Ch. 8) quietly maintains the wall and pretends the Nine is a structural condemnation; Nyx routes around it and sells the danger; HALO's feeds insist it isn't there. (Ch. 1, 3): the place “The Tithe” and “The Foundation Fault” point toward, the horror set-piece, the reason the Sinks are feared, and the ticking clock — every session it is a little larger. A crew that goes into the Nine and comes out changed is the campaign's coming-of-age. The wasteland settlement at the gates — Cinderhold. Where the Reach's lowest habitable levels open out onto the poisoned wastes of Veyra (Ch. 6) sits Cinderhold — a scrappy, half-free settlement clinging to the hive's outer gate, built from the Reach's cast-offs and the wasteland's salvage. It is the way out of the box and the closest thing to unowned ground the campaign has: too poor for the Ten to bother annexing, too useful to destroy — the last stop before the wilds and the first market for anything the wastes drag in. Verdant Provision's Greenline Rangers (Ch. 8) use it as a forward post; Nyx runs contraband through it; wasteland caravans and hive-exiles meet here to trade.
- Who lives there. Cinderhold is the home of the cast-out: burned-SIN humans, Mutants exiled from the hive's clean levels (Ch. 5, Ch. 16), Changer packs and Goliar kinship-crews who'd rather be free and poor than owned and fed, and Revenants who frighten the tidy Crown. It is prejudiced, dangerous, and real in a way the sedated hive is not — the one place in the default setting where the underclass the Founding built (Ch. 1) governs itself, badly and freely. It is, quietly, the most hopeful place on the map: people who chose (Ch. 1) over people who were kept.. Cinderhold's protector — Ranger-Captain Cael Marrow, “the Gate.” Cinderhold has no mayor and no council that anyone obeys; what it has is Cael Marrow, a former Greenline Ranger field-captain (Ch. 8, Verdant) who worked this stretch of frontier for twenty years, buried too many crews to reclaimed ground that came back wrong (Ch. 3), and one day simply stopped filing his reports and stopped going back inside. Verdant lists him as lost on survey; the wastes know him as the reason Cinderhold is still standing. He went native in the truest sense — not gone feral, but gone loyal, to the cast-out settlement instead of the corp that trained him. He holds the gate with an ad-hoc militia of retired Rangers, Goliar kinship-crews (Ch. 19), and anyone who can hold a line, and he governs the only way the place can be governed: by being the one person hard enough, fair enough, and feared enough that the raiders, the cartels, and the corps all decide Cinderhold is more trouble to take than to leave alone.

chunks.heading: The worst corrupted zone — Deadfall Nine
chunks.text:
- His authority. Marrow's power is not a title — it's that he is the settlement's living early-warning system.
He still reads the ground the way a Ranger does; he is the first to know when a caravan route has gone quiet, when the wastes are pushing something toward the gate, when the dead-air is spreading (Ch. 3). Cinderhold obeys him because the times it didn't, it got hurt. He keeps an uneasy back-channel to Verdant (old comrades who still slip him seed, water-tech, and ammunition off the books) and a colder one to Mama Cassavir up in the Flats (Ch. 8) — the two of them are the settlement's and the hive's twin switchboards, and they trust each other exactly as far as professionals do.
- The threat leaning on it — the Clean Route (Ch. 8, Kestrel Dynamics). Cinderhold's slow-motion existential threat is not raiders and not (yet) the Incursion — it is Kestrel Dynamics, whose autonomous-transport expansion (the “Clean Route,” Ch. 8) has finally noticed that the cheapest corridor from the hive into the deep wastes runs straight through the gate Cinderhold sits on. Kestrel doesn't want to conquer Cinderhold; it wants to civilize it — to buy it, brand it, insure it (a Sanctum partnership), pave its market into a logistics depot, and put the free settlement on the ledger at last. It comes not with an army but with contracts, clean water, and reliable pay — an offer that would end the raider threat overnight and end Cinderhold's freedom just as fast, splitting the settlement between those exhausted enough to take the deal and those who fled the hive precisely to never be owned again. Marrow is the fulcrum: the Falcon's people court him (a Ranger-captain is exactly the credible local face Kestrel needs), and Marrow knows the thing Kestrel doesn't — that the route it's so eager to pave runs through ground that is going quiet (Ch. 3). He is sitting on the same truth as the “Clean Route” run hook, from the other side of the gate. creeps closer, and the crew's own choices — do they help Kestrel prove the corridor safe, help Nyx keep it “dangerous,” or help Marrow keep the gate free — decide whether their home stays unowned. Marrow is the patron who gives wasteland work, the hard-but-fair authority who can bar a crew from the one safe settlement in the wastes, and, if the Incursion surfaces at the gate, the veteran who has seen it before and will finally have to say so out loud.

chunks.heading: What the Flats Are
chunks.text:
Come up out of the transit tube and the first thing that hits you is the weight of the light. It does not fall from a sky — there is no sky, this low — it comes from everywhere at once: a hundred thousand signs stacked forty stories deep, noodle-stall holos and blessing-tier ads and simsense come-ons in six tongues, all of it bleeding pink and cyan and sodium-gold into the standing rain. The rain never really stops on the Flats. It falls from the condensation of a million air-scrubbers on the levels above, warm and faintly chemical, and it drags the neon down the girders in long smeared ribbons until the whole street looks like it is melting.

This is the fourth stratum down — **Lifestyle 4, Low** — the semi-lawless underlevel where the Machine's grip loosens just enough for a person to disappear into it. Above you, the **Grid** hums with wage-bodies who still have something to lose. Above them, the **Spires**; above them, the **Crown**, and the Halo burning at the top of the hive like a second sun so far away it reads as a rumor of morning that never actually arrives. Below you, the **Warrens** thin out into the written-off dark, and below that the **Sinks**, sunless and Signal-dead, where Nyx runs the Churn and worse things settle in the deep floors.

The Flats are the seam. Watched enough to be dangerous, dark enough to work in. This is the edgerunner's natural country — the place most runs begin, and the only place in the Reach where nobody chose the shape they were born to but everybody, at last, gets to choose.

chunks.heading: Getting to & from the Flats — The Vertical Is the Obstacle
chunks.text:
In the Reach, altitude is the class system, and movement is **vertical first, horizontal second**. You do not simply walk to the Flats or away from them — you ride the strata, and every boundary between them is a wall the Machine built to keep the wrong bodies on the wrong rungs. Understanding that wall is the first thing a crew learns and the last thing a run turns on.

**The two ways down, the two ways up.** There are only ever two kinds of passage between levels, and a crew's whole plan lives in the choice between them.

**The licensed spines — the corp way.** The great **transit spines** are the Machine's arteries: corp-run lift-stacks, maglev tubes, and cargo conveyors that move the wage-body up and down the tower on schedule. They are fast, clean, well-lit, and watched to the millimeter. Every one of them charges a fare on the bright ledger and, worse, every tier-boundary along the route is a **checkpoint**. To ride a spine is to trade time for exposure — you arrive quickly and you arrive seen.

**The grey transit — the runner's way.** Beneath and beside the spines runs the Flats' own circulatory system: **unlicensed lifts, smuggler's shafts, maintenance ways, and dead freight-conveyors** that fixers and runners use precisely because they do not scan you. Mama Cassavir knows every one of them, and access to the good ones is a favor, a fee, or a Renown check. Grey transit is slow, filthy, sometimes structurally unsound, and occasionally someone else's territory — but it is quiet, and quiet is the runner's native currency.

chunks.heading: Getting to & from the Flats — The Vertical Is the Obstacle
chunks.text:
**Coming in.** Most crews first arrive on the Flats the way the book opens: up out of a dead transit tube into the weight of the neon and the warm chemical rain, or down a grey shaft from the Grid with the wrong SINs already burning in their pockets. Coming into the Flats is the easy direction — the Machine does not much care who sinks to the Low levels, only who tries to rise. A body drifting downward is a body giving up on the ledger, and the checkpoints going down are lighter for exactly that reason.

**Going up (inward — the hard climb).** This is where a run lives. To take a Flats crew — with visible chrome, borrowed identities, and gear that should not exist — up into the Grid, the Spires, or the Crown is to pass a rising wall of scrutiny, and the check gets harder with every rung:

**The SIN-scan.** Every boundary gate reads your System Identification Number. A blank simply will not transact — the gate won't open for a ghost. A crew moves up on **fake, burner, or spoofed SINs**, and a run can live or die on whether a borrowed identity survives one more scan. A **Wanted** flag on any crew member lights the scanner up like a flare.

**The posture-check.** Higher boundaries add a security-posture read on top of the SIN — dress, chrome, behavior, the company you keep. A Flats loadout reads wrong in a Spire lift, and the higher you climb the more the gate expects you to belong.

chunks.heading: Getting to & from the Flats — The Vertical Is the Obstacle
chunks.text:
**Going down and out (outward — the gate to the wastes).** Below the Flats the passages stop being checkpoints and start being dangers. The **Warrens** and **Sinks** have no gates because they have no order — descending means the cameras die, the Signal thins, the maintenance stops, and local power (gangs, level-bosses, the Churn) fills the gap the corps abandoned. And at the very bottom of the map the hive opens outward at **the gate — Cinderhold**, the wasteland settlement where Ranger-Captain Cael Marrow holds the seam between the inner game and the wastes beyond. To leave the Reach entirely is to pass through Cinderhold onto the open ground, where the law is thinner, the Signal is thinner, and the war is in the open.

**Documents that will pass.** At least one clean **fake or burner SIN** per crew member (¥100–300 each, single-scan and disposable), matched to the tier they mean to reach. A SIN that reads Flats-Low will not open a Spire gate.

**A route, licensed or grey.** Decide the direction of exposure: buy fare and speed on the spine and plan to beat the checkpoints, or buy quiet on the grey transit and plan to survive the shaft. Cassavir sells routes as readily as she sells jobs.

**Chrome discipline.** Visible street chrome that reads proud on the Flats reads criminal in the Grid. Crews climbing high either run subtle 'ware or plan to talk (or hack) around the posture-check. What you wear is part of your cover.

chunks.heading: Getting to & from the Flats — The Vertical Is the Obstacle
chunks.text:
**The specialist for the gate.** Know before you leave which door-opener you're leaning on — the Face for the talk, the Hacker for the spoof, the Scout for the bypass. A crew with no answer to a checkpoint is a crew that gets turned back at the first boundary.

**Gear for the vertical itself.** For the grey shafts and the outward climb, a **grapple-and-line or ascension rig** (~¥2,000) turns a lethal drop into a traversal. The vertical is terrain, and terrain kills the unprepared.

chunks.heading: The Black Water — The Cistern-Sea, the Flood-Cycle, and What Lives Below
chunks.text:
Ask anyone in Slackwater where the water comes from and you'll get a shrug; ask where it goes and they'll lower their voice. The Flats sit on the drowned floor of the hive, and the black water that fills Slackwater's piers, the Drowned Market, and the culverts of the Spillway is not a river, not a sea, not a reservoir — it is all three and none of them, an engineered body of water the Reach has been quietly managing, and quietly lying about, for a thousand years.

**What the water actually is.** The Reach was built upward on the fossilized levels of everything it stood on, and the lowest of those old levels never drained — they drowned. What the docks call the **cistern-sea** is the flooded remains of the hive's own foundations: dead sub-levels, older ruins, and pre-Founding structure, filled to a black mirror whose bottom the charts stop pretending to know. It is not natural water. It is runoff, condensation, the endless warm chemical rain sheeting off every level's underbelly, and the slow weep of a thousand years of leaking infrastructure, all pooled in the dark and stirred by machines. It is warm in places it shouldn't be, and near the Sinkmouth it steams where something warmer wells up from below.

chunks.heading: The Black Water — The Cistern-Sea, the Flood-Cycle, and What Lives Below
chunks.text: **Where it goes — down, not out.** Here is the thing the corps don't advertise: **the water does not flow out to the wastes. It flows down.** The Flats are the ground-level seam where the hive meets the poisoned wastes through the outer gate at Cinderhold — but the outer gate is a dry gate, a wall onto open ground, not a river mouth. The black water instead drains inward and downward, through sluices and culverts and the great sealed throat of the **Sinkmouth**, into the half-flooded dark of the **Warrens and the Sinks** below. Slackwater is not the bottom of the water; it is a landing on the way down. Everything that pools on the Flats is destined, eventually, for the deep dark — which is precisely why the deep dark is half-flooded, and precisely why the things stirring down there are so often described as rising through black water.

chunks.heading: The Black Water — The Cistern-Sea, the Flood-Cycle, and What Lives Below
chunks.text: **Self-contained, cleaned, and rationed — the Ferrum machine.** The whole system is **corp-managed infrastructure, run by Ferrum Dynastic** through its dock authority and hydraulics crews. It is closed-loop by design: pumps lift and circulate, sluice gates route the flow, drains carry the overflow down, and reclamation plants skim the top layer clean enough to matter. But "clean" is a corporate word. The reclaimed water that reaches the Flats is expensive and rationed — a working freshwater still (like Dassa Wynn's in the Drowned Market) sells clean water at a price that's "either extortion or mercy depending who's asking," and the purest stills are quietly tapping unlicensed **Caduceus runoff lines** that aren't supposed to exist. The rain you can catch off a tarp is the only water most of the Flats can truly count on. Below the reclamation layer, the black water is not clean — it carries contaminants, disposed corp waste, and the occasional thing pulled up on a barge that makes people sick in ways a ripperdoc can't explain.

chunks.heading: The Black Water — The Cistern-Sea, the Flood-Cycle, and What Lives Below
chunks.text: **The flood-cycle — the heartbeat under the heartbeat.** The single most important game-fact about the water is that **it moves on a schedule.** Ferrum's tidal system counts down to a **scheduled flood** — pumps and sluice gates cycling the water level up and down through the culverts and drains on a published timetable.
