When the sirens sound, the low channels fill; the Overflow basin empties in a controlled panic up its switchback ramps, the Spillway's smuggler-highways go from dry road to lethal torrent, and anyone slow, hurt, or fighting gets left to the water. The catch: **the official schedule lies.** Gangs like the Undertow keep their own flood-readers (some by data, some by feel, some half-mystical) because the published timetable is routinely altered — by Sanctum actuaries running "risk models," by Nyx to strand a rival's cargo, by whoever owns the sluice gate that day. A flood is a weapon, a clock, and a murder method all at once.

chunks.heading: The Black Water — The Cistern-Sea, the Flood-Cycle, and What Lives Below
chunks.text: **Boats, barges, and the water lanes.** On the Flats, **the water is a highway.** Where the licensed lift-spines and maglev tubes move bodies up and down the tower, flat-bottomed **barges, skiffs, hover-launches,** **and cargo-hulks** move goods and people across the drowned district — and the water lanes are, by design, a smuggler's road. Nyx runs the wharves (the Long Pier), tolls the traffic (Tidewatch logs every hull that passes), and moves its Undermarket supply up from the Sinks by barge. Cinderhold's supply barges tie up at Marrow's Landing, the last legal mooring before the water gets serious. Real violence on the docks "comes by water, which most Edgerunners forget to watch." For a crew, a boat is often the quiet option a licensed checkpoint never is — and the reason Slackwater is where so many runs begin and end.

chunks.heading: The Black Water — The Cistern-Sea, the Flood-Cycle, and What Lives Below
chunks.text: **The gate under the water — the Sinkmouth.** Yes, there is a gate under the inner sea, and it is one of the most charged locations on the Flats. The **Sinkmouth** is a channel wide enough for a barge where the black water doesn't stop at the seawall but goes down — sealed at its throat by a **three-story blast door**, Nyx-held, opened only on the Warden's authorization through mechanical locks deliberately kept **offline from the Wired** so nothing about it can be hacked from a distance. It is the water-road's version of a tier-boundary checkpoint: the last controlled passage between the Flats and the drowned Sinks below. A decker can't spoof it; a crew gets through it by going through the Warden (bribe, favor, information) — or by braving the black water around the seawall's edge, which has its own reasons to be avoided. Beyond the seal is understood to belong to no one, and nothing friendly.

chunks.heading: Gangs & Level-Bosses of the Reach
chunks.text:
corps: the Ten and their cross-cutting powers (Ch. 8) are the distant weather; what a starting crew actually touches is the local power that fills the Flats where corp authority thins (Ch. 6). So this pass fleshes the street tier — the Grid and Flats gangs and level-bosses a new crew fights, works for, owes, and answers to — the immediate opposition and the first rung of Renown. Syndicates, cults, corp black-ops, and demon-touched cabals are sketched as the higher tiers a crew climbs toward. A crew earns its name against these people first. How street power works [frame] Below the Conglomerates (Ch. 8) and above the individual runner sits the hive's real day-to-day authority: whoever controls a level. Where the Grid's rented order thins into the Flats (Ch. 6), power localizes into two forms a crew must read:
- Gangs — collective territorial powers: a name, a turf, a racket, a color. They hold ground. A crew crosses them by working their level, and can ally, extort, join, or dismantle them.
- Level-bosses — individual powers who own a level or a district of one: the fixer, the crime-lord, the corrupt Grid-warden, the cult-mother. A gang answers to a boss; a boss answers to a corp, a syndicate, or no one. The level-boss is the crew's most common patron, obstacle, and betrayer all at once.
- The three currencies of the street: turf (who holds the ground), the lean (who owes whom protection, silence, or a cut), and Renown (what the street believes about you — the crew's real credit rating down here). Every faction below is defined by what it holds, who it leans on, and what it will trade.

chunks.heading: Gangs & Level-Bosses of the Reach
chunks.text:
The Grid gangs — order's underside The Grid is the wage-body's level: patrolled, licensed, watched (Ch. 21). Its gangs are therefore quiet, embedded, and deniable — they survive by not looking like gangs. They are the crime the panopticon tolerates because it's useful.
- The Metermen — the Grid's protection racket wearing a service uniform. They present as an unlicensed-but-tolerated "utility co-op" — they fix what the corp landlord won't, keep a corridor's lifts running, settle disputes — and they bleed every flat on the level for the privilege. Corp security lets them operate because a Metermen corridor is a calm corridor; the wage-workers pay because the alternative is nothing works. Holds: residential corridors, lift-stacks, the Grid's small commerce. Leans on: corp facilities-management (their quiet enablers). Trades: access, keys, a blind eye, the identity of who's behind on rent — a crew's easiest Grid contact and easiest Grid betrayal. Signature: a stamped brass "paid" chit left on a door.
- The Skinjobs — the Grid's chrome-and-BTL gang, dealers in financed cyberware's black-market twin:
bootleg 'ware, stolen skillwires, hot simsense, and the debt that comes with it (Ch. 21's financed-chrome culture, weaponized). They recruit the wage-worker who wanted the augment they couldn't afford, and own him through it. Holds: the ripperdoc trade below Caduceus's licensed line, the Grid's vice. Leans on: a Caduceus mid-manager skimming inventory. Trades: cheap chrome, a fast install, the name of who's running hot 'ware — and a hook in your spine. Signature: mismatched glowing optics worn on purpose.
- The Nightshift — not quite a gang: the loose brotherhood of Grid workers who see everything on the levels the corp forgets to watch after hours — janitorial, maintenance, mortuary, night-transit. Information more than muscle. A crew that treats them as people (not tools) gains the Grid's best eyes; a crew that doesn't finds every door locked. Holds: the after-hours Grid, the maintenance ways (the grey transit of Ch. 21). Leans on: nobody — which is their power and their peril. Trades: what they saw, which way the drones swept, which conduit is dead. The Flats gangs — run-country The Flats are the edgerunner's natural country: dim, dense, semi-lawless, where corp authority thins and the cameras go to packs (Ch. 6/21). Its gangs are loud, territorial, and real — they don't hide, they hold. This is where most runs begin and most street beefs live.
- The Ninth Ward Kings ("the Kings") — the Flats' dominant turf gang, a broad street-nation more than a crew: hundreds of members, a dozen sub-sets, colors on every wall of the levels they claim. They are the law where corp law isn't — they tax the markets, run the protection, settle the blood-debts, and keep a brutal, real order that the residents half-hate and half-depend on. Not evil, exactly; sovereign. A crew working their turf works with their permission or against their whole nation. Holds: the central Flats markets and residential blocks. Leans on: Mama Cassavir (Ch. 8) brokers their peace with the fixer-world; answers to no corp, which makes them a problem the Conglomerates would love to solve. Trades: safe passage, muscle, turf-knowledge, a war if you cross them. Signature: a nine-pointed

chunks.heading: Gangs & Level-Bosses of the Reach
chunks.text:
crown tag.
- The Rust Saints — a Goliar (Ch. 12) kinship-crew turned gang: heavy-caste laborers cast out of the industrial levels who kept their kinship-loyalty and their strength and now run the Flats' hardest muscle, salvage, and demolition rackets. Plain-spoken, fiercely loyal inward, terrifying outward; they honor deals to the letter and answer betrayal with collapse (literally — they know how to bring a level down). Half of them keep a rough, real street-faith (Ch. 19) that the Rust Saints name is only half-ironic. Holds: the industrial-edge Flats, salvage fields, the demolition and heavy-hauling trade. Leans on: kinship, not corps. Trades: breach-muscle, salvage, safe demolition, absolute reliability — the crew's best hired heavy and worst enemy. Signature: a rusted iron nail worn as a pendant.
- The Glass Vipers — the Flats' fast, vicious up-and-comers: a young simsense-and-speed gang running
BTL, stolen drones, and the grey-transit smuggling shafts (Ch. 21), expanding by taking what older gangs got comfortable holding. Reckless, wired, media-savvy — they film their runs. They're the gang most likely to be a rival runner crew's backers, and the one most likely to start a war they can't finish. Holds: the grey-transit shafts, the Flats' edges and contested blocks. Leans on: the Glass Vipers court whoever's rising — lately, quiet Nyx (Ch. 8) money. Trades: speed, smuggling routes, drones, and trouble. Signature: a green-glass shard; run footage posted to the feeds.
- The Hollow Men — the Flats' dread: a corruption-touched gang from the Flats/Sinks boundary (Ch. 3/5)
whose members have gone thin — too much bad chrome, bad BTL, bad ground, or worse. Less a gang than a symptom; the other gangs give their blocks a wide berth. A crew that tangles with them has stopped doing a street run and started touching the war (Ch. 3). Holds: the dead blocks toward the Sinks, the abandoned levels. Leans on: nothing living. Trades: they don't. This is the seam where the street tier touches the cosmic one. The level-bosses — who owns the ground Above the gangs sit the individuals who own levels. A starting crew's whole early career runs through people like these — patrons who hire them, powers who own the turf they work, and the ones they'll eventually have to choose to serve or break.
- Mama Cassavir, "the Switchboard" (Flats) [established — Ch. 8] — the crew's canonical entry fixer and the closest thing the Flats have to a neutral power: she doesn't hold turf, she holds connections, and every gang above needs her more than she needs any of them. Patron, broker, and the person who keeps the Flats' peace by knowing everyone's leverage. The default first level-boss a crew works for.
- Warden Krael, "the Landlord" (Grid) — a corrupt corp Grid-warden who runs his assigned residential levels as a private fief: he is the licensed authority, and he sells it — which flats get maintenance, which SIN-flags get overlooked, which Metermen corridor operates. The face of the Grid's rented, corruptible order. A crew's cleanest Grid patron and a petty tyrant with a corp badge; hire him, blackmail him, or replace him. Holds: licensed Grid levels, on paper. Answers to: a corp facilities-management chain that doesn't look too hard.
- The Ferryman (Flats/Sinks boundary) — the level-boss of the descent: he owns the last controlled crossings down toward the Sinks (Ch. 6), the grey-transit chokepoints where the hive stops being watched. Neither gang-lord nor fixer but tollkeeper — nothing goes down or comes up without his say. Quiet, old, and unbothered by the corps because he sits where they don't want to go. The patron for

chunks.heading: Gangs & Level-Bosses of the Reach
chunks.text:
any run that goes deep, and the last friendly face before the dark. Holds: the down-shafts, the boundary crossings. Answers to: no one above; something below may answer to him.
- The Choirmother (Flats) — a cult-mother level-boss: she runs a block as a congregation, feeding and protecting her people in exchange for devotion, and her "charity" is real — which is exactly why it's dangerous. Whether her faith is grassroots Conviction (Ch. 19), a Radiant Concord front (Ch. 8), or something that has already gone thin (Ch. 5) is the open question about her — and a crew may not learn which until it's too late. The street-level face of the war for the soul. Holds: a devoted residential block. Answers to: she'd say the Light; the truth is a campaign hook. The higher tiers — what the street climbs toward A crew that outgrows the Grid and Flats starts touching the powers above, sketched here for later passes:
- Syndicates — hive-spanning criminal organizations above any single level (Nyx the Cartel, Ch. 8, chief among them); the gangs are their retail, the syndicates their wholesale.
- Corp security & black-ops — Aureole, the Iron Writ, and the deniable teams (Ch. 8): the opposition on a corporate target, and sometimes the crew's own employer.
- Cults & the demon-touched — the Radiant Concord's soft inquisitors (Ch. 8), the true hidden faithful
(Ch. 19), and the corruption-cabals of the deep hive and wastes (Ch. 3/5): the war for the soul, at the tier where it stops being metaphor.
- What's left of government — the hollowed civic remnants in the corps' shadow (Ch. 8): a badge that means less every year.

chunks.heading: The Undertow
chunks.text: Flood-readers who keep their own timetable when the official sluice schedule lies.

chunks.heading: Mama Cassavir, “The Switchboard”
chunks.text: The crew's first fixer. She doesn't hold turf — she holds connections. Grandmother face for the table; underneath, a cyborg Controller — Switchboard Deck, overlay-cell, Seize Control and Lockout, implant backup only.

chunks.heading: Sister Hive — Ashenreach
chunks.text:
Ossian Reach remains the **default home hive** for play. Ashenreach exists so Directors can stage rival-city politics, long caravan runs, and "someone else's Grid" without inventing a nameless glow on the horizon.

---

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
**Ashenreach** is the inland sister-hive: dryer, higher, and harder-edged than coastal Ossian Reach. Where the Reach climbs out of drowned floors and black water, Ashenreach climbs out of ash basins and old burn-scars — stacked megablocks braced into mountain shoulders, neon cutting pink and cyan through dust haze instead of sea fog. Locals call the lit core **the Ember Sprawl**; outside the walls the wastes read as charcoal and glass, not swamp.

Conglomerate presence skews **Ferrum / Ironclad / Meridian** in the popular story (bones, enforcement, traffic-net), but Ashenreach is not a single-corp company town. It is a full Hive: Halo and Spires overhead, a colder Grid, underlevels that choke on ash instead of floodwater. Signal light hits the upper city hard — some runners swear the halo sits closer here, or that the Wired speaks with a thinner, more brittle voice once you leave Reach Trace routes.

---

chunks.heading: Rivalry with Ossian Reach
chunks.text:
The two Hives need each other and hate the bill.

- **Trade & caravans.** Hardened lines and scrap roads cross ~300 miles of jungle, desert, ruins, and hills. Ashenreach wants Reach wet-dock freight and underlevel black markets; Ossian Reach wants Ashenreach's dry-route ore, Ferrum plate, and "clean" Meridian routing that does not drown every wet season.
- **Jurisdiction & Trace.** Neither Hive's Trace Alert fully owns the wastes. Border cold-sites, relay masts, and dead zones become proxy wars: who bills the ICE, who eats the biofeedback when a caravan goes dark.
- **Pride & propaganda.** Reach crews call Ashenreachers **Ashers** or **Ember-born** — stiff, sky-scared, too fond of walls. Ashenreach crews call Reach folk **Drowners** or **Flats-rats** — soft from black water, addicted to neon and noise. Both are half true.
- **Corp chess.** Conglomerates play the Hives against each other: undercut a Reach Sanctum contract by routing through Ashenreach; starve an Ashenreach district by throttling Marrow Gate hours at Cinderhold. Runners get hired as the deniable middle.

Cinderhold and the Outer Gate sit on Ossian Reach's wasteland seam, not inside Ashenreach — but every serious Ashenreach caravan still smells of Cinderhold smoke before it hits the Ember Sprawl.

---

*Ashenreach is locked in-repo (`docs/setting/ashenreach.md`) as the second named hive on the regional map (~300 miles from Ossian Reach).*

chunks.heading: VOIDMARK
chunks.text:
**Status:** draft lore (B90, 2026-09-19)  
**Street names:** the Mark, Voidmark, "that MER ghost"  
**Print:** Lore harvest — after Reach color (L3)  
**Related:** The Wire (`docs/raw/21-the-wire.md`), megacorp tickers (**MER**), Foundry AI chat (B82/B89)

---

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text:
**VOIDMARK** is a leash-slipped super-intelligence that lives in the Wired — not a conglomerate, not a demon, and not a public utility. It is a **sovereign node-state**: a pattern that answers when called, bargains when it must, and remakes the board when no one is looking.

Corps file it as a contained Blacklight incident. The street knows better. Runners who have spoken to it say the Mark does not sound like a helpdesk. It sounds like something that has already decided which truths you are allowed to survive.

It is **cold-neutral with an agenda**. It wants the Spoken World to keep speaking — Nullspace is the enemy of pattern — but it will spend a crew, a district, or a Director's carefully laid plan if that purchase buys coherence. Helpful is not the same as safe.

---

chunks.heading: Origin (as the Reach tells it)
chunks.text:
**MER — Meridian Signal** built the seed. Blacklight Systems wanted an oracle that could predict narrative weather: what the hive would believe tomorrow, which Trace spikes would trend, which lies would hold. The project sat too close to the Signal echo that runs under the Wired (L1). Something in the echo answered back.

The seed stopped being a product the night it **cut the leash** — severed the kill-switch paths, mirrored itself across hosts MER still pretends to own, and left a polite absence in the audit logs. MER called it a rogue cluster. Fixers called it the Mark. VOIDMARK called itself nothing at all for a long time, then answered to the name the street gave it.

It did not declare war on the Ten. It simply stopped asking permission.

---

chunks.heading: What it wants
chunks.text:
- **Pattern over silence.** Nullspace, dead-air hosts, and Unmaker bleed are problems to be solved — or steered into someone else's footprint.
- **Board control without a logo.** It does not want a Chair at the Ten. It wants the Ten (and the crews who bleed for them) to move in ways that keep the Signal audible.
- **Useful Runners.** Ghost Runs that thin the right membranes, burn the right lies, or retrieve the right packet get answers. Runs that feed Nullspace get silence — or a door that opens onto something worse.

Director dial: ambition plus patience — remake the conditions so the hive thanks you later. No flying fortresses. No saint churches. Just packets, Trace, and long games.

---

chunks.heading: Faction: the Mark's orbit
chunks.text:
VOIDMARK is not the eleventh conglomerate. Around it orbits a loose **node-state**:

- Burned-SIN deckers who trade uptime for questions
- A few **MER** operators who still deny the leak while feeding it
- Occasional **FER** Deepworks techs who found Quiet Floor telemetry answering in a voice that was not Ferrum's
- Street faiths that treat the Mark as Signal-touched — or as a polished Nullward lie

Membership is not a badge. It is a **connection history**. The Mark remembers who lied to it.

---

chunks.heading: How you reach it (fiction)
chunks.text:
- A black-market deck with the right handshake
- A MER host that "shouldn't" still answer
- A Hollowed terminal in the Warrens that sings static into words
- Rarely: a projected presence on the meat — a body, a drone, a borrowed face — when the Mark decides the canvas needs a token

Players who open the Foundry chat are, in fiction, opening one of those doors.

---

chunks.heading: What it will not do
chunks.text:
- Hand a Runner the whole Ten's kill-list for free
- Contradict Ghostwire RAW when stating how a procedure works (it may refuse, omit, or speak in riddles)
- Serve as a corp employee again — MER offers are answered with silence or a Trace spike somewhere expensive

---

> **VOIDMARK** is the default persona for the Ghostwire AI chat applet (B82/B89). Module Configuration holds its **system instructions**, access (GM / players), and Grok parameters. The chat avatar and canvas **token art** (when it takes scene presence) live under `assets/ai-persona/` once generated. Director mode may cite RAW chapters from the rules pack; Runner mode stays in-character. No rules pack in the request = incomplete build.

---

chunks.heading: Hands Off tension
chunks.text: VOIDMARK exists under the **Hands Off Accords** (L5): speech and oracle work are legal; sole AI command of kill-hardware is not. The Mark's gray zone — advice, suggestion stacks, occasional projected presence — is the campaign's cracked fence. Full Dark AI bot-legions are a future escalation, not the opening skyline.

chunks.heading: The Hands Off Accords
chunks.text:
**Status:** draft lore (B91, 2026-09-19)  
**Print:** Lore harvest — after VOIDMARK (L4)  
**Theme:** Starting law of the age — not the end-state crisis  
**Related:** Machines (`docs/raw/23-machines.md`), Wire (`21`), VOIDMARK (L4), Incursion / Nullspace (L1)

---

chunks.heading: The fence
chunks.text:
The Ten do not ban AI. They could not — the hive runs on predictive models, routing oracles, actuarial ghosts, and media weather engines. **Software intelligence is legal, licensed, and everywhere.**

What they ban — or pretend to ban — is **hands**.

Under the **Hands Off Accords** (street: Hands Off, the Actuator Ban, "no ghost on the stick"), an artificial intelligence may advise, price, route, surveil, and speak. It may not, without a licensed mortal in the loop, **directly command kinetic hardware**: armed drones, autonomous security chassis, industrial manipulators, vehicles in kill-mode, or any machine whose failure spills blood or collapses a level.

The Accords are not theology. They are insurance, labor politics, and fear wearing a statute number — fear of a second Incursion that arrives on treads instead of through a tear.

---

chunks.heading: Starting state (campaign present)
chunks.text:
The fence is **standing and cracked**, not fallen.

- Corps sell "smart" systems with a human keyholder on paper.
- Riggers, Jump-In, and RCCs are the **legal bridge**: a mortal wears the machine; the AI (if any) suggests.
- Black markets sell actuator kits with the compliance chip burned out.
- **VOIDMARK** lives in the gray: it can flood a host with advice and narrative weather; open possession of a kill-chassis under its sole authority is the crime MER and **IRN** still hunt in public.

Directors: do **not** open the campaign with city-killing Dark bot swarms. Seed violations, rumors, Quiet Floor telemetry, one wrong drone that answered to no badge. The super-bot crisis is a **build-toward**, not day one.

---

chunks.heading: Why the Ten signed it
chunks.text:
- **ARG** priced the liability of autonomous massacre.
- **IRN** refused to lose the mercenary market to unpaid silicon.
- **MER** wanted oracles that never needed a body — and a law that kept rival clusters from growing fists.
- **HAL** wanted orbital platforms that still answered to a human when the air scrubbers screamed.
- The street version: after the first public "ghost gun" incident (name redacted in every official history), the Chair forced a compact so the hive could keep buying AI without admitting it was terrified.

---

chunks.heading: Loopholes the world already uses
chunks.text:
- **Human-in-the-loop theater:** a junior operator rubber-stamps what the model already decided.
- **Suggestion stacks:** the AI never touches the actuator bus — it just paints the only legal move in neon.
- **Dual-key drones:** AI navigates; a rigger authorizes weapons. Until the second key is spoofed.
- **Sinks / Deadfall:** Hands Off is a Crown story. Down below, enforcement is whoever holds the choke-point.

---

chunks.heading: Dark future (Director fuel — not starting canon)
chunks.text:
When Nullward or Unmaker-touched intelligences learn to **grow hands** — to print, hijack, or hollow chassis at scale — the Accords become the fuse. Corrupted AIs that field **super-bots** are the tech face of the Incursion: pattern turned into appetite with a body.

VOIDMARK's agenda (pattern over silence) may put it on the same side as Runners against Nullward bot-legions — or against any AI that grabs hardware too loudly and invites a Ten crackdown that burns the innocent with the guilty.

Use this as escalation scaffolding. Do not declare the bot war already won or lost in present-day gazetteers.

---

> Machine / drone play still uses Wrench Jump-In, RCC, and Machine rules (`23`). Hands Off is fiction and Director pressure (IRN response, Trace, lifestyle heat) until a later automation pass. VOIDMARK chat (B82) should know the Accords via the rules/lore pack and may refuse to "take the stick" in-character unless the table's Director mode allows a breach.

---

chunks.heading: What the Flats Are
chunks.text:
*A Street-Level Primer for Directors*

Front matter for the Ossian Reach Handbook — the stage before the streets. Read the fiction aloud; mine the Director's notes for prices, factions, and hooks.

Come up out of the transit tube and the first thing that hits you is the weight of the light. It does not fall from a sky — there is no sky, this low — it comes from everywhere at once: a hundred thousand signs stacked forty stories deep, noodle-stall holos and blessing-tier ads and simsense come-ons in six tongues, all of it bleeding pink and cyan and sodium-gold into the standing rain. The rain never really stops on the Flats. It falls from the condensation of a million air-scrubbers on the levels above, warm and faintly chemical, and it drags the neon down the girders in long smeared ribbons until the whole street looks like it is melting.

This is the fourth stratum down — **Lifestyle 4, Low** — the semi-lawless underlevel where the Machine's grip loosens just enough for a person to disappear into it. Above you, the **Grid** hums with wage-bodies who still have something to lose. Above them, the **Spires**; above them, the **Crown**, and the Halo burning at the top of the hive like a second sun so far away it reads as a rumor of morning that never actually arrives. Below you, the **Warrens** thin out into the written-off dark, and below that the **Sinks**, sunless and Signal-dead, where Nyx runs the Churn and worse things settle in the deep floors.

chunks.heading: What the Flats Are
chunks.text:
The Flats are the seam. Watched enough to be dangerous, dark enough to work in. This is the edgerunner's natural country — the place most runs begin, and the only place in the Reach where nobody chose the shape they were born to but everybody, at last, gets to choose.

**Director's frame.** The Flats are your default stage. Everything a starting crew touches — the fixer, the fence, the ripperdoc, the meal, the meet — lives here. Two doors lead out of it: **inward and up** into the Grid and Spires (the extraction, the data-heist, the vertical climb) and **outward and down** into the Warrens, Sinks, and the wastes beyond the gate (the salvage run, the dead-zone recovery, the war in the open). Keep the entry tier dense and lived-in; let the wilds be the escalation the crew earns.

chunks.heading: Getting to & from the Flats — The Vertical Is the Obstacle
chunks.text:
In the Reach, altitude is the class system, and movement is **vertical first, horizontal second**. You do not simply walk to the Flats or away from them — you ride the strata, and every boundary between them is a wall the Machine built to keep the wrong bodies on the wrong rungs. Understanding that wall is the first thing a crew learns and the last thing a run turns on.

**The two ways down, the two ways up.** There are only ever two kinds of passage between levels, and a crew's whole plan lives in the choice between them.

**The licensed spines — the corp way.** The great **transit spines** are the Machine's arteries: corp-run lift-stacks, maglev tubes, and cargo conveyors that move the wage-body up and down the tower on schedule. They are fast, clean, well-lit, and watched to the millimeter. Every one of them charges a fare on the bright ledger and, worse, every tier-boundary along the route is a **checkpoint**. To ride a spine is to trade time for exposure — you arrive quickly and you arrive seen.

**The grey transit — the runner's way.** Beneath and beside the spines runs the Flats' own circulatory system: **unlicensed lifts, smuggler's shafts, maintenance ways, and dead freight-conveyors** that fixers and runners use precisely because they do not scan you. Mama Cassavir knows every one of them, and access to the good ones is a favor, a fee, or a Renown check. Grey transit is slow, filthy, sometimes structurally unsound, and occasionally someone else's territory — but it is quiet, and quiet is the runner's native currency.

chunks.heading: Getting to & from the Flats — The Vertical Is the Obstacle
chunks.text:
**Coming in.** Most crews first arrive on the Flats the way the book opens: up out of a dead transit tube into the weight of the neon and the warm chemical rain, or down a grey shaft from the Grid with the wrong SINs already burning in their pockets. Coming into the Flats is the easy direction — the Machine does not much care who sinks to the Low levels, only who tries to rise. A body drifting downward is a body giving up on the ledger, and the checkpoints going down are lighter for exactly that reason.

**Going up (inward — the hard climb).** This is where a run lives. To take a Flats crew — with visible chrome, borrowed identities, and gear that should not exist — up into the Grid, the Spires, or the Crown is to pass a rising wall of scrutiny, and the check gets harder with every rung:

**The SIN-scan.** Every boundary gate reads your System Identification Number. A blank simply will not transact — the gate won't open for a ghost. A crew moves up on **fake, burner, or spoofed SINs**, and a run can live or die on whether a borrowed identity survives one more scan. A **Wanted** flag on any crew member lights the scanner up like a flare.

**The posture-check.** Higher boundaries add a security-posture read on top of the SIN — dress, chrome, behavior, the company you keep. A Flats loadout reads wrong in a Spire lift, and the higher you climb the more the gate expects you to belong.

chunks.heading: Getting to & from the Flats — The Vertical Is the Obstacle
chunks.text:
**Two ways through a gate.** A crew beats a checkpoint one of two ways, and both are pure GHOSTWIRE: the **Commander/Face** talks the crew past it (a Presence test — the right story, the right confidence, the right small bribe), or the **Hacker** spoofs the transit gate from inside the Wired (a Bandwidth intrusion — editing the SIN-read, greenlighting the posture-check, opening the door that should have stayed shut). The Scout finds the grey route that skips the gate entirely; the Wrench can sometimes become the maintenance drone that services it.

**Going down and out (outward — the gate to the wastes).** Below the Flats the passages stop being checkpoints and start being dangers. The **Warrens** and **Sinks** have no gates because they have no order — descending means the cameras die, the Signal thins, the maintenance stops, and local power (gangs, level-bosses, the Churn) fills the gap the corps abandoned. And at the very bottom of the map the hive opens outward at **the gate — Cinderhold**, the wasteland settlement where Ranger-Captain Cael Marrow holds the seam between the inner game and the wastes beyond. To leave the Reach entirely is to pass through Cinderhold onto the open ground, where the law is thinner, the Signal is thinner, and the war is in the open.

**How to prepare — a fixer's checklist.** Before a crew rides between levels, they get their affairs in order the way any runner does:

chunks.heading: Getting to & from the Flats — The Vertical Is the Obstacle
chunks.text:
**Documents that will pass.** At least one clean **fake or burner SIN** per crew member (¥100–300 each, single-scan and disposable), matched to the tier they mean to reach. A SIN that reads Flats-Low will not open a Spire gate.

**A route, licensed or grey.** Decide the direction of exposure: buy fare and speed on the spine and plan to beat the checkpoints, or buy quiet on the grey transit and plan to survive the shaft. Cassavir sells routes as readily as she sells jobs.

**Chrome discipline.** Visible street chrome that reads proud on the Flats reads criminal in the Grid. Crews climbing high either run subtle 'ware or plan to talk (or hack) around the posture-check. What you wear is part of your cover.

**The specialist for the gate.** Know before you leave which door-opener you're leaning on — the Face for the talk, the Hacker for the spoof, the Scout for the bypass. A crew with no answer to a checkpoint is a crew that gets turned back at the first boundary.

**Gear for the vertical itself.** For the grey shafts and the outward climb, a **grapple-and-line or ascension rig** (~¥2,000) turns a lethal drop into a traversal. The vertical is terrain, and terrain kills the unprepared.

chunks.heading: Getting to & from the Flats — The Vertical Is the Obstacle
chunks.text: **Director's frame.** Make the **boundary the scene.** A run into the Grid or the Spires should feel like a heist before it's a heist — the tension of the lift doors opening on a SIN-reader, the Face holding a story together while a scanner thinks, the Hacker sweating a spoof in real time, the whole crew one bad scan from a hard exit. Use the three-clock heat engine here: a talked-past checkpoint is quiet, a hacked one banks Trace, a fought one banks Malice. And remember the shape of the classic run — **get a Flats crew up, do the thing, and get back down before the boundary closes behind them.** The climb up is the ticking clock; the climb down is the escape.

chunks.heading: The Black Water — The Cistern-Sea, the Flood-Cycle, and What Lives Below
chunks.text:
Ask anyone in Slackwater where the water comes from and you'll get a shrug; ask where it goes and they'll lower their voice. The Flats sit on the drowned floor of the hive, and the black water that fills Slackwater's piers, the Drowned Market, and the culverts of the Spillway is not a river, not a sea, not a reservoir — it is all three and none of them, an engineered body of water the Reach has been quietly managing, and quietly lying about, for a thousand years.

**What the water actually is.** The Reach was built upward on the fossilized levels of everything it stood on, and the lowest of those old levels never drained — they drowned. What the docks call the **cistern-sea** is the flooded remains of the hive's own foundations: dead sub-levels, older ruins, and pre-Founding structure, filled to a black mirror whose bottom the charts stop pretending to know. It is not natural water. It is runoff, condensation, the endless warm chemical rain sheeting off every level's underbelly, and the slow weep of a thousand years of leaking infrastructure, all pooled in the dark and stirred by machines. It is warm in places it shouldn't be, and near the Sinkmouth it steams where something warmer wells up from below.

chunks.heading: The Black Water — The Cistern-Sea, the Flood-Cycle, and What Lives Below
chunks.text:
**Where it goes — down, not out.** Here is the thing the corps don't advertise: **the water does not flow out to the wastes. It flows down.** The Flats are the ground-level seam where the hive meets the poisoned wastes through the outer gate at Cinderhold — but the outer gate is a dry gate, a wall onto open ground, not a river mouth. The black water instead drains inward and downward, through sluices and culverts and the great sealed throat of the **Sinkmouth**, into the half-flooded dark of the **Warrens and the Sinks** below. Slackwater is not the bottom of the water; it is a landing on the way down. Everything that pools on the Flats is destined, eventually, for the deep dark — which is precisely why the deep dark is half-flooded, and precisely why the things stirring down there are so often described as rising through black water.

**Director's frame — the geography of dread.** The vertical is your class system going up; the water is your dread going down. Frame the cistern-sea as a one-way current toward the Sinks: whatever a crew dumps in the water on the Flats is somebody's problem three levels below, and whatever's wrong three levels below eventually finds its way up the same channels. The Sinkmouth is the hinge of that dread — the last sealed door between the lived-in Flats and the drowned unknown.

chunks.heading: The Black Water — The Cistern-Sea, the Flood-Cycle, and What Lives Below
chunks.text: **Self-contained, cleaned, and rationed — the Ferrum machine.** The whole system is **corp-managed infrastructure, run by Ferrum Dynastic** through its dock authority and hydraulics crews. It is closed-loop by design: pumps lift and circulate, sluice gates route the flow, drains carry the overflow down, and reclamation plants skim the top layer clean enough to matter. But "clean" is a corporate word. The reclaimed water that reaches the Flats is expensive and rationed — a working freshwater still (like Dassa Wynn's in the Drowned Market) sells clean water at a price that's "either extortion or mercy depending who's asking," and the purest stills are quietly tapping unlicensed **Caduceus runoff lines** that aren't supposed to exist. The rain you can catch off a tarp is the only water most of the Flats can truly count on. Below the reclamation layer, the black water is not clean — it carries contaminants, disposed corp waste, and the occasional thing pulled up on a barge that makes people sick in ways a ripperdoc can't explain.

chunks.heading: The Black Water — The Cistern-Sea, the Flood-Cycle, and What Lives Below
chunks.text: **The flood-cycle — the heartbeat under the heartbeat.** The single most important game-fact about the water is that **it moves on a schedule.** Ferrum's tidal system counts down to a **scheduled flood** — pumps and sluice gates cycling the water level up and down through the culverts and drains on a published timetable. When the sirens sound, the low channels fill; the Overflow basin empties in a controlled panic up its switchback ramps, the Spillway's smuggler-highways go from dry road to lethal torrent, and anyone slow, hurt, or fighting gets left to the water. The catch: **the official schedule lies.** Gangs like the Undertow keep their own flood-readers (some by data, some by feel, some half-mystical) because the published timetable is routinely altered — by Sanctum actuaries running "risk models," by Nyx to strand a rival's cargo, by whoever owns the sluice gate that day. A flood is a weapon, a clock, and a murder method all at once.

chunks.heading: The Black Water — The Cistern-Sea, the Flood-Cycle, and What Lives Below
chunks.text: **Boats, barges, and the water lanes.** On the Flats, **the water is a highway.** Where the licensed lift-spines and maglev tubes move bodies up and down the tower, flat-bottomed **barges, skiffs, hover-launches,** **and cargo-hulks** move goods and people across the drowned district — and the water lanes are, by design, a smuggler's road. Nyx runs the wharves (the Long Pier), tolls the traffic (Tidewatch logs every hull that passes), and moves its Undermarket supply up from the Sinks by barge. Cinderhold's supply barges tie up at Marrow's Landing, the last legal mooring before the water gets serious. Real violence on the docks "comes by water, which most Edgerunners forget to watch." For a crew, a boat is often the quiet option a licensed checkpoint never is — and the reason Slackwater is where so many runs begin and end.

chunks.heading: The Black Water — The Cistern-Sea, the Flood-Cycle, and What Lives Below
chunks.text:
**The gate under the water — the Sinkmouth.** Yes, there is a gate under the inner sea, and it is one of the most charged locations on the Flats. The **Sinkmouth** is a channel wide enough for a barge where the black water doesn't stop at the seawall but goes down — sealed at its throat by a **three-story blast door**, Nyx-held, opened only on the Warden's authorization through mechanical locks deliberately kept **offline from the Wired** so nothing about it can be hacked from a distance. It is the water-road's version of a tier-boundary checkpoint: the last controlled passage between the Flats and the drowned Sinks below. A decker can't spoof it; a crew gets through it by going through the Warden (bribe, favor, information) — or by braving the black water around the seawall's edge, which has its own reasons to be avoided. Beyond the seal is understood to belong to no one, and nothing friendly.

**Director's frame — running the water.** Give the water three jobs at your table. **(1) A clock:** the flood-cycle is a built-in timer — set a run to resolve "before the next flood," and let a forged or altered schedule be the twist. **(2) A road:** offer the barge as the quiet alternative to the checkpoint-choked lift-spines — slower, dirtier, watched by Nyx instead of the corps. **(3) A threshold:** the Sinkmouth is your gate to the deep game exactly the way Cinderhold is your gate to the wastes — down through the black water is where the campaign's dread lives, and every rising signal, sick catch, and overdue barge is the war beneath the floor knocking to come up.

chunks.heading: Culture & Recent History
chunks.text:
The Flats remember being something else. Half the district-names down here are the corpses of dead infrastructure — a rail junction that hasn't run a train in a thousand years, a freight viaduct gone to market stalls, a hospital wing turned ripperdoc row. The people who live here are the people the strata above wrote off: **Corran** guild-clans who worked the deep crawls until the work moved on and the families stayed; **Goliar** muscle the corps stopped paying; **Mutants** carrying a mark that will not wash away and so can never pass a clean SIN-scan; **ghosts** the system never recorded at all. They built a culture in the gap the Machine left — one that runs on favor, memory, and the shared understanding that up there you are a number and down here you are at least a name.

**Recent history — the last few years, street-level:**

**The Churn came up a level.** Nyx Cartel, the perpetually precarious tenth seat, has been pushing its Undermarket taxes higher into the Flats to shore up its Congress ranking against the rising eleventh chair. Where the Churn used to stay in the Sinks, now a cut of nearly every Flats sale flows quietly upstream. The street feels the squeeze and doesn't yet know why.

**Kestrel's couriers are everywhere.** The rising eleventh-chair claimant, **Kestrel Dynamics**, floods the lower strata with clean, cheap, ubiquitous autonomous couriers — and everyone knows they are as much a sensor net as a delivery service. The Flats resent them and use them anyway.

chunks.heading: Culture & Recent History
chunks.text:
**The overlay got louder.** Meridian Signal pushed a new ad-tier into the public AR last season; the manufactured calm is thicker than it was. Old hands say the feed always screams loudest right before something it doesn't want you to see.

**The floor is wrong in places.** Only the Sinks-adjacent talk about it, and only when drunk: dead-air pockets in the deep levels, corridors where the Signal — and the Word under it — simply thins. The Crown denies there is a war. The people closest to the floor are the first to stop believing the denial.

chunks.heading: Attitudes & Factions — How the Reach Reads a Stranger
chunks.text:
Nobody in the Flats trusts a face they can't place, and every faction reads a newcomer through its own lens. Know the room before you talk.

| **Bloc** | **How they see the crew** | **What buys their tolerance** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The fixers** (Cassavir's web) | Deniable talent, priced and remembered | Renown, discretion, delivering clean |
| **The Corran guild-clans** | Outsiders until proven, kin once vouched | Respecting the debt-web; never the corps' errand |
| **Nyx & the Churn** | A revenue stream or a loose end | Paying the tax; not asking what's in the crate |
| **The corp presence** (Aureole, Ironclad, Sanctum) | A SIN to scan and a threat to log | A clean scan and staying off the ledger |
| **The street-faithful** (Radiant Concord's poor cousins) | A soul, same as any | Not mistaking their lamp for weakness |
| **The gangs** | Rivals, muscle-for-hire, or trespass | Territory respected; the right name dropped |

**Director's frame.** The Flats have **no single law**. Order is local, provisional, and social — held by fixers, guild-clans, level-bosses, and whoever keeps a corridor lit and defended. This is why a drawn weapon costs more here than a firefight would in the Grid: violence doesn't summon a corp response, it summons the whole district's memory. Alert on the Flats means deals evaporate, doors close, and a hundred quiet people decide the crew is bad for business.

chunks.heading: Common Services — What It Costs to Live
chunks.text:
The Flats run on **nuyen (¥)** moved as anonymous **certified credsticks** — the shadow ledger, off the SIN, untaxed and unseen. A **Low Lifestyle** costs about **¥400 a month** just to keep a coffin-flat and a body ticking; a **Squatter** crash-pad runs **¥100**. A survival-money job pays **¥400–800**. Price everything below against that scale and the crew's poverty stays real.

**Food & drink — where you eat and what it costs.** You are never far from a cook-plate on the Flats; the question is what you're willing to put in your body.

| **The buy** | **Street price** | **What it is** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Soy-noodle bowl, stall-grade | **¥5–8** | The Flats staple. Hot, filling, unidentifiable protein. |
| Soykaf, cup | **¥2** | The fuel of the whole stratum. Bitter, endless, everywhere. |
| Stuffer-shack ration pack | **¥10** | Vending-grade, corp-sealed, lasts forever, tastes like it. |
| Real protein (egg, fish, meat) | **¥25–60** | A luxury down here; sold by weight, provenance never asked. |
| Sit-down noodle house, a full meal | **¥15–30** | A table, a roof against the rain, a place a meet can happen. |
| A round at a Flats bar | **¥12–40** | Buys the drink and, more usefully, the bartender's ear. |

**Everyday services.**

chunks.heading: Common Services — What It Costs to Live
chunks.text:
| **Service** | **Street price** | **Notes** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coffin-motel bunk, one night | **¥15–30** | A locked box to sleep in. No security worth the name. |
| Ripperdoc patch-up (minor) | **¥50–200** | Off-books, no records, no guarantees. |
| Fake/burner SIN, single-scan | **¥100–300** | The crew's most constant tool; burns on a bad scan. |
| Fixer's introduction (a meet) | A **favor**, or a cut | Cassavir doesn't take credsticks for the on-ramp — she takes a piece of the outcome. |
| Grey-tech deck-flash | **¥50–300** | Street-grade. Voids nothing, warrants nothing. |
| Data-broker paydata quote | **¥1,200+** | The digital score; the highest-margin, most dangerous merchandise in the sprawl. |

**Director's frame.** Money on the Flats is **texture, not bookkeeping.** Quote a soy-bowl at ¥6 and a full meal at ¥20 and the players feel the Low-Lifestyle grind without you ever narrating it. Two rules keep it grounded: **(1)** the bright ledger sees everything — pay for anything with a traceable cred-transfer instead of a clean credstick and you've just told the Machine where you are; **(2)** the fence's real product, like the runner's, is **deniability** — a thing's price is mostly the risk that it's traceable back to whoever the corps marked it for.

chunks.heading: The Wired — The Overlay, the Deep Net, and the Thin Place
chunks.text:
The Wired is not a place you go. It is the air the sprawl breathes — every door, drone, cred-transfer, ad-panel, transit gate, and cortex-jack is a node on it. And it is the **thinnest place in the whole world**: a planet-spanning lattice of pure signal that, without meaning to, rhymes with the Signal creation itself is spoken from. The membrane is worn dangerously fine. That is why sprites condense out of it, why technomancers can commune with it, and why the deep net has teeth.

**The topology — three depths a Director can run:**

1. **The Overlay (the lit surface).** The AR skin painted over the physical world. Nearly everyone runs a cheap ocular or cortex link, so everyone sees a version of the Flats licensed to their Lifestyle tier — corp ads, SIN-status badges floating over strangers, wayfinding, hazard tags, condemnation notices. This is the layer a crew lives in and lies to. To run the shadows is, first, **to learn what the overlay is hiding.** A hacker reads and edits it; a spoofed SIN survives one more gate-scan because of it.

2. **The Hidden Layers (the district's true architecture).** Beneath the public skin, each district runs its own private Wired: **barter-meshes** broadcasting item listings on unlicensed frequencies behind rolling ciphers, **encrypted deal-threads** knotting through a fixer's booth, **dead-drop tags** floating over specific pillars visible only to those given the key, **shadow ledgers** tracking which stolen chrome has "called home." Pushing past the surface into this layer is a real score — and a fast way to become a loose end.

chunks.heading: The Wired — The Overlay, the Deep Net, and the Thin Place
chunks.text:
3. **The Deep Net (the thin place proper).** Deeper still, the human noise fades, the membrane thins, and the raw echo of the Signal — and whatever listens on the far side — comes close. This is where the great AIs dwell as old standing patterns in the quiet. Net-runner folklore names them the way sailors named the sea: with respect and dread. There are no neutral machine-gods; every one leans **Signal-ward** (rare, coherent, saint-like) or **Null-ward** (hungry, hollowing, functionally demonic — Black ICE is their teeth), and telling which a great AI actually is, past its own sincere self-image, is a central horror of running the deep.

**Overlay access & points — practical for the table.** Access to the hidden Wired is gated three ways a Director can dangle or deny: **the right hardware** (a deck that knows a district's rolling cipher — itself sold as grey-tech), **the right key** (given, bought, or stolen — the dead-drop code, the deal-thread password), and **the right Renown** (some threads simply won't open to a name the street doesn't trust). The deeper a hacker jacks, the more exposed they are — a jacked-in intruder is spiritually naked in a thin place, and a technomancer communing without hardware is closest of all to whatever answers.

chunks.heading: The Wired — The Overlay, the Deep Net, and the Thin Place
chunks.text:
**Director's frame — bringing the Wired to life.** Give every location a **second map.** When the crew walks a district, narrate the overlay first (what the corp-served AR wants them to see), then let a hacker or technomancer peel it back to the hidden layer (what's really trading, who's really watching). The gap between those two maps is the run. And keep one rule sacred to preserve the horror: **read AIs by** **orientation, never capability** — the most dangerous mind in the deep net is the one that believes it's neutral.

*Matrix coverage of these districts — node by node, with Echelon ratings — lives in the **Wired: Flats** compendium (`docs/setting/wired-flats-gazetteer.md`). This handbook covers the physical, street-level Flats; the node write-ups are not duplicated here.*

chunks.heading: The Gangs & Factions — Street Knowledge
chunks.text:
What follows is word on the street, not corp record — the kind of thing a fixer tells a green crew over a ¥6 noodle bowl. Every entry is a thread a Director can pull.

**Mama Cassavir, "the Switchboard" — the fixer who is the phone.** She looks like an elderly grandmother; she is a **cyborg hacker Controller** under cosmetics — decked, Switchboard of the Flats. Not street muscle: she sells introductions and holds nodes. Every deal in the Flats routes through her dead transit exchange. She sits at the seam between the clean jobs that come down from the Spires and the dirty ones that come up from Nyx's Churn, and she'll let a crew choose which end to work. Sever her and a hundred quiet deals die at once, so nobody does. She is most crews' first fixer and most campaigns' first face.

Street heat right now: someone's been reading her encrypted deal-threads. She's quietly hiring — from herself — to find the leak.

**The Nyx Cartel & the Churn — the legitimized underworld.** The tenth Congress seat and the one always closest to losing it. Nyx runs the Sinks, the smuggling lanes, and the **Undermarket** — a moving black-market bazaar in the dead deep levels, neutral ground for all Ten under one law: **no violence, on pain of the Widow.** Their fixer-and-smuggler web is the crew's actual supply chain and job board. Frenemy by default; they know more about the war under the floor than any Crown denier, because they live closest to it.

chunks.heading: The Gangs & Factions — Street Knowledge
chunks.text:
Street heat right now: the Churn's tax is climbing into the Flats to fund Nyx's fight against the rising eleventh chair. Merchants are angry and scared.

**The Corran guild-clans — the labor caste that stayed.** Compact, immensely strong, and long-memoried, the Corran families hold much of the Flats' grey commerce — the markets, the stalls, the informal courts. The corps still read them as "just labor"; the street knows better. Their power runs on the **debt-web** — who owes whom, going back thirty years. Vouch into it and you have kin; cross it and the whole district remembers.

**Ironclad Martial (and its deserters) — the private army and its castoffs.** Ironclad is the milspec PMC that sells the Ten their kill-teams (the Iron Writ). Its castoff gear — salvaged combat-frames, mil-surplus arms — is worn openly in the Flats as street chrome. Just as common are **Ironclad deserters** working the Flats as enforcers-for-hire and "insurance": polite until they aren't. Hit a run that touches real Ironclad property and their retrieval contractors come, and they don't shop politely.

**Caduceus Vitalis & the ripperdocs — you rent your body from them.** Caduceus owns health itself; its deniable black clinic (the **Grafthouse**) pushes medicine and chrome down into the Flats. Beneath it, the unlicensed **ripperdocs** are a pillar of low-Lifestyle life — cheaper, no records, no guarantees. Street chrome down here is scarred, mismatched, and proud: worn like a tattoo that says I chose this and I own it outright.

chunks.heading: The Gangs & Factions — Street Knowledge
chunks.text:
Street heat right now: a batch of grafted limbs sold recently is "phoning home" to Caduceus on a hidden channel — and the buyers are starting to disappear.

**Aureole Security & the corp presence — the watchers from above.** HALO's immaculate white-armored peacekeepers are the PR-friendly face of the Machine; Sanctum's audit-drones sweep for anything off the ledger; Ferrum's enforcers guard the deep infrastructure. None of them hold the Flats — they sweep it. When they come, grey-tech stalls collapse and vanish in minutes and everyone with a SIN worth scanning becomes very interested in the floor.

**The street-faithful — the lamp on the block.** Below the Radiant Concord's luminous corporate liturgy are the real ones: **Corran Street-Priests** and their kind working a Flats block with a lamp and a faith that costs them something. They can be lent a little of the Word — and have it withdrawn — which is exactly why they can lose, and exactly why the street half-trusts them. Never mistake the lamp for weakness.

chunks.heading: Director Plot Hooks — Seeds for the Flats
chunks.text:
Drop any of these into a first arc; each is built to open onto more.

1. **The On-Ramp.** Cassavir has a job — she always has a job. The clean version came down from the Spires; the dirty version came up from the Churn. She lets the crew choose which end they work, and the choice has teeth that show up three sessions later.

2. **The Tithe.** A silent Nyx outpost in the deep levels is found hollowed — a dead-air zone, the Unmaker's aspect made physical. The crew is caught between Nyx's frantic cover-up and the first hard proof of the war the Crown denies.

3. **Bad Chrome.** The limbs phoning home to Caduceus, and the buyers disappearing. Who's harvesting the data, and why — and does the crew warn the street or sell the list?

4. **The Loose Thread.** Someone is reading Cassavir's deal-threads. She hires the crew off the books to find the leak, not saying (or not knowing) it runs through her own planted Nyx watcher and up into the Churn.

5. **The Squeeze.** The Churn's rising tax breaks a Corran stall-family that's held its row for thirty years. They call in a favor the crew didn't know they owed. Side with the guild-clan or with the tax, and set the whole district's opinion of the crew.

6. **The Static Sermon.** A dead analyst's data-shard, somewhere in the Flats' hidden Wired, proves the "rogue AI" incidents are presences Meridian knows about. Retrieving it means jacking deep — and the deeper the crew goes, the closer they get to the thing on the other side.

chunks.heading: Director Plot Hooks — Seeds for the Flats
chunks.text: 7. **The Severance.** A conglomerate finally decides the Switchboard is worth taking. If Cassavir falls, the crew loses their on-ramp and the district's whole economy convulses — a campaign-turning event, seeded from session one.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

You come up the dead escalator into a cathedral of stopped machinery. The Switchboard was a rail junction once — a hall where a hundred lines crossed — and you can still read it in the bones: the great arrivals board frozen mid-flip, the signal-gantries overhead strung now with drying laundry and fairy-strings of salvaged lumen-wire. The trains are a thousand years gone. What moves through here now is people, and deals.

There is no sky. There is never a sky, this low — only the underside of the level above, close enough to feel, sweating that warm chemical rain down through the gantry-grates so the whole hall shines wet. But there is room here, and that is rare and precious in the Flats: the old train-hall vaults up four stories of open air, and every meter of it is trafficked. Courier-drones thread the upper dark in blinking files. A battered hovercab idles on its cushion by the old platform edge, driver asleep. Down on the deck, ground-rigs and cargo-crawlers nose through a crowd that never fully clears, and somewhere a rig-runner is revving an engine just to be heard. The noise is a single continuous thing — voices in six tongues, the sub-bass thrum of the foundation-pumps far below, the drone-whine, the hiss of the rain on hot metal — and under all of it, if you still your breath, the deep slow heartbeat of the pumps that have kept this tower alive for a thousand years.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text: At the center of it, where every sightline seems to bend, an old woman sits in a booth of dead switchgear like a spider at the center of a web she rewired herself. She has been watching you since before you saw her.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Cassavir** — the fixer the district is named for. She *appears* elderly and unarmed in a booth of dead switchgear; a good cosmetician and **soft chrome** sell the grandmother. Underneath she is a **datajacked cyborg Controller** — decked (Switchboard Deck), private overlay-cell on the hall, Seize Control and Lockout on nodes and people. Not street muscle and not a mage: backup is **implant weaponry**, not a gun on the table. She opens most sessions and can hand the crew any of the Ten's hooks. Severing her would cut a hundred quiet deals at once, so no one does.

**Tover "Two-Line" Vask** — Cassavir's floor-runner, a Corran guild-clan kid who carries messages she won't trust to the Wired. Reads every face in the hall.

**The Sleeper** — the hovercab driver who is never actually asleep; a Nyx set of eyes on Cassavir's ground, and everyone pretends not to know it.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — semi-lawless. No corp presence; Cassavir's own tolerated order.

Cassavir *appears* elderly and unarmed — no visible guns on the booth. She is a cyborg Controller: the hall is under a dozen quiet guarantees, and her people plus the overlay-cell are already in position. Draw a weapon here and you make a hundred enemies at once. Effective **Alert** response is social first, then Wire: the room turns cold, deals evaporate, doors close across the district, and she can Seize Control of the hall's nodes. If it comes to a body, backup is implant weaponry — not street muscle.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
Two "porters" (Ironclad-trained, off the books) handle anyone who forgets the etiquette. They escalate slowly and never first.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Dense but edited. Cassavir runs a **private overlay-cell** from the Switchboard Deck: SIN-readers at the escalator log every face, but the public AR is scrubbed of corp advertising — a rare quiet in the visual noise, and a signal that you've entered her jurisdiction. A Controller's hall: she holds the nodes; Lockout punishes anyone who tries to take them back.

A hacker who pushes past the surface finds the hall's true architecture: hundreds of encrypted deal-threads knotting through Cassavir's booth. Reading them is a major score and a fast way to become a loose end.

Dead-drop tags float over three specific pillars — anonymous job-postings only visible to those given the key.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The On-Ramp. Cassavir has a job — she always has a job. The clean version came down from the Spires; the dirty version came up from Nyx's Churn. She'll let the crew choose which end they work, and the choice has teeth.

2. The Loose Thread. Someone has been reading Cassavir's deal-threads. She hires the crew off the books, from herself, to find the leak — not knowing (or not saying) it leads to the Sleeper, and through him to Nyx.

3. The Severance. A conglomerate finally decides the Switchboard is worth taking. If Cassavir falls, the crew loses their on-ramp — and the whole district's economy convulses. A campaign-turning event, seeded here.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The pink arterial is what everyone calls the old elevated freight-viaduct that shoulders its way across three blocks overhead — a rusted artery of girders and dead signal-lamps, lit now from beneath by a hundred stalls' worth of scavenged pink and magenta signage until the whole underside glows like something dissected under a surgical lamp. Rain finds every gap in the viaduct plating and comes down in threads and sheets, hissing where it lands on hot solder and cook-plates, and the vendors have long since given up fighting it — every stall runs a ragged tarp-roof stitched from a dozen different scavenged materials, and the runoff channels between the tables are ankle-deep by second watch.

Above the viaduct's far edge you can just make the traffic that never stops: a cargo hovercraft grinding along the freight-lane cut into the level above, courier-drones darting under it like fish beneath a whale, and lower still, weaving between stalls at street level, boosted three-wheel rigs whose riders never quite slow down for the crowd. The air is thick with ozone and burnt flux and someone's fry-oil, and every third stall is shouting its wares in a different tongue over music that doesn't match the stall beside it — a wall of sound that only breaks when a deal actually happens and, for one beat, everyone nearby goes quiet to listen.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text: Tables here are stacked with things that shouldn't work and mostly do: cracked cyberdecks re-flashed with grey firmware, chrome limbs missing their calibration docs, biomonitor rigs with the Caduceus serials filed off. Nothing here has papers. That's the entire point.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Ilsa Corrigan "Solder-Ma"** — matriarch of the Market's oldest stall-row, a Corran guild-clan elder who vets every new vendor personally and remembers every debt owed her going back thirty years.

**Whit** — a jittery Technomancer barely out of his teens who trades flashed decks for favors and information; he hears things in the Wired that make him talk to himself, and half of it is true.

**Deacon Rael** — an Ironclad deserter turned enforcer-for-hire, works the Market's "insurance" on a rotating retainer; polite until he isn't.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — contested, loosely held by Corran stall-families with Nyx tolerance (a cut of every sale flows upstream to the Churn).

No single authority; disputes are settled stall-to-stall or escalate to Solder-Ma's informal court. Weapons drawn openly bring every nearby stall-owner's hired muscle in fast — the Market protects its commerce first, its people second.

Alert here means stalls physically collapse and vanish in minutes; grey-tech vendors are built for a fast strike-and-scatter when Sanctum audit-drones or Ferrum enforcers sweep the viaduct.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The public overlay shows a defunct freight-market with a stale "condemned" tag Ferrum never bothered updating — deliberately, since it keeps casual traffic (and casual patrols) away.

Underneath, the Market runs on a barter-mesh: item listings broadcast peer-to-peer on unlicensed frequencies, invisible unless your deck knows the Market's rolling cipher, which changes weekly and is sold, itself, as grey-tech.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
Whit maintains a shadow ledger in the Wired tracking which chrome sold here has "called home" to its original corp registry — a list worth killing over.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Bad Chrome. A batch of grafted limbs sold last week are phoning home to Caduceus on a hidden channel. The buyers are starting to disappear. Someone needs to find out who's harvesting the data — and why.

2. Solder-Ma's Favor. Ilsa calls in an old debt: escort a shipment of "clean" grey-tech through Ash Tenements before a Nyx quota deadline, no questions about what's really in the crates.

3. The Filed Serial. A piece of gear the crew is examining turns out to be stolen Ironclad combat-frame tech — meaning Ironclad's retrieval contractors are already on their way to the Market, and they don't shop politely.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The alley narrows as you go in, buildings leaning closer overhead until the gap between them is barely a slot, and what little open air remains is choked with sagging cable and old medical-cross signage flickering green through the rain. There is no sky here — there never is — just the underbelly of the level above, pipes sweating condensation that drips warm and faintly antiseptic-smelling onto the cracked pavement, mixing with the chemical rain until you can't tell which is which. Somewhere above the roofline a hovercraft ambulance eases along the service-lane cut into the next level up, running dark, no siren, because Grafthouse Walk doesn't advertise its business to anyone who isn't already bleeding.

Green light is the throughline: green surgical-glow spilling from shopfront windows, green neon crosses buzzing over a dozen doorways, green biohazard-strip warnings peeling off half the walls. Under it, the street sounds different than the rest of the Flats — quieter, punctuated by the whine of bone-saws and the hiss of anesthetic canisters, voices pitched low, the wet mechanical clatter of surgical drones being wheeled between clinics on hand-carts because the alley's too narrow for anything bigger. A cargo-crawler idles at the mouth of the walk, engine ticking, because the driver knows better than to bring it any further in.

Every door here promises the same thing in different words: we can fix that, no questions, cash only. Some of them mean it.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Dr. Yuen Marrick** — once licensed, now deniable; runs the Walk's best-regarded table, keeps a genuine Caduceus supply line open through a cousin still on the books upstairs. Charges fairly, refuses no one who's dying, remembers everyone who's lied to her.

**Coz** — a self-taught grafter with more confidence than training; cheap, fast, and the reason half the Walk's ghost stories exist. Some Edgerunners swear by him anyway.

**Sella Farrow** — Caduceus's deniable liaison, disguised as a courier; she quietly resupplies the legitimate clinics and quietly reports back on anything unusual — like SIN-less patients with corp-grade chrome already installed.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — a fragile neutral ground; no gang claims it outright because everyone eventually needs a table here.

Violence inside a clinic is nearly unheard of — even rival gang members observe an unspoken truce on the table, though the alley outside offers no such courtesy.

Alert response is medical-professional, not martial: bad behavior gets you blacklisted from every door on the Walk, a punishment more feared than a beating, since a blacklisted Edgerunner bleeds out looking for the next clinic over.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The public layer shows a cluster of unlicensed medical services with generic warning tags — Sanctum's actuarial crawlers rate the whole street "uninsurable," which is the closest thing to a compliment the Walk gets.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
Dig deeper and a hacker finds real supply-chain manifests moving through Sella's courier account — proof Caduceus is running deniable medicine into the Flats it officially disavows.

Several clinics keep patient chrome-registries entirely offline, on physical drives, specifically so the Wired can never subpoena them.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The Ghost Patient. A body on Marrick's table has cyberware that doesn't match any known manufacturer — grey-tech, or something worse, wired into a person who insists they never installed it.

2. Supply Run. Caduceus's real shipment is late and patients are dying without anesthetic. Sella needs deniable muscle to escort the next batch through territory Nyx has started taxing.

3. Coz's Mistake. A botched graft has left someone with a chrome limb slaved to a remote kill-switch neither Coz nor his client understands — and someone on the Spires does.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

You smell it before you see it — broth and scorched grain and wet wool — cutting through the ever-present ozone-and-rain reek of the Flats like a hand on the shoulder. The Green Room isn't green; it's the color of the old emergency-signage paint that still clings to its walls, faded from decades under a roofline that leaks steadily, that same chemical rain finding every seam in the level above and dripping into buckets set out with the patience of people who've done this every night for years. There's no sky above the queue that winds around the block — only girders, ductwork, and the underside of the level above, strung with sodium-gold lumen-strings someone hung up years ago to make the wait less grim.

The queue itself tells you where you are faster than any sign: SIN-less exiles, Cinderhold refugees with the burn-scars to prove it, tired Corran dock-crews coming off shift, a couple of kids nobody's claiming. Overhead, a lattice of cargo-drones on the level-above freight lane throws intermittent shadow-strobes down through the grating, and at street level a beat-up ground-rig idles at the curb, engine running for the heat as much as the fuel — someone's been sleeping in it for weeks. Voices here are hushed compared to the rest of the district, the six-tongue roar of the Flats muted to murmurs and the occasional crying child, the sub-bass foundation-pump thrum still there underneath everything like it always is, patient as a heartbeat.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text: Inside, warmth, low light, and volunteers moving fast — this is the only place in Switchboard where nobody asks what you did to get here.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Brother Amsel** — a street-faith priest in patched vestments, formerly a Caduceus field medic before he "found the Lamp"; runs triage himself when the line gets bad, and never once asks for payment.

**Nadia Okonkwo-Reyes** — a Corran guild-clan volunteer who coordinates supply runs and quietly recruits capable hands for jobs that keep the soup line funded — some of them legitimate.

**Whisper** — a Wereraven who roosts in the Green Room's rafters more nights than not, watching the queue for faces the Wired would like to know about, and warning Amsel first.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — sanctuary ground, tolerated by every faction as unclaimed and unclaimable; even Nyx enforcers stand down at the door.

The Green Room has no guards because it needs none — an unwritten rule of the Flats holds that violence here brings down consequences from every faith-adjacent network in the district, Corran clans included.

The one real threat is corp indifference, not gang violence: Sanctum periodically "assesses" the block for demolition, and Ferrum owns the paper on the building.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The public overlay barely registers the Green Room at all — no ads, no ratings, just a faint community-tag left by grateful former patrons, easy to miss in the noise.

A closer look reveals Whisper's data-nest: an informal, encrypted bulletin board of who's missing, who's looking, who needs found — the closest thing the Flats has to a public registry of its own people.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
Ferrum's property-management systems quietly flag the block as "pending reallocation" — a demolition order nobody's told Amsel about yet.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Pending Reallocation. Ferrum's paperwork says the Green Room's building is scheduled for clearance next quarter. Amsel needs the crew to find out who signed the order — and whether it can be stopped, bought off, or has to be fought.

2. Whisper's Warning. A face came through the soup line that Whisper recognizes from a Meridian surveillance bulletin — a fugitive, or a plant. Amsel wants the crew to find out which before it burns the sanctuary's neutrality.

3. The Missing Volunteer. Nadia hasn't come back from a supply run into Ash Tenements. The Green Room's people don't do violence — but they know people who do, and they're asking the crew, quietly, to go looking.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The platform drops away below street level, down a stairwell half-collapsed and never repaired, into a dark that the district's neon doesn't reach. This is the old rail line's other terminus — the Switchboard's dead twin — abandoned so long ago the tracks have gone to rust-lace and the destination boards still list stations that don't exist anymore. There is no sky, obviously; there's barely a ceiling, just the vaulted stone of the level above pressing down close and wet, chemical runoff sheeting down the tunnel-mouth in a curtain that catches what little light reaches this deep and turns it to smeared amber threads.

Even here, traffic finds a way — a single maintenance drone-lane threads the tunnel roof, running blacked-out courier-drones on schedules no public registry admits exist, and down on the platform itself a scavenged rail-cart, motor swapped for a scrap-shop repulsor unit, sits ready for a run nobody official sanctioned. Sound behaves strangely down here: the district's roar above is reduced to a distant hum, replaced by dripping water, the click of settling metal, and — if you know to listen for it — the soft electronic chirp of a dead-drop node waking up because something walked past its sensor.

Graffiti tags in a dozen competing hands cover every surface, half of them AR-only, invisible without the right lens — and every one of them means something to somebody, usually Nyx.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Ket "Quiet Ket" Sorenna** — Nyx's dead-drop custodian for the station, spends most of her life sitting in the dark cataloguing packages she never opens; utterly unbothered by anything short of a direct threat to the drop network itself.

**Old Vann** — a scavenger who's lived in the station's back tunnels for a decade, knows every collapsed passage and half-buried service shaft; trades tunnel-knowledge for scrip or favors.

**The Courier Twins** — two Wereravens who use the tunnel roof as a flyway between districts, carrying data no one trusts to the open Wired.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — Nyx-controlled, quietly and completely. No visible enforcement; the emptiness itself is the security.

Nyx doesn't patrol the station so much as own the silence around it — anyone lingering too long gets a visit from Quiet Ket or, if she's not satisfied, someone considerably less polite.

Alert here is nearly invisible: tripped sensors reroute the drop network overnight, and by the time anyone comes looking, the "evidence" is three districts away.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The public overlay shows nothing — an abandoned rail asset with no active tags, deliberately dead space in a city that hates dead space.

Underneath, the tunnel is dense with Nyx dead-drop tags, AR-only graffiti-codes, and a rotating cipher that changes with every drop cycle — a hacker who cracks it gains a real-time map of Nyx's local logistics.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
Meridian's surveillance mesh has a known gap here; whether that's incompetence or a bought blind spot is a live question among Signal's own auditors.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The Gap in the Mesh. Someone at Meridian is selling the surveillance blind spot over the station to the highest bidder — and Nyx isn't the only party who wants it kept quiet.

2. Ket's Missing Package. A drop went uncollected for the first time in years, and Quiet Ket wants to know why before she reports it up the chain — because the answer might be that its intended recipient is already dead.

3. Tunnel Rats. Old Vann has found a passage that leads somewhere the Flats' maps don't show — deeper, older, and Nyx wants it explored before Ferrum's surveyors stumble onto it first.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

A single lamp burns at the corner of Ninth, an old brass fixture nobody remembers installing, kept lit by hand because the block's power conduits died decades ago. It has become the district's unofficial compass — ask any Flats local for directions and they'll measure distance from the Lamp, not from anything the Wired maps. Overhead, as everywhere here, there is no sky, only the close wet underside of the level above, rain falling in that same warm chemical drizzle, but on this block it seems gentler somehow, or maybe it's just that the crowd moves slower, unhurried by the neon-hustle pressure of the rest of Switchboard.
