Fights here are common and rarely fatal — the crowd is too dense and too indifferent for anything but a beating to happen before it's broken up by sheer foot traffic. Serious violence draws Kreel's own enforcers fast, since a body in the court is bad for everyone's business.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The dead menu-boards still broadcast ghost-ads for a defunct restaurant chain, a corrupted loop that's become part of the court's ambient noise floor in both light and sound.

Underneath, Kreel runs an order-and-delivery layer disguised as food-delivery traffic — dust orders routed and paid for exactly like a meal, invisible to anyone not looking for the pattern.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
Fingers Aoi's information trade leaves a light data-footprint that a sharp hacker could use to reconstruct half the court's client list — valuable, and likely to get someone killed if it leaked.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Cut Too Far. Kreel's latest dust batch is causing seizures, and Chef Odalys — furious that it's scaring off her customers too — wants the crew to find out why and make it stop, one way or another.

2. Fingers's Ledger. Aoi has been selling information to too many sides at once, and someone's finally decided she's more valuable dead than talking. The crew can save her, silence her, or buy her ledger before either happens.

3. The Supply Squeeze. Odalys's Corran supply chain has been cut off by a Ferrum checkpoint shakedown, and without real food, the court tips entirely into Kreel's dust economy. The crew's choice of who to help decides what the Food Court becomes.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The fountain hasn't run on its own power in a century, but it still holds water — rigged now with filtration hoses and collection barrels feeding off a cracked main, so that the dry marble basin where shoppers once tossed coins for luck has become the single most valuable piece of infrastructure in Glasshook. Every gang, every faction, every desperate soul in the district needs this water, and that single fact has made the Fountain Court the one place in the arcade where nobody starts a fight.

The dome above the court is more intact than most, a scarred but unbroken shell that gathers the warm chemical rain into channels someone engineered decades ago to feed the fountain's original plumbing — a rare piece of the old arcology still doing, however crudely, the job it was built for. Around the court's edge, the district's layered traffic slows out of unspoken respect: courier-drones circle wide rather than crossing the open basin airspace, hovercabs land at a designated distance rather than pushing close, ground-rigs queue politely at water-collection hours instead of jostling for position — a strange, fragile pocket of order in a district defined by its lack of one.

The sound here is almost gentle by Glasshook's standards — running water, the creak of hand-pumps, quiet transactional murmurs, rain on the intact dome overhead — a hush that makes the ever-present sub-bass heartbeat feel, for once, less like a threat and more like a held breath.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Old Marrin** — the fountain's self-appointed keeper, ancient and Corran-rooted, who maintains the filtration rig and enforces the neutral-ground truce through sheer accumulated moral authority.

**Tessa Blackwell** — a Cinderhold representative who negotiates water-rights on behalf of the district's exiled and SIN-less population, ensuring the truce holds even for those with no gang to protect them.

**The Broker** — an unaffiliated fixer who uses the fountain's neutral ground to arrange meetings between rival factions too hostile to meet anywhere else in Glasshook.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — universally respected neutral ground; no single faction controls it, and all factions enforce its peace collectively.

The truce is self-policing: anyone who draws a weapon here loses access to water for their entire crew, permanently, by unanimous district consensus. That threat has held for longer than anyone can remember, and it works better than any armed guard could.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The court runs an unusually clean, cooperative AR layer — a shared, faction-neutral scheduling system for water access that multiple gangs maintain jointly, a rare piece of the Wired here used exactly as intended.

A hacker probing deeper finds The Broker's meeting-arrangement threads, encrypted negotiations between factions that would never admit to speaking otherwise.

Old Marrin keeps a private log of every faction's water usage down to the liter — quiet leverage that has, more than once, prevented a fight before it started.

#### Plot Hooks

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
1. Poisoned Well. Someone has tampered with the filtration rig, and the water's starting to make people sick. Old Marrin needs the crew to find the culprit before the truce collapses in a district-wide panic.

2. The Broker's Meeting. Two warring factions have agreed to negotiate at the fountain, and someone wants that meeting to fail violently — a perfect setup for a hired disruption, or for the crew to play unlikely peacekeepers.

3. Rights and Runoff. Ferrum has quietly asserted ownership of the fountain's original plumbing infrastructure and is threatening to shut it down unless the district starts paying for "their" water — a slow-motion crisis that could unite Glasshook's gangs against a common enemy for the first time.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

A hand-painted sign reading LOST & FOUND hangs over what used to be a mall service counter, and the joke, if it ever was one, curdled long ago. This is where Glasshook's missing go looking for each other, and where the district's body trade quietly does its business under the same roof — photographs pinned three-deep across every wall, hand-scrawled descriptions of the vanished, and behind the counter, a woman who has learned to tell, just by the way a client asks, whether they want their missing person found alive.

The ceiling here sags lower than anywhere else in the district, a single collapsed floor pressing close enough that you could touch it standing on a chair, and the warm chemical rain seeps through in slow dark stains across the drywall rather than proper drips — this room feels buried in a way the rest of Glasshook, for all its ruin, doesn't quite. Outside the doorway, the usual layered traffic passes with a kind of unconscious avoidance: courier-drones rarely stop here, ground-rigs don't idle at the curb, as if the whole district has agreed, without saying so, to keep Lost & Found at arm's length.

Inside, the sound wall drops to something closer to a hospital waiting room than a marketplace — hushed questions, the shuffle of photographs, a distant drip, and underneath, so faint you might mistake it for imagination, the same tower-heartbeat sub-bass that runs beneath everything else in the Flats, patient as ever.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Maren Cole** — Lost & Found's proprietor, ex-Caduceus records clerk who lost her license in a scandal she's never explained; brokers missing-persons cases and, discreetly, the sale of unclaimed bodies and their harvestable chrome to the district's ripperdocs.

**The Cataloguer** — Cole's silent assistant, a heavily augmented figure of uncertain gender who catalogs every photograph and every body with the same clinical patience, rumored to have once worked Caduceus's official morgues.

**Whit Sarrow** — a grief-hardened Cinderhold father who's been searching Lost & Found's boards for his daughter for two years, and has become an unofficial fixture — and unofficial guard — of the place.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — independent brokerage, unaffiliated with district gangs, protected by universal discomfort rather than force.

Almost no one bothers Lost & Found; there's an unspoken understanding that everyone might need it someday. The few who've tried to rob Cole found the entire district's grief turned against them fast — Whit Sarrow alone has driven off more than one attempt with nothing but sheer refusal to back down.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Cole maintains a private missing-persons database that vastly outperforms any corp SIN-registry for the Flats' population — the Wired's official record simply stops caring about people down here, and her handwritten photographs fill that gap.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
A hacker who accesses her files finds not just the missing but a shadow ledger of body-trade transactions — who sold, who bought, what chrome was harvested from whom, an ethically radioactive but valuable data-cache.

The Cataloguer maintains a second, hidden layer: cross-references to Caduceus's own deniable "acquisition" programs, connecting missing Flats residents to legitimate corp research in ways no one up-tower would want confirmed.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Whit's Daughter. After two years, a photograph matching Whit Sarrow's daughter finally surfaces — in the Cataloguer's hidden body-trade ledger, not the missing-persons wall. Whit hires the crew to find out what really happened, whatever the cost.

2. Caduceus's Ledger. The Cataloguer's hidden cross-reference file, if it got out, would prove Caduceus has been sourcing "volunteer" test subjects from the Flats' missing-persons pool. Someone wants that file, and someone else wants it destroyed forever.

3. Cole's Confession. Maren Cole is dying and wants to make something right before she goes — she offers the crew her entire archive, decades of secrets, in exchange for one impossible last favor: finding the person whose disappearance she caused, back when she still worked for Caduceus.

chunks.heading: Wireside
chunks.text:
*The Flats // Ossian Reach // The Data Slums*

*Matrix coverage of these districts — node by node, with Echelon ratings — lives in the **Wired: Flats** compendium (`docs/setting/wired-flats-gazetteer.md`). This handbook covers the physical, street-level Flats; the node write-ups are not duplicated here.*

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The Cold Stack announces itself before you see it — a bass-deep exhale of chilled air rolling out between two shanty-towers, and under it, a hum that isn't quite sound, more a pressure behind your back teeth. When the alley opens up you understand why: a server-farm the size of a cathedral, forty stories of scavenged rack-cabinets welded into the tower's dead structural bones, wrapped floor to ceiling in cable like ivy grown feral. There is no sky above it — only the black gasket-seams of the level overhead, sweating that warm chemical rain down onto the stack's roof in fat, hissing drops that flash to steam a foot from the hottest vents.

Between you and the Stack, the district's traffic sorts itself into a strange, layered ballet. Courier-drones hug the ceiling-dark in blinking lines, threading around a Meridian relay-gantry strung with a hundred jury-rigged antennae. A cargo-crawler grinds past at knee height, dragging a sled of coolant drums, forcing pedestrians up onto cable-spool sidewalks that sway underfoot. Somewhere close a hovercab noses down out of the murk, running lights smeared to long pink-and-cyan streaks in the standing rain, and lands nowhere in particular because there is nowhere in particular to land. Every wall here glows — not with ads, but with the Stack's own status-runes, cyan data-conduit lines pulsing along the gutters like exposed veins, carrying the district's lifeblood of bandwidth out to a thousand shanty-hab feeds.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text: Up close, the cooling-mist rolling off the Stack's louvers beads on your jacket and tastes of ozone and machine oil. Somewhere inside that wall of humming metal, a hundred people are sleeping, dreaming, working, or dying wired into something that isn't quite a place.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Auntie Ferro** — a Corran guild-clan elder who "owns" the Stack the way a shepherd owns a flock: she doesn't control it, she tends it, brokering rack-space, settling disputes, and feeding anyone who keeps the cooling fans running. Everyone in Wireside owes her a favor or fears losing one.

**Deckhand Priya** — a self-taught Technomancer barely out of her teens who lives inside the Stack's crawlspaces, running diagnostics in exchange for a cot and deep-net access. She hears things in the noise-floor no one else does.

**Warden Oyelaran** — Ferrum's nominal landlord-rep, a tired mid-boss who collects "structural tax" and otherwise leaves the Stack alone because shutting it down would black out half the district.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — community-held. Auntie Ferro's informal authority, tolerated by Ferrum as long as the tax gets paid.

No standing guard, but the Stack is watched constantly — a hundred residents with a stake in it. Theft or sabotage draws a fast, physical, and collective response, not corp Alert. Ferrum sends an enforcer crew only if the tax stops; they come loud, in a cargo-rig, and leave once paid or once someone bleeds.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
The Cold Stack is one of the brightest nodes in Wireside's data-map — a visible knot of traffic any hacker's overlay will flag on sight. Public AR shows only maintenance schematics and Ferro's barter-board; the real traffic (deep-net relays, black-market bandwidth resale, three dead-drops in the coolant-duct access panels) sits one layer down, guarded by Priya's homebrew ICE.

Technomancers describe the Stack's noise-floor as "haunted" — ghost-packets that don't resolve to any known protocol, looping in the deep architecture. Most call it corrupted legacy code. Priya isn't so sure.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Ferro's Favor. Auntie Ferro calls in an old debt: someone is skimming rack-space contracts to funnel bandwidth to an unknown buyer uptower. She wants the crew to find out who — and whether Meridian is already watching.

2. The Noise-Floor. Priya has isolated a recurring ghost-signal that resembles a corrupted Technomancer's sending — impossible, since the last known Stack diver of that skill died six years ago. The signal is getting louder, and it's asking for help.

3. Structural Tax. Ferrum quietly triples the Stack's tax, timed to a citywide "infrastructure audit" tied to the war effort above. If the crew can't find leverage fast, Auntie Ferro's people go dark — literally and financially.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The street here doesn't so much have a ceiling as a lid — the sagging underbelly of the district above, patched in places with corrugate sheeting where the original structure gave out decades ago, dripping its endless warm rain into gutters that hiss and steam. Cable Souk fills the gap beneath it wall to wall: stall after stall of salvaged spool-wire, bootleg decks, cracked optics, and coils of fiber sold by the meter off spindles taller than a man, every table lit by its own cheap sign bleeding sodium-gold and cyan into the wet.

Overhead, in the narrow slot of open air the souk's canopies leave clear, the traffic never stops — courier-drones weaving single-file above the stalls, a hovercab drifting sideways to avoid a low gantry, and below them all a line of ground-rigs crawling bumper to bumper, horns and hawkers' cries fighting for the same air. The noise is layered like the traffic: engine-whine under vendor-chant under the wet slap of tarps under, always, that deep foundation heartbeat thrumming up through the souk's cracked pavement.

You feel the souk clock you before you've taken ten steps in — a dozen vendors' eyes flicking to your rig, your chrome, the cut of your jacket, doing the math on what you're worth to rob, to sell to, or to warn away.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Broker Yuen** — runs the souk's unofficial exchange rate for bandwidth futures; a Nyx-adjacent fixer who trades favors as often as scrip and remembers every debt down to the decimal.

**Big Marsh** — a hulking ex-Ironclad quartermaster turned rig-parts dealer, selling combat-frame components that "fell off a convoy." Everyone knows better than to ask which convoy.

**The Twins** — two identical, unnervingly quiet vendors who deal exclusively in grey-tech decks and never give the same name twice; rumored Cinderhold couriers laundering gear through the souk.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — lawless-by-consensus. No single gang rules it; the vendors police each other because a riot is bad for everyone's business.

Petty theft gets mob justice on the spot. Anything bigger — a shootout, a corp raid — scatters the souk in seconds, stalls folding into mobile carts and vanishing down side-alleys within a minute. Alert here means the souk simply isn't there anymore.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Public AR is a chaotic flea-market of floating price-tags, fake reviews, and vendor reputation scores, half of them gamed. Underneath, the souk runs a private barter-ledger on a pirate mesh-net that never touches the corp backbone — a hacker who finds the mesh finds an unregulated, untaxed economy worth a fortune to expose or exploit.

Meridian's official coverage of the souk is thin by design — a "dead patch" bought and maintained by pooled vendor bribes, one of the few blind spots in the Wired this far down.

#### Plot Hooks

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
1. Grey Market Audit. A batch of "fallen off a convoy" combat-frame parts from Big Marsh turns out to be tagged Ironclad war matériel headed for the front. Someone up the chain wants it back quietly — or wants the leak found loudly.

2. The Twins' Ledger. The Twins go missing along with their entire stock, and their mesh-net dead-drop starts broadcasting a garbled distress loop. Cinderhold wants the crew to find out if it's a corp snatch or something in the deep-net that got out.

3. Blind Patch. Someone is buying up the souk's Meridian bribe-fund from the outside, threatening to flood the blind spot with surveillance. The vendors need muscle, money, or a miracle before their dead patch goes live.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

There's no sign, just a hole in a cooling-tower's foundation wall where a door used to be, and a stairwell going down instead of up — which in Wireside is the closest thing to a landmark you get. Rain sheets off the tower above in ropes, catching cyan light bounced off the data-conduits running along the gutter, and by the time you've crossed the street your boots are soaked through. Above the doorway a single flickering holo-sign reads THE DIVE, half the letters dead.

The street traffic here is thinner but no less layered — a lone courier-drone parked on a ledge like a roosting bird, a boosted ground-rig idling at the curb with its Technomancer owner still half-jacked into its dash-deck, eyes rolled back, lips moving to a conversation happening somewhere else entirely. Somewhere above, unseen, an aircraft's running lights slide across the underside of the level-ceiling, gone before you can track it.

Down the stairs the air changes — cooler, drier, humming with deck-fans and old amp static. A dozen jacks are plugged into a dozen skulls at the bar, bodies slack, minds somewhere in the Wired. The bartender doesn't look up. He already knows why you're here.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Sable** — the Dive's owner-bartender, an old Technomancer who "retired" from deep-net running after something down there left half his face numb; now he brokers net-runner contracts for a cut and never explains the numbness.

**Kess Oduya** — the Dive's best working net-runner, young, arrogant, brilliant, freelance for hire to anyone who can meet her price; despises corp work but will take it if the money's obscene enough.

**The Hollow Man** — a regular who never removes his jack, speaks only in half-sentences, and is either the best diver in the district or something that used to be a person and now just wears one's face. No one's checked closely enough to be sure.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — Technomancer-informal. Sable's word is law inside; outside is whatever gang controls that block that week.

Violence inside the Dive is almost unheard of — jacked-in patrons are catatonic and utterly defenseless, and everyone knows it, so an unwritten code protects them fiercely. Break it once and you're barred from every deep-net den in Wireside within a day; Technomancers talk.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

To a normal AR scan, the Dive reads as an unlicensed net-café, nothing more. To anyone jacked in, it's a doorway — Sable maintains one of the district's cleanest, fastest deep-net on-ramps, a rarity worth protecting.

Under the surface, the Dive's private board lists net-runners for hire by reputation, not name — a hacker who cracks it finds real identities, blackmail-grade information on half the district's talent.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
Kess's persona in the Wired burns unusually bright — Technomancers who've crossed her signature say it doesn't feel entirely human anymore.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Hire the Diver. A client needs a net-runner for a job too hot for their usual talent. Sable will broker the introduction to Kess — for a price, and a favor owed to the house.

2. The Hollow Man's Errand. The Hollow Man surfaces from a jack-in for the first time in months, hands the crew a data-shard, and says only "finish it" before going under again. What's on the shard implicates a Meridian watch-captain in something ugly.

3. Sable's Numbness. Something from Sable's old final dive is resurfacing in the deep-net — a signature only he'd recognize. He wants the crew to escort him back in, one more time, to close a door he never properly shut.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

You smell Mist Alley before you see it — hot metal and coolant chemical, sweet and acrid together — and then you're in it, and the world goes soft-edged and gold. The alley runs between two cooling-tower blocks whose overflow vents dump superheated exhaust straight into the standing rain, and the collision boils up a fog that never fully clears, lit sodium-gold by a string of caged bulbs no one's bothered to steal. There is no sky here, less than anywhere — just the fog, and above the fog, somewhere, the black gasket-seam underside of the level overhead, invisible tonight behind the mist.

Shapes move through it at every height: a courier-drone's running lights smear to a soft halo as it threads overhead, a ground-rig's headlamps become two golden smudges before the vehicle itself resolves out of the murk close enough to graze your shoulder, gone again just as fast. Voices arrive before faces do. Footsteps arrive before voices. You can hear the alley's whole life happening around you — a transaction, a laugh, a scuffle — and see none of it until it's three feet away.

Everyone in Wireside knows what Mist Alley is for. Half the deals in this district happen in this fog because no camera holds a clean image here — and so does every ambush that ever needed the same cover.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Whisper Cole** — a Nyx-affiliated broker who conducts sensitive meets exclusively in the mist, trusting the fog more than any encryption; pays well for discretion and punishes its absence personally.

**Dredge** — a scavenger who works the alley's runoff grates for anything dropped, lost, or hidden in a hurry; knows the fog's blind spots better than anyone alive and sells that knowledge cheap.

**Captain Reyes** — leads a small Ironclad-contracted patrol that sweeps the alley twice a night on paper and once in reality; corruptible, exhausted, and one bad night from snapping.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — contested/no-man's cover. No faction truly holds it; everyone uses it, so everyone tacitly protects the fog's usefulness by not clearing it.

The mist defeats most visual security entirely — thermal and sonar work poorly through the coolant-vapor turbulence. Violence here escalates fast and unseen; by the time anyone reacts, it's usually already over. Ironclad's patrol responds to gunfire, not screams.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The fog is a literal blind spot in the visual-surveillance net, and Meridian's coverage maps show it as a known, tolerated dead zone — too expensive to fix, too useful to certain corp interests to actually want fixed.

AR overlays degrade badly in the mist's particulate interference; tags flicker, ghost, and sometimes show stale data hours or days old — an Edgerunner reading the alley's AR layer may be looking at a version of the street that no longer exists.

#### Plot Hooks

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
1. The Fog Meet. Whisper Cole wants the crew as muscle for a meet gone paranoid — a Meridian defector trading data for a new SIN, and someone's already tipped off the buyer's rivals.

2. What Dredge Found. Dredge surfaces a corp ID-chip from the runoff grates, still warm, belonging to someone who was never reported missing. Following the thread means finding out who's disappearing people in the mist and why no one's looking.

3. Reyes's Breaking Point. Captain Reyes is about to snap and either flip on Ironclad or get someone innocent killed trying to prove he hasn't gone soft. The crew gets pulled into his last patrol, one way or the other.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The block around Ghost Node is too quiet, and in Wireside that's its own kind of scream. The chemical rain still falls from the level-underside above, the data-conduit veins still glow along the gutters — but here they flicker wrong, stuttering cyan-to-black-to-cyan in a rhythm that makes your eyes want to look away. The building itself was a relay substation once, Meridian-built, abandoned so long ago that even the salvage crews stopped coming back for parts. Its rooftop dish still turns, slow, servo-grinding, pointed at nothing anyone can name.

The traffic thins here too, and that's wrong as well — courier-drones detour a full block around the airspace above the substation, and the one hovercab you see takes the long way rather than cross it. Only ground traffic still uses the street below, and even the cargo-crawlers seem to pick up speed passing the door. Somewhere behind you, faint under the rain and the district's usual wall of noise, you could swear you hear a voice that isn't on any frequency you own.

Every net-runner in Wireside has a story about Ghost Node. Most of them end with someone jacking in whole and coming out wrong, or not coming out at all.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Old Voss** — the last Meridian technician assigned here before the substation was scrapped off the books; never left, never ages visibly, and speaks to visitors through the building's dead intercom in a voice that matches nobody's memory of him.

**Reth** — a Technomancer exile who camps at the substation's edge, believing the Node holds a fragment of something that died in the Wired long ago and refusing all offers of help or reason.

**The Cull** — a small gang of scavenger-kids who dare each other to jack in for seconds at a time, daring death for street cred; one of them hasn't woken up right in months.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — unclaimed, avoided. No gang wants it, no corp will admit owning it.

There is no conventional security because there is nothing here worth conventionally guarding — the danger is entirely in the deep-net, not the street. Anyone jacking in draws no corp Alert at all, which is itself the warning: nobody official is watching, because nobody official wants to be found here.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Ghost Node is a literal dark spot in Wireside's data-map — a dead zone that shouldn't exist on infrastructure this dense, showing as a null address that some systems render as an error and others simply omit.

Divers who go deep report a presence: fragmentary, recursive, aware of being observed. Some Technomancers insist it's a corrupted AI ghost, a dead relay's leftover process looping forever; others insist it's something that was never a program at all — a piece of the Wired's substrate that woke up wrong.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
Old Voss's intercom voice matches no biometric on file. Meridian's own maintenance logs list him as decommissioned, not deceased, forty-one years ago.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The Cull's Dare. One of the scavenger-kids doesn't wake up from a Ghost Node dare, still breathing, still jacked in, mind gone somewhere the crew has to follow to bring back.

2. Voss's Request. The intercom voice asks the crew, politely, to find out who decommissioned Old Voss — and why the paperwork says he's still technically employed.

3. What Reth Believes. Reth has finally found a way to jack all the way in, convinced he can speak to whatever's in there. Whether he's right, mad, or about to feed something in the deep-net a very dangerous amount of power is the crew's problem now.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

After a district's worth of glow and static, the silence hits you first. Faraday Chapel sits inside a decommissioned signal-shielding vault — Meridian copper mesh still lining every wall, ceiling, and door, a birdcage big enough to live in — and inside that mesh, the Wired simply isn't. No AR tags. No ambient hum. No ghost-flicker of a hundred thousand signals brushing past your skin without you ever noticing they were there, until they're gone and you notice everything.

Outside, the district goes on as it always does — chemical rain sheeting off the level above, cyan conduit-veins pulsing along the street, a cargo-crawler grinding past under a courier-drone's blinking transit lane, a hovercab's downwash scattering steam off a grate. But at the Chapel's copper threshold all of it seems to hush, muffled, like stepping underwater. Candlelight — real flame, real smoke, startling in its rarity — throws warm gold instead of neon, the only warm light for blocks.

A street-priest in patched vestments meets you at the door before you've decided whether to knock. "No signal here," she says, like a blessing. "Come in and be unwatched a while."

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Sister Amako** — the Chapel's keeper, Corran-rooted street-faith, running soup lines and washing-rites for anyone who crosses the threshold regardless of SIN status; her calm is a deliberate, hard-won discipline against a district built to fray it.

**Brother Ilya** — a former Meridian signal-engineer who built the Chapel's shielding himself after his faith and his employer parted ways violently; maintains the mesh with an engineer's precision and a convert's zeal.

**Nameless Tomas** — a SIN-less refugee who's lived inside the Chapel's shielding for two years, terrified of what re-entering the Wired's surveillance will mean for him; the congregation's living argument for why this place matters.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — sanctuary, tacitly respected. No faction claims it; violating it costs social standing across nearly every faction in the district.

The copper mesh is the real security — it makes the Chapel useless as a target for anyone who needs a live surveillance feed or an AR-tracked mark, which covers most predators in Wireside. Physical violence inside is rare and reflexively punished by whoever's present, faction lines forgotten for the duration.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

From outside, the Chapel is simply gone — a null patch in the data-map, the one true dead zone in a district defined by signal. Hackers scanning the block get nothing, not even an error; the shielding is that complete.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
This makes it precious and dangerous in equal measure: a perfect place to go dark, meet unseen, or hide someone the Wired is actively hunting — and a perfect trap if someone learns to watch the physical entrance instead of the data one.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Sanctuary for Tomas. Someone has learned Nameless Tomas is hiding inside the Chapel and is watching the physical door, patiently, since the digital one is closed to them. The crew has to get him out — or get the watcher gone.

2. Ilya's Old Employer. Meridian wants its shielding technology back — specifically, wants to know how a disgraced engineer built a dead-zone this clean, since it has applications far beyond one chapel.

3. The Unwatched Meeting. A Nyx broker and a war-weary Ironclad deserter want to negotiate something explosive, and both insist on Chapel neutrality. Sister Amako allows it on one condition: the crew keeps the peace inside her walls.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The transition is sudden and total. One block you're in Wireside's usual amber murk, cable-strung and grimy — the next you're bathed in hard violet-white floodlight bleeding down from a checkpoint gantry, and every shadow you own snaps into sharp, watched relief. Blacklight Fringe is Meridian's line in the sand: the last stretch of street before their sub-corp watch-post, and they want you to know it, feel it, from a hundred meters out.

The rain still falls from the level-ceiling above — you can see it catch the floodlight in sheets, blacklit and strange, chemical residue fluorescing faintly where it beads on exposed skin. Overhead the air-traffic thins and straightens, courier-drones flying in disciplined transponder-lanes now instead of loose formation, a Meridian patrol-craft holding station on repulsors with a slow, deliberate menace. Ground traffic funnels through a single checkpoint lane, engines idling, drivers' hands visible on wheels, everyone very carefully not looking nervous.

Every wall here is tagged in real-time AR readouts only Meridian credentials can fully see — status codes, threat-flags, biometric pings — and even without a jack you can feel it, that specific prickling sense of being catalogued. In Wireside, that feeling has a name: the Fringe.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Watch-Captain Idris Halloran** — runs the Blacklight checkpoint with cold professionalism, more interested in data than drama; will let almost anything through if the paperwork and the biometrics agree, and burns anyone who makes him look bad.

**Analyst Nkemdirim** — a young Meridian data-analyst stationed at the Fringe who's started noticing patterns in the traffic that shouldn't be there — and is scared of what filing an honest report might mean for her.

**Ghost-Runner Jax** — a smuggler who's mapped every blind angle of the checkpoint's sensor sweep and sells safe-passage timing to anyone willing to pay Meridian-adjacent prices for Meridian-adjacent risk.

#### Security

Zone: Flats border — Meridian sub-corp controlled. The most heavily surveilled ground-level checkpoint in the district.

Biometric and SIN scanning is dense and active; false credentials or flagged status trigger immediate, escalating Alert — first a hold-and-verify, then armed Meridian response drones, then a full lockdown of the checkpoint lane. Halloran's people are drilled, calm, and will shoot to stop rather than to kill, which doesn't make it survivable to test twice.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The Fringe is one of the most information-dense nodes in Wireside — full AR threat-tagging, live biometric overlays, transponder-lane guidance, all visible to Meridian credentials and heavily obfuscated to everyone else.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
Analyst Nkemdirim's flagged "anomalous pattern" is a subtle but real one: a statistically improbable number of SIN-verified travelers through the Fringe are, weeks later, turning up as unregistered dead in the Sinks. Someone is laundering people through a legitimate checkpoint on their way to disappearing.

Ghost-Runner Jax's blind-spot map is itself a hot commodity — worth a fortune to a rival corp, and worth Jax's life if Meridian ever traces the leak back to him.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Nkemdirim's Report. The analyst wants to file her findings but knows it'll get buried or get her killed. She needs deniable outside help to make noise the right way — loud enough to force action, quiet enough not to trace back to her.

2. Jax's Map. Someone stole a copy of Jax's blind-spot map, and now Halloran's checkpoint is about to get a very unwelcome audit tracing exactly how it leaked — with Jax and anyone who's used his routes in the blast radius.

3. The Laundering Line. Following Nkemdirim's pattern leads toward a Meridian internal unit quietly feeding "verified" people into a black program tied to the war above — deniable, dangerous, and exactly the kind of thing a fixer would pay very well to expose or bury.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

Every cable in Wireside seems to end at the Battery eventually, and looking at it, you believe it — a block-long tangle of tapped power lines, jury-rigged transformers, and stacked capacitor banks scavenged from three different eras of the tower's construction, humming loud enough to feel in your fillings. There's no sky above it, only the usual black underside of the level overhead, but here the chemical rain hisses to steam a full meter off the ground, boiled by heat the Battery's illegal draw throws off like a fever.

The light is all its own — not neon selling anything, just raw arc-glow and fault-flicker where insulation's worn through, gold and white and occasionally, alarmingly, violet. Overhead a courier-drone gives the block extra clearance, wary of the electromagnetic soup; a hovercab's systems visibly stutter passing too close, dash-lights flickering before it clears the interference. Ground traffic detours around exposed cable-runs snaking across the street like something alive, half-buried under runoff and steam.

A line of people waits at a folding table with a charge-meter bolted to it, paying scrip by the watt to a woman who looks like she could rewire the tower's dead heart with her bare hands and has probably tried.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Voltess** — runs the Battery's charge-market with iron-fisted fairness, tapping power from a dozen sources (some corp, most not) and selling it back to the district at rates everyone can afford; a folk hero to residents, a headache to Ferrum and HALO's grid auditors alike.

**Sparkjaw Denny** — Voltess's chief rigger, missing an arm to an arc-flash and replaced with cheap grey-tech chrome that still throws sparks when he's angry, which is often.

**Auditor Chen** — a HALO-contracted grid inspector sent to find the Battery's illegal taps; competent, quietly sympathetic, and under increasing pressure from above to stop finding excuses to file inconclusive reports.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — community-defended, informally armed. Voltess's people guard the taps directly; the district as a whole protects the Battery because losing it means losing cheap power district-wide.

Sabotage or theft draws fast collective retaliation. Corp response is bureaucratic rather than violent — Ferrum and HALO send auditors, not soldiers, at least for now — but that patience visibly thins with every inspection Auditor Chen fails to close.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The Battery's power draw is a glaring anomaly on any utility-grid overlay — impossible to fully hide, managed instead through a rotating shell of falsified meter data that Voltess's people update constantly.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
A hacker digging into the grid data finds a decade of increasingly creative fraud, and beneath that, evidence the original "loss" the Battery taps into was budgeted for and never reported missing — someone upstream has been covering for Wireside's theft for reasons no one down here understands yet.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Chen's Last Report. Auditor Chen is being forced to finally close the case against the Battery. She'd rather leak Voltess a warning than watch a war-footing crackdown level a district's power supply — if the crew can make the warning look like it came from anywhere else.

2. The Budgeted Loss. Someone has been quietly funding the "missing" power the Battery taps for years. Finding out who — and why — leads uncomfortably close to a black-budget line item tied to the war climbing the foundations.

3. Sparkjaw's Grudge. Denny's convinced a rival tapper crew is bleeding the grid dry and blaming it on the Battery's usual overdraw, risking the whole operation. Proving it — or proving him wrong before he starts a turf war — falls to the crew.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The building has no windows, which in a district with no sky shouldn't matter, but somehow it does — Deep Dream feels sealed, deliberately, like something that doesn't want light or attention finding its way in or out. Pink and violet signage bleeds down its face in the rain, half advertisement and half warning, promising DREAMS DEEPER THAN THE FLATS in a script that drips like it's melting. Chemical rain sheets off the level above and pools black at the entrance, catching that pink glow and holding it like something bruised.

The street outside keeps its usual rhythm — a courier-drone's lights blinking past overhead, a boosted ground-rig idling at the curb with its engine ticking, a hovercab discharging a customer who won't quite meet anyone's eyes on the way in. But the crowd near Deep Dream moves differently than the rest of Wireside's foot traffic: slower, softer-footed, some of them clearly still coming down off whatever they bought last time.

A tout in a stained silk jacket peels off the wall to meet you before you've committed to stopping. "First dive's on the house," he says, and something about the way he says house makes it sound like a place you don't leave from easily.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Madam Solene** — runs Deep Dream as an Obsidian-licensed front with unlicensed extras in the back rooms; charming, dangerous, genuinely believes she's selling relief rather than harm, which makes her more dangerous, not less.

**The Tout, "Silk" Ferro** — no relation to Auntie Ferro despite the name, works the street pulling in customers, paid per head, increasingly uneasy about what's actually happening to the regulars.

**Dr. Anh Behar** — a disgraced Caduceus ripperdoc who keeps Deep Dream's deepest divers alive after sessions that should have killed them, for a price that is never just money.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — Obsidian-licensed, self-policing. Legitimate on the surface; the back rooms are a different jurisdiction entirely.

Front-of-house security is minimal and professional — bouncers who de-escalate, cameras that see everything. The back rooms have no such rules; anything that happens there, happens, and Alert only comes if a body turns up somewhere a corp has to notice it.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Public AR shows a fully licensed, faintly seedy simsense lounge — legitimate Obsidian branding, real health disclaimers, real (if minimal) safety certifications.

Underneath, Deep Dream runs an unlicensed feed of BTL-adjacent full-immersion product that doesn't exist on any manifest — dives so deep some customers don't fully surface, their minds lingering somewhere in the recording long after the session ends.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
A hacker digging into the back-room feed finds recordings that shouldn't be legally possible to make — sensations recorded from donors who, per hospital and precinct records the deep-net still holds, are already dead.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The Deepest Dive. A client's sibling went into Deep Dream's back rooms and hasn't fully come back — physically present, mentally elsewhere. Getting them out means finding what recording they're stuck inside, and why Dr. Behar keeps them breathing instead of letting go.

2. Dead Donors. Someone has traced Deep Dream's most extreme product to recordings taken from people listed as deceased — meaning either the records are wrong, or the recordings were taken from someone who wasn't dead yet when it happened.

3. Silk's Crisis of Conscience. The tout wants out, and wants to take evidence with him — but Madam Solene doesn't let go of assets that easily, and Obsidian doesn't let go of a licensed front that's making this much quiet money.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

You find Relay Roost by looking up, which nobody in the Flats does by habit anymore — there's nothing up there but the level above, close and dark and dripping. But here, high on the skeleton of a long-dead broadcast tower still bristling with dish and antenna, shapes perch and shift against the black: too still to be birds, too many joints in the wrong places to be anything the Wired would call human. Wereravens. Watching the street the way a hawk watches a field, patient and unbothered by the rain sheeting off the tower's ribs in cyan-lit ropes.

Below them, Wireside's usual layered churn continues, oblivious or pretending to be — a courier-drone flight skimming low along a data-conduit line glowing like a vein in the wet street, a cargo-crawler grinding past under a string of gantry lights, a hovercab settling to discharge a fare who doesn't look up either. The noise wall is the same as everywhere in the district: six tongues of voices, drone-whine, hiss of rain on hot metal, the deep pump-heartbeat underneath it all — except here, if you listen past it, there's a second sound: the soft, dry rustle of feathers that aren't quite feathers, shifting on a girder forty feet up.

One of them drops from the tower in a controlled, silent fall and lands in front of you already mid-transformation, human enough by the time its boots hit the pavement to ask, quite politely, what you're doing under its roost.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Corvin Ashwake** — the Roost's senior scout, Wereraven-born, ancient by their kind's reckoning; trades data and information for favors, coin, or good stories, and remembers every debt across decades.

**Little Pinion** — the youngest scout at the Roost, still learning the discipline of the perch, eager to prove herself on a courier run more dangerous than her elders would assign her.

**Handler Ostrowski** — a Nyx logistics contact who uses the Roost as a trusted dead-drop relay point, paying the Wereravens in favors and protection rather than scrip, which the Roost values more.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — Wereraven-held airspace, informally respected. No one owns the ground beneath the tower, but no one contests the sky above it either.

The scouts see everything approaching from a considerable distance and simply won't engage unless the Roost itself or a courier in flight is threatened; then they respond fast, from above, and are gone before ground-level backup can arrive. There is effectively no "Alert" here — just consequences, delivered personally.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Relay Roost functions as a physical dead-drop node bridging the digital and the real — data-shards, encrypted courier packages, and whispered intel change hands here precisely because the Wereravens' perch sits above most ground-level surveillance angles and their flight patterns read as wildlife noise to automated tracking.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
A hacker who identifies the Roost's actual traffic pattern (rather than dismissing it as sensor clutter) finds a startlingly complete map of who's moving what through Wireside's underworld — a treasure and a death sentence in equal measure.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Little Pinion's Run. The young scout takes a courier job above her experience level and doesn't check in on schedule. Corvin asks the crew, as outsiders the Roost can deny knowing, to retrace her route without drawing attention to the network itself.

2. Ostrowski's Package. A Nyx dead-drop routed through the Roost goes missing between hand-offs, and Handler Ostrowski suspects someone inside the scout network — an accusation that could shatter the trust the whole relay depends on.

3. Eyes on the Sky. Meridian has started test-flying a new drone-swarm pattern that reads Wereraven flight signatures with unsettling accuracy — the Roost's centuries-old blind spot may be closing, and Corvin wants to know exactly how much the corp already knows before it's too late to move the network.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The street simply stops believing in itself about a hundred meters ahead of you, the neon thinning block by block like a signal losing signal, and then there is the plaza — the last one, the one every map of the Flats draws with a small dotted warning around its edge. Above, there is no sky, only the underside of the Ninth Grid pressing down close and black, sweating its warm chemical rain onto a cracked concrete bowl ringed by the tallest, oldest signs left standing this far down: a triple-stacked Obsidian dream-den ad still running a loop nobody's paid for in a decade, a Cassavir relay-flag hung from a girder by someone with a sense of humor, a Nyx toll-marker burning steady cyan. The rain drags all three colors down into the puddles until the whole bowl looks like it's on fire underwater.

Traffic still finds this place, stubbornly, layer on layer — a courier-drone flock threading the black overhead in a tight defensive V, an Ironclad gunship idling far up on a routine sweep it never actually descends for, a string of cargo-crawlers grinding along the last real road grumbling under chains because the street surface gives out to gravel and bone-white rubble past here. Ground level is thick with rig-runners double-parked nose-out, ready to floor it back toward the lit Grid at the first wrong sound. Six languages of shouting, the sub-bass foundation-thrum, the drone-whine, the hiss of rain on hot iron — all of it a little quieter here than it should be, like the plaza itself is listening for something underneath the noise.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text: At the bowl's center, raised on a dais of stacked shipping plate, a floodlight burns steady and merciless — the actual Last Light, the fixture the whole plaza is named for, powered off a line nobody can trace and guarded by nobody who'll admit to guarding it. Past its throw, the dark starts. You can feel the edge of the district in your teeth before you ever see the barricades.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Mother Kessa** — self-appointed "boss of the edge," a former Ferrum dock-forewoman who lost her SIN in a foundation collapse and now runs the plaza's unofficial council of last-block holdouts. Trades safety and light for tithe and information; genuinely protects who she can.

**Old Renn** — keeps the floodlight running, claims descent from the original maintenance crew who wired it before the Warrens sealed off. Speaks to the light like it's a person. Knows every splice in the district's power grid.

**Vashti "Two-Toll" Orn** — a Nyx-aligned toll-runner who taxes anyone moving goods toward Barricade Row or the Drop, in exchange for a "clean word" that keeps them off gang watch-lists for a night.

**Deacon Ishii** — itinerant street-priest of the Lamp tradition who preaches nightly at the dais steps about what waits below; half the plaza thinks he's mad, the other half leaves him offerings anyway.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — contested/lawless, held loosely by Mother Kessa's council rather than any single gang or corp. The last patch of ground with functioning municipal power before the Warrens.

No formal law. Kessa's council enforces a single rule — nobody kills under the Light — with numbers, not guns; break it and every hand in the plaza turns against you before Ironclad or anyone else could respond. Real violence draws scavenger gangs from Barricade Row within minutes, drawn by the noise like sharks to blood in dark water.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
The Wired flickers and stutters this close to the edge — official Grid maps mark the plaza "unverified," and SIN-readers here are old, patched, and easy to spoof. It's the last place upstream from the Warrens where the overlay still mostly works.

A hacker who digs finds a graveyard of dead account-pings — SINs that checked in here once and never again, their last known location frozen forever at the plaza's edge.

AR tags left by Kessa's council mark safe stalls, known toll-runners, and — in a private layer only she controls — a live tally of who currently owes her.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The Last Toll. Mother Kessa wants the crew to shadow a caravan of Warrens-salvage traders through the plaza to Salvage Gate without Vashti's toll-runners bleeding them dry — but the real threat is a Barricade Row warband testing whether the Light's truce still holds.

2. Dead Reckoning. Old Renn's floodlight is failing, and with it the last verified ground-truth marker the Grid recognizes this deep. Losing it would let the Warrens' dead-air creep swallow the plaza within weeks — someone upstream (possibly Meridian, possibly worse) wants exactly that.

3. The Council's Debt. Kessa's tally of favors has grown too large for her to control, and a Nyx broker is quietly buying up the debts of half the plaza. The crew is hired — by Kessa, or by Nyx — to find out who really owns the Last Light now.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

You smell the Row before you see it — scorched plastic, gun-oil, and the wet-mineral reek that bleeds up out of the dark past the wire. It used to be three parallel streets; now it's one fortified wall of stacked containers, sandbagged rubble, and salvaged plate welded into a crooked rampart that runs the width of the district, broken only where the old roads punch through in chokepoints nobody crosses without being seen first.

There's no sky here, same as anywhere this low — just the black underbelly of the Grid above, dripping its warm chemical rain onto razor coils and gun positions, the neon reduced to hazard-strobes and targeting-lume in sullen red and amber instead of the seductive color up-Flats. But the air is still busy: a pair of Ironclad-surplus drones on loan to the line-bosses patrol in slow figure-eights above the wall, a hovercab won't come within two blocks of the checkpoint no matter what you pay, and every so often a heavy cargo-rig grinds up from the plaza behind you loaded with something the crews on the wall want badly enough to open a gate for. The wall of sound here is different too — less voices, more machinery: generator-thrum, the clack of somebody racking a weapon just to remind you they can, and under everything, that same thousand-year heartbeat of the foundation pumps, steady as a held breath.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text: Past the wire, past the checkpoint lights, the street doesn't so much end as stop existing — the pavement gives way to broken plate and then to nothing your eyes can resolve. Every gun on the Row points that way. That should tell you everything.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Corvo Ashwell** — warlord of the Ferronail Crew, the largest gang holding the central barricade; ex-Ironclad contractor who "retired" with a stolen combat-frame and a grudge. Runs the Row like a siege, because he believes it is one.

**Sera "Latch" Nkemdi** — Corvo's quartermaster and the only person on the Row who talks to outsiders civilly; brokers passage deals and mercenary contracts through the checkpoints.

**The Widow's Boys** — a smaller rival crew holding the eastern chokepoint, rumored to trade directly with things that come up from the Warrens rather than just guard against them.

**Tomas Greel** — Meridian stringer who's paid the Ferronail Crew for exclusive footage rights to "whatever comes through," and is visibly disappointed most nights.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — gang-fortified, effectively a private front line. The Ferronail Crew and Widow's Boys hold their sections as sovereign territory; no corp will contest it because no corp wants the job.

Security here is total and immediate: armed checkpoints, sightlines covering every approach, and standing orders to shoot anything that comes over the wall from the wrong side without waiting for ID. Alert response is instant and lethal — the Row doesn't do warnings, because warnings are how people used to die before they learned better.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
The gangs run their own jury-rigged sensor mesh layered over what's left of the Grid's overlay — motion-tags, heat-ghosts, and a private comm channel that lights up red the instant something crosses the wire from the dark side.

Officially the Wired shows Barricade Row as a "structural hazard zone, access restricted" — corp language for we stopped mapping this and so should you.

A skilled hacker can tap the gangs' sensor mesh and get earlier warning of Warrens activity than the defenders themselves — valuable, and a very good way to get shot by someone who assumes you're one of the things they're watching for.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Relief Line. The Ferronail Crew is bleeding numbers to something that's started probing the wall at irregular hours, and Corvo needs deniable guns willing to hold a chokepoint for one bad night while he figures out what it is.

2. The Widow's Deal. Evidence surfaces that the Widow's Boys are trading captured Edgerunners — or worse, live SINs — to something below the wire in exchange for safe passage. Someone wants proof, and someone else wants it buried.

3. Breach of Contract. Sanctum's actuaries have quietly classified the entire Row as an "uninsurable total loss zone," which means the conglomerates have stopped caring who wins here — opening the door for a third faction, human or otherwise, to make a play for the wall itself.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The shaft-house looks like a tomb because that's more or less what it became. It was a freight lift once — one of the old bones-of-the-tower elevators that used to run supplies down into levels the Reach has since disowned — and someone, a long time ago, welded its doors shut with plate three layers thick and painted a warning across it in six languages and one that isn't a language at all, just a symbol every child in the Flats learns to fear before they learn to read.

Overhead there's the same ceiling every street down here has to live under — no sky, just the dark underbelly of the level above, chemical rain sheeting off the shaft-house's corrugated roof in curtains lit orange by a single flickering sodium lamp. But the air over the Drop is wrong in a way you feel before you can name it: courier-drones give the shaft-house a wide, deliberate berth, arcing around it rather than over it; the one hover-rig idling nearby has its running lights pointed away, like even light doesn't want to look down that hole. Ground traffic avoids the block entirely except for the vigil-keepers' foot patrols and the occasional Nyx supply crawler making its last delivery before turning back. The sound-wall that blankets the rest of the district — the voices, the drone-whine, the hiss of rain on hot metal — goes strangely thin here, swallowed by something under the plate that never quite goes silent and never quite resolves into a sound you can name.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text: Stand close enough, in the wet and the cold sodium light, and you'll swear you can feel a draft coming up through the seams in the door. Warm, when the air on your face is cold everywhere else. Nobody has ever explained that, and everybody who works this block has stopped asking.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Warden Iyoba Cresh** — self-titled "Warden of the Drop," a burned-SIN former Sanctum risk-assessor who took it upon herself to log everything that happens at the shaft. Keeps meticulous, slightly unhinged records. Will trade information for almost anything.

**The Vigil Three** — a rotating trio of Lamp-tradition street-priests who keep a permanent watch on the shaft-house door, never fewer than one at a time, praying and logging disturbances in a shared ledger.

**Renny Oskol** — a Nyx-connected fixer who occasionally arranges "sealed cargo" drops through a maintenance grate beside the main doors — the only sanctioned traffic still moving through the Drop in either direction.

**The Knocker** — not confirmed to be a person; the name given to whatever periodically strikes the sealed doors from the inside, three times, always at the same measured interval, always stopping before a fourth.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — nominally unclaimed, functionally held by the vigil-keepers' quiet authority and general terror. No gang wants the block; even the toughest crews on Barricade Row treat the Drop as neutral, cursed ground.

There's no armed security in the conventional sense — the deterrent is dread, reputation, and the Vigil Three's ledger, which every faction in the district respects because nobody wants their name in it next to something that came out. If the seal is ever breached, the Alert cascades district-wide within minutes: every barricade crew, every Nyx waystation, every vigil shrine will know before the corps do.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The Wired goes almost dead over the shaft — a true dead-air pocket, one of the few places in the Reach where the overlay simply refuses to render, showing only a grey error-glyph where the map should be.

Hackers who push into that dead zone report fragments of old data — pre-collapse maintenance logs, a lift schedule for a floor that officially doesn't exist, and, more than one has claimed, something that pings back.

Cresh maintains her own private overlay-log of every disturbance, timestamped and geotagged, that she'll share for the right price — the closest thing the district has to hard data on what the Drop actually is.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Three Knocks. The Knocker's pattern has changed for the first time in years — a fourth strike, faint, was heard last night. Warden Cresh wants deniable contractors to investigate before the vigil-keepers' panic spreads to the whole district.

2. The Sealed Cargo. Renny Oskol's last sanctioned drop through the maintenance grate didn't come back up on schedule, and Nyx wants to know if it's a Warrens problem or if Renny's skimming — either answer is a job.

3. Breaking the Seal. A Ferrum survey team, escorted by Ironclad muscle, arrives with orders to reopen the shaft for "resource assessment." The vigil-keepers see it as unforgivable heresy; the crew is caught between a corp contract and the fury of everyone who's kept watch here for a generation.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The gate isn't a gate anymore so much as a marketplace that grew around one — a old maintenance checkpoint whose actual doors were scrapped decades back for the very trade that now fills the block: things carried up out of the dark and sold to whoever's buying. Tarps strung between girders keep the worst of the rain off stalls piled with pre-Collapse alloy, dead tech nobody can identify, bone-white fragments that might be structural composite or might be something else entirely, and hand tools worn smooth by hands that don't work here anymore.

There is no sky above the Gate, only the low black ceiling of the level overhead, sweating its warm chemical rain through gaps in the tarps onto buyers haggling under strings of scavenged lumen-wire that throw a sick, uneven glow — cyan where the wire's still good, dead brown where it's not. The vertical space over the block is thinner than uptown but still crowded in its own cramped way: a single tired courier-drone weaves between support struts on autopilot, a scrap-hauler rig backs in through the crowd with its horn blaring continuously, and everyone on foot has long since learned to move without looking up, because looking up here just means rain in your eyes. Voices haggle in six languages over the price of a rusted control panel; somewhere a generator coughs and catches; the sub-bass foundation-thrum underlies it all, patient as ever.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text: Every buyer here asks the same unspoken question of every seller: how far down did you go for this, and what did you leave down there. Nobody answers honestly. Nobody expects them to.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Auntie Ferro** — matriarch of the Gate's trading families, a Corran guild-clan elder who set the first rules of "clean salvage" decades ago and still enforces them with a cane and a reputation. Buys, sells, and settles disputes.

**Digger Voss** — a scarred, taciturn salvager who goes deeper than anyone else still walking and always comes back with the strangest hauls; trusted for his goods, feared for what he might have picked up down there besides scrap.

**Ilse Marrow** — Caduceus-trained field medic who works the Gate unofficially, patching up salvagers who come back wrong before Auntie Ferro's rules force them to be quietly turned away.

**Baxa Ohn** — a Nyx buyer with standing orders to acquire anything electronic or "informational" that comes up, no questions, top price, immediate pickup.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — an independent trade-zone under Auntie Ferro's guild-clan authority, tolerated by the surrounding gangs because everyone profits from the Gate staying open and neutral.

Ferro's rule is simple and absolute: no violence in the market, no unvetted salvage sold without inspection, no questions about where anyone's cut came from. Breaking it means permanent exile from the only marketplace in the district that will still buy Warrens goods. Real threats — contaminated salvage, something that "came up wrong" — trigger an immediate, practiced quarantine drill the traders have run more than once.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
The Gate's overlay is a patchwork of private trade-tags — item listings, price histories, seller reputations — laid over a Grid map that officially still shows the old maintenance checkpoint and nothing else.

A hacker who digs finds an unofficial ledger of "flagged" salvage — items sold through the Gate that later did something they shouldn't have — kept quietly by Ferro's own people as insurance against her own market.

Nyx runs a discreet standing data-tap here, buying not just objects but the metadata of where they were found, building a slow, patient map of the Warrens no corp survey team could ever legally produce.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Digger's Last Haul. Digger Voss has gone quiet after his latest run and Auntie Ferro wants someone to check on him before Baxa Ohn's buyers realize what he might be carrying — and try to take it themselves.

2. Contaminated Lot. A batch of "clean" salvage turns out to be actively hazardous — data-active, possibly Wired-linked, possibly something the Warrens didn't want brought up. Ferro needs it traced back through every hand it's passed through before it causes a district-wide incident.

3. The Buyer's Ledger. Someone has stolen Ferro's private flagged-salvage ledger. In the wrong hands it's blackmail material on half the traders at the Gate — and proof of exactly what's been quietly surfacing from the Warrens for years.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The shrine occupies what used to be a transit substation, its old control room gutted and refitted with pew-benches made from packing crates and a single, patient lamp burning in the window that faces the dark. It's a daughter-house of the Lamp on Ninth, the street-faith tradition that keeps its soup lines and its washing rites and its vigils no matter how far down the Flats go — and here, at the literal edge of everything, that vigil means something more specific: they watch the chasm, in shifts, every hour of every day, so that no one ever has to look into it alone.

There's no sky above the shrine, only the close black underside of the level above, the rain coming down warm and faintly chemical the way it always does, streaking the shrine's single lit window and pooling in the gutters outside where a line of the hungry and the sleepless waits for the soup kettle no matter the hour. The vertical space above the block still carries its share of traffic — a Meridian relay-drone passes overhead on its fixed patrol route, indifferent; somewhere out past the barricades a hovercraft's running lights blink low and slow, probably a smuggler's rig giving the shrine's watch-lamp a wide, respectful berth. The sound here softens, almost reverently — voices low, the sub-bass foundation-thrum still present but muted, like the building itself is holding its breath along with everyone inside it.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text: Through the window, past the lamp, you can just make out where the street gives way to the dark. Someone is always there, watching it. Right now, it's your turn to wonder why.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Brother Amadi Vell** — the shrine's keeper, a former dock-worker who lost his crew to a Warrens breach years ago and has kept the vigil ever since; gentle, exhausted, unshakeable in his faith that watching matters.

**Sister Priya Nakash** — runs the soup line and the shrine's small clinic, trained informally by Caduceus field medics; the practical half of the shrine's work, and the one who actually keeps people alive.

**Old Mattis** — a blind vigil-keeper who claims he can hear things in the dark the sighted watchers miss, and has been right often enough that nobody argues anymore.

**Deacon Ishii** — the wandering priest also seen at the Last Light, considers the Vigil Shrine his true home parish and returns here between his plaza sermons.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — a recognized sanctuary under street-faith custom; even the hardest gangs on Barricade Row observe the old rule that shrines are neutral ground, a courtesy extended more out of superstition than piety.

The shrine keeps no weapons and wants none. Its only defense is the custom of sanctuary and the fact that every faction in the district, at some point, needs the soup line, the clinic, or the vigil's honest word about what's moving in the dark. Violating the sanctuary is a fast way to lose every ally you have left down here.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The shrine keeps almost no digital footprint by choice — the Lamp tradition distrusts the Wired on principle — so the overlay here shows little beyond a generic "community shelter" tag, deliberately unremarkable.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
Off the books, Brother Vell keeps a hand-written ledger of every disturbance the vigil-keepers have logged at the chasm's edge over the years — a physical record the Wired has never touched and can't erase.

Wereraven scouts are known to rest here between runs, trading news of the deep Warrens for a hot meal — making the shrine an unlikely but reliable source of current intelligence on what's actually moving below.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Old Mattis Hears Something. The blind watcher reports a new sound from the dark — rhythmic, patterned, unmistakably deliberate — and Brother Vell wants it investigated quietly before panic spreads down the soup line.

2. The Ledger's Worth. A Meridian researcher offers Vell serious money for access to the vigil's decades of handwritten disturbance records. Selling it would fund the shrine for years; it would also hand a conglomerate the district's only real historical data on the Warrens' edge.

3. Sanctuary Broken. A wounded fugitive — Warrens salvager, burned-SIN, or worse — claims sanctuary at the shrine while a Barricade Row warband hunts them through the streets outside. The crew must decide whether the old rule still holds, and what it costs to enforce it.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The building has no sign, which is the point — everyone who needs to find it already knows its name, and everyone else has no business here. It sits low and windowless behind a curtain of hanging chain-plastic that clatters in the wind off the chasm, the entrance marked only by a hand-painted line on the pavement that everyone calls the Deadline itself: cross it, and whoever you were on the other side stops mattering.

Above, there's the same close black nothing every street this deep has instead of a sky, rain sheeting warm and chemical off the building's corrugated overhang, catching a single dim red bulb above the door and turning the puddles the color of old rust. The air over the block carries a thin, careful trickle of traffic — a courier-drone drops something through a chute in the roof and leaves without circling back, a hover-rig sits dark and idling two streets off, engine running, driver watching the door rather than the road. Ground level stays deliberately quiet; nobody loiters near the Deadline who doesn't have to. The sound-wall thins here the way it does near the Drop — voices dropping to murmurs, the sub-bass foundation-thrum the loudest thing left, like the whole block has agreed to stop making noise about what happens inside.

Somewhere behind that chain-plastic curtain, someone is deciding whether your SIN — the six-digit thread of everything you ever were on the Grid's books — is about to stop existing. For some people, down here, that's the whole point of coming.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**The Clerk** — the broker who runs the Deadline, identity unknown even to regulars, always masked, always calm; erases SINs, forges new identities, and — for the right price — makes people disappear entirely, sometimes permanently, sometimes just administratively.

**Foss Ardan** — the Clerk's enforcer, a hulking ex-Ironclad washout who searches everyone at the curtain and has never once been seen to speak.

**Yuen Ratha** — a Meridian data-ghost who trades the Clerk clean SIN-templates skimmed from real deaths up in the Grid, in exchange for a cut of every erasure.

**Dez** — a nervous, half-erased regular who haunts the block outside, technically SIN-less but not quite gone, a walking cautionary tale for anyone considering the same transaction.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — a fiercely independent operation the Clerk defends personally; not aligned with any gang, tolerated by all of them because everyone eventually needs an eraser.

Foss Ardan is the only visible security, but the Clerk's real protection is leverage — everyone who's used the Deadline has something to hide, which means everyone has a reason to keep its existence quiet and its operator alive. Trouble here draws a slow, patient kind of retaliation rather than a loud one.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The building doesn't exist on any official Grid map — a genuine blank tile, deliberately scrubbed, which is itself the most reliable way to find it if you know what you're looking for.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
The Clerk's actual erasure-work happens on an isolated, air-gapped rig inside — the one piece of infrastructure in the district that never touches the open Wired, making it nearly unhackable from outside and nearly untraceable once a job is done.

Dead SIN-threads that pass through here occasionally resurface months later, reused, on someone else entirely — a quiet trade the corps would very much like to shut down if they could ever prove it existed.

#### Plot Hooks

1. A Ghost's Favor. The Clerk needs a SIN erased fast and clean for someone too important to be seen anywhere near Gallows End — and wants deniable contractors to escort them in without anyone, including the crew, learning who it is.

2. Yuen's Supply Problem. The templates Yuen Ratha has been feeding the Clerk are running dry, and Yuen wants the crew to help "acquire" fresh ones from a source that's very much still alive.

3. The Recycled Name. A SIN erased at the Deadline years ago has just resurfaced attached to someone with a very public, very dangerous profile — and the Clerk wants it quietly traced back before Sanctum's actuaries notice the anomaly and start asking who's really behind the mask.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The block feels wrong before you can say why. The neon is still there, technically — half-lit signs stuttering over shuttered storefronts, an old lumen-strip flickering its last colors into the wet — but something about the way sound behaves here sets your teeth on edge, a faint, wrong hush where the district's usual roar should be. This is the Quiet Fringe, and everyone who works Gallows End will tell you the same thing without being asked twice: don't be here after the lights change color.

No sky, of course — just the flat black underside of the level above, rain dragging down thin trails of dead neon until the street looks like it's bleeding out slowly. What passes for air-traffic up here has thinned to almost nothing: a courier-drone that strays too close to the block visibly corrects course and climbs, like something in its routing algorithm has learned to be afraid; a single stubborn ground-rig crosses the block at speed, headlights cutting twin tunnels through the rain, and does not stop for anything. The wall of sound every other block in the district takes for granted — voices, drone-whine, the hiss of rain on hot metal, the deep pump-heartbeat below — is all present here too, but thinned, delayed, wrong, like you're hearing it a half-second after it happened rather than as it happens.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text: Your comm implant hiccups once, quietly, as you cross into the block — a data packet arriving a fraction of a second late, or not quite arriving at all. Whatever's causing the dead-air creep here, it's spreading. Everyone agrees on that much. Nobody agrees on what it means.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Ondrej Fask** — a Meridian signal-tech obsessed with mapping the Fringe's expanding dead-air pocket, convinced it's an early warning of something structural, or worse, deliberate.

**The Watcher-Kids** — a loose crew of street children who dare each other to run through the Fringe after dark and always come back with a slightly different story about what they saw; harmless, or an early sign, depending who you ask.
