**Iolanthe Grey** — a technomancer squatting in one of the block's dead buildings, drawn here by something in the Wired's silence that the rest of the district can't perceive at all; half oracle, half hazard.

**Sergeant Okafor** — leads an Ironclad "signal integrity" patrol that sweeps the Fringe on an irregular schedule, officially to protect Meridian relay infrastructure, unofficially unnerved by every pass.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — unclaimed by any gang; nobody wants ground that swallows signal, but Ironclad maintains a nominal, reluctant patrol presence tied to nearby relay assets.

There's no real security here in the human sense — the danger isn't armed. Alert response, when it happens, is technical and confused: comms drop, drone escorts lose lock, and reinforcements sent to the Fringe often arrive later than their own dispatch timestamp says they should.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

This is dead-air creep made visible — a slowly, measurably expanding pocket where the Wired's overlay lags, glitches, or fails outright, spreading a few meters further each month by Ondrej Fask's careful measurements.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
Hackers who probe the edge of the pocket report the same disorienting symptom: their own tools respond a half-second slow, as if the Fringe itself has a kind of localized latency to reality.

Iolanthe Grey claims the silence isn't empty — that something in the Wired's underlying structure here has gone quiet on purpose, not broken, and that the difference matters enormously.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Fask's Measurements. Ondrej Fask needs deniable contractors to plant sensor relays deeper into the Fringe than he's willing to go himself, to prove — or disprove — that the dead-air pocket is accelerating.

2. The Watcher-Kids' Dare. One of the street children who ran into the Fringe after dark hasn't come back, and the others swear they saw someone waiting for her in the static. Her family wants her found before the search becomes a search for a body.

3. Iolanthe's Warning. The technomancer surfaces with a fragmentary, urgent message pulled from the Wired's silence — something about the Drop, or the Warrens, or both — and insists it has to reach the vigil-keepers or the Nyx Waystation before the next tide of dead-air creep arrives.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

Before you see the stalls you see the gear hanging off every available surface — coiled rope in a dozen grades, climbing harnesses salvaged and re-webbed a hundred times over, breather masks with their filters proudly displayed like trophies, lumen-flares bundled in dozens, grapples and winch-rigs and hand-crank descenders racked along improvised pegboards made from scavenged girder-mesh. This is the Rope Market, the last place in the district — in the Flats — where you can outfit yourself properly for a trip down, and everyone working here knows exactly what that means for the person buying.

The sky, as ever this low, doesn't exist — just the close dark underside of the level above, chemical rain sheeting down onto tarps stretched between stalls, catching neon-price-tags in cyan and gold that swim and blur in the wet. Traffic here skews low and heavy: a cargo-crawler backs in to make a bulk delivery of rope-stock, its horn blaring; a scrap-hauler idles nearby loaded with recovered descent gear bought back cheap off Warrens salvagers too spooked to go down again; overhead, a courier-drone or two threads between support cables strung for exactly that purpose, careful not to catch a line. Voices haggle hard and fast over rope-grade and rot-resistance, over which breather filters actually work below the Drop's dead-air line, over whose gear failed on whom and why — a market conversation that is, underneath the haggling, entirely about survival.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text: The vendor nearest you holds up two coils of rope, one twice the price of the other, and asks without much ceremony: how far down are you actually planning to go? It's not a sales question. It's the only question that matters here.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Big Halsey** — the market's most respected vendor, a former Warrens salvager himself who quit the deep runs after losing partners to bad gear and now sells only rope and rigging he'd trust with his own life.

**Petra Voss** (no relation to Digger) — runs the market's breather-mask stall, sourcing filters from a Caduceus supply contact and modifying them to handle the Warrens' worse air; expensive, but reliable.

**Nix** — a teenage runner who tests returned/salvaged gear before resale by using it herself on short drops, functionally the market's unofficial quality-control department and far too reckless about it.

**Corran Aldis** — a guild-clan negotiator who brokers bulk gear contracts for salvage crews and Barricade Row alike, keeping the market's prices from spiraling during gear shortages.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — an independent trade block, loosely protected by the vendors' mutual interest in staying open; too useful to every faction in the district to be worth attacking.

No dedicated muscle, but theft here is rare and punished informally and thoroughly — steal rope that might save someone's life and the whole market turns on you fast. Real trouble draws a crowd of armed customers before it draws any organized security.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

A brisk, practical trade-tag layer covers the market — gear reviews, failure reports, and a crowd-sourced (if grim) rating system for which rope grades have actually held up on real Warrens descents.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
A hacker digging deeper finds Nix's informal testing logs — an unofficial but startlingly accurate record of which gear survives the Drop's dead-air zone and which doesn't, information worth real money to serious salvage operations.

Big Halsey keeps no digital records at all by preference, trusting only his own memory and reputation — making him a rare, entirely un-hackable source of expertise in the district.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Bad Rope. A batch of counterfeit "premium" descent gear has entered the market, indistinguishable from Halsey's real stock until it fails under load. Someone's dying because of it, and Halsey wants the source found before it's his reputation, too.

2. Nix's Test Run. Nix has gone missing after a solo test-drop near the Drop's dead-air boundary, and the market's vendors — unofficially, off the books — want her found before her family or the vigil-keepers turn it into a bigger incident.

3. The Bulk Contract. Corran Aldis needs deniable escorts for a shipment of rope-stock coming up from a Cinderhold supply barge — cargo that a Barricade Row gang has decided it would rather take by force than pay for.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The bridge earns its name honestly — a long, narrow span of pale structural composite, salvaged and re-poured so many times over the centuries that it's gone the bleached white-grey of old bone, arching out over the chasm to a dead block on the far side that the district map simply marks as unclaimed. Cables strung with warning-flags and old prayer-ribbons run its length, snapping wet in a wind that comes up from below rather than from anywhere you'd expect wind to come from.

Above, no sky — only the black underside of the level overhead, rain coming down warm and chemical, sheeting off the bridge's low guardrails into the dark on either side, which is somehow worse than rain falling anywhere else in the district, because here you can watch it fall and never see it land. The vertical space over the bridge is thin but not empty: a Meridian relay-drone crosses at altitude, running lights blinking a steady rhythm; a hover-rig crew, paid well and nervous about it, ferries salvage across at low altitude rather than trust the span's old composite; on the bridge itself, foot traffic moves in a tight, purposeful line, nobody lingering, nobody looking down for longer than they have to. The sound here strips down to almost nothing but wind and rain and the groan of old structural composite settling under weight it was never rated for — the district's usual roar fading behind you with every step you take out over the gap.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text: Halfway across, if you stop — and something about the place makes you want to stop, just for a second — you'll notice the far side of the bridge is dark. Not unlit-dark. Dark like the lights over there stopped working for a reason nobody's fixed.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Toll-Keeper Bram** — collects an informal crossing toll at the bridge's near end, ostensibly to fund the bridge's upkeep, actually because he's the only one with the nerve to stay posted there full-time.

**The Far-Siders** — a small, insular community of squatters and burned-SINs who've made a life on the dead block across the bridge, distrustful of outsiders, protective of whatever they've built over there.

**Yusra Okonkwo-Vale** — a Ferrum structural engineer sent, against her own better judgment, to assess whether the bridge is salvageable or should be demolished before it fails and takes crossers with it.

**Wereraven scout Kiel** — uses the bridge as a regular crossing point on runs between the district's shrine and points further into the unclaimed dark; one of the few who crosses without paying Bram's toll, by mutual unspoken agreement.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — nominally unclaimed on both ends; Bram's toll is tolerated custom rather than enforced law, and the Far-Siders defend their block fiercely but only if actually threatened.

The bridge itself is the danger — structural failure is a constant, quietly acknowledged risk, and nobody in authority has inspected it properly in years. Social friction is low; physical risk is high. The real "security" is the Far-Siders' watchfulness over who actually makes it across.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The bridge registers on official Grid maps as condemned and closed, a designation everyone ignores because the alternative is a much longer, much more dangerous route around the chasm.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
The dead block on the far side is an actual overlay blank — no SIN-readers, no AR tags, nothing, which is either why the Far-Siders chose it or a result of choosing it, nobody's sure which came first.

A hacker checking the bridge's old structural sensors — if any still function — could get real warning of an imminent collapse; so far, nobody's bothered, which itself worries the few engineers who know the sensors exist.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Structural Assessment. Yusra Okonkwo-Vale needs escorts to complete her survey of the bridge without the Far-Siders — who correctly suspect Ferrum wants an excuse to demolish their only way home — running her off first.

2. The Toll Dispute. A Barricade Row gang has decided Bram's informal toll should belong to them, and the Far-Siders have made it clear that if the bridge falls under gang control, they'll cut the near-side cables themselves rather than allow it.

3. What Kiel Saw. The wereraven scout crossed the bridge on a routine run and came back changed — quiet, evasive, unwilling to say what she saw on the dead block beyond its usual dark. Someone needs to know if the Far-Siders are still themselves.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The Waystation used to be a freight depot, and Nyx never bothered changing much beyond the signage — a squat, reinforced block of a building with loading bays still scarred from decades of cargo traffic, now the literal last stop for supply, information, and deniability before the district runs out of ground entirely. Its cyan sigil, the cleanest, best-maintained light on this entire stretch of the Flats, burns steady over the main bay door like a promise nothing else down here can make.

There is no sky above the Waystation — just the low dark underside of the level overhead, chemical rain sheeting off the depot's reinforced roof in thick warm sheets, pooling silver-black in the loading yard where cargo-rigs idle in a neat, disciplined row that looks almost wrong this deep in the district, where nothing else runs on schedule. Overhead, the air stays busy in Nyx's usual efficient way: a tight formation of courier-drones lifts off on a fixed rotation, a hovercraft with cargo netting slung beneath it eases down onto the yard's landing cradle with practiced precision, and ground-rigs queue for loading with none of the chaos you'd expect from any other block this close to the edge. The sound here has its own particular texture — less the district's ragged wall of noise and more a controlled hum, forklifts and loading cranes and quiet, professional voices running manifest checks, the sub-bass foundation-thrum underneath it all like it's just another piece of machinery Nyx has learned to schedule around.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text: A quartermaster in a rain-slicked Nyx jacket clocks you before you've finished crossing the yard, already running your face against a manifest you didn't know you were on. Whatever you're here for — gear, information, a way down, a way to disappear — the Waystation has almost certainly handled it before, for someone else, last week.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Quartermaster Devra Solis** — runs day-to-day operations at the Waystation with brisk, unsentimental efficiency; answers to Nyx's regional cartel structure and treats every transaction, human or cargo, with the same professional detachment.

**"Ledger" Okonkwo** — the Waystation's information broker, trading intelligence on Warrens conditions, salvage routes, and gang movements to anyone Nyx has cleared to buy it.

**Big Tarn** — chief of the loading crew, an ex-dock worker built like a cargo-crawler himself, who personally vets every crew heading down through the Waystation's supply channel and has a good instinct for who's about to get themselves killed.

**The Courier Cell** — a tight rotation of Nyx-run drone and hover-pilots who make the actual final supply drops into Warrens contacts, seen by almost nobody, spoken of by everyone.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — solidly Nyx-controlled, the most orderly and well-defended point in the entire district by a wide margin, because Nyx cannot afford to lose its last supply artery into the deep.

Security is professional, not showy — quiet cameras, disciplined loading-crew muscle, and a standing arrangement with Barricade Row's gangs that keeps the Waystation off-limits to raiding in exchange for preferential trade terms. Real threats trigger a fast, coordinated Nyx response rather than a chaotic one; this is corporate-grade organized crime, not street chaos.

Alert here means Nyx's regional enforcers arrive, not just local muscle — a tier of consequence most of the district can't match.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Nyx runs its own clean, private overlay-cell here, similar in spirit to Cassavir's at the Switchboard — public AR shows only a generic freight-depot tag, while the real manifest data, cargo-tracking, and personnel logs stay locked inside Nyx's proprietary layer.

A hacker who breaches it finds the district's most valuable dataset: real-time Warrens supply-route intelligence, drop coordinates, and a running list of which Warrens contacts are still answering their comms — priceless, and exactly the kind of theft that ends careers permanently.

The Waystation also hosts one of Nyx's dead-drop relay nodes, feeding intelligence up into the wider Churn network in the Sinks — making it a quiet nerve-node in Nyx's larger operation, not just a local outpost.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The Last Run. Nyx needs a deniable crew to escort a critical supply shipment down past the Drop to a Warrens contact who's gone dangerously quiet — and wants to know why before writing the contact, and the shipment, off as a loss.

2. Ledger's Leverage. Ledger Okonkwo has been secretly selling Warrens intelligence to a Meridian buyer behind Nyx's back, and Quartermaster Solis wants proof before she decides whether to handle it quietly or make an example of him.

3. Supply Line Under Siege. A rival cartel faction is testing whether it can choke off the Waystation's supply route from the plaza side, betting Nyx won't risk open war this deep in the Flats to defend one outpost — and Solis needs to prove them catastrophically wrong.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The gate is the biggest single made-thing you have ever stood beneath. After a lifetime under the hive's low ceilings, the Marrow Gate opens upward — a canyon punched clean through the Reach's forty-foot outer wall of black iron, poured concrete, and heavy industrial plate. This is no simple door: it's a **massive** **hydraulic blast-gate**, twin armored slabs driven by external pistons and rams the size of buildings, flanked by gatehouse control-towers bristling with watch-platforms, floodlights, and the long silhouettes of mounted guns pointed outward. And it runs on a **timer** — the higher-ups inside the hive decide the hours, and when the great pistons sigh and the slabs grind shut, they shut for everyone. This is the only place in the Reach where the wall's job is written plain: not to keep people in, but to keep something out.

There is sky here — the real, terrible open sky, the first most Flats-born ever see — and it does not comfort. It hangs vast and bruise-colored over the poisoned scrubland, and on the horizon the black wall of the jungle stands like a second, living wall, its huge trees lost in mist. The rain that falls here is cleaner than the hive's and somehow worse for it. Traffic through the gate is slow, checked, and watched: caravans queue in the checkpoint lanes, salvagers haul their wasteland finds in for inspection, and everyone — everyone — is logged by the hard-eyed militia in Ranger field-coats before the inner door will cycle.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text: Above the main blast-door, someone has welded three words in salvaged letters, and they are the first law of Cinderhold: **THE GATE CLOSES AT DARK.**

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Ranger-Captain Cael Marrow** (human), "the Gate" — commands the gate and, through it, Cinderhold. Former Greenline Ranger, keeps a cold back-channel to Mama Cassavir inside the wall, and personally decides who passes. Fair, hard, and utterly unbribable on the one rule that matters: the gate closes at dark.

**Gate-Sergeant Odell Rusk** (Goliar) — Marrow's second, who runs the checkpoint lanes and the inspection crews; built like a blast-door himself and twice as immovable about paperwork.

**The Watch** — Marrow's ad-hoc militia of retired Rangers, Goliar kinship-crews, and hard cases with nowhere else to go; disciplined by frontier necessity, not corp pay.

#### Security

Zone: Cinderhold — outside all corp authority; Marrow's law is the only law, enforced by the Watch and the plain fact that everyone here needs the gate to hold.

Response is military, not corporate: the guns point outward at the wilds, but they turn inward fast for anyone who threatens the gate mechanism itself. The gate is Cinderhold's heart, and Marrow will spend lives to protect it.

Alert here is the wall alarm — the horn that means the treeline has moved. When it sounds, every other concern stops.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The Wired is thin and getting thinner the closer you stand to the outer door; past the threshold it fails entirely. Public AR shows Marrow's own hand-maintained gate-tag and a stark corruption-warning boundary.

Marrow's hardened comm-line to Cassavir terminates in a strongbox in the gatehouse — the single most secure node in Cinderhold.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
A technomancer near the open door feels the Wired go strange, Veil-corruption bleeding in from the wilds; the deep net out here does not speak in the hive's voice.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Passage. Getting a crew, a cargo, or a person through the Marrow Gate — in or out — against Marrow's judgment is a run in itself. He cannot be bribed, but he can be convinced, and he owes Cassavir. Worse if they arrive as the timer runs down and the great pistons are already sighing shut.

2. The Door That Wouldn't Close. Someone sabotages the hydraulic mechanism at dusk, jamming the slabs half-open, and the crew is the only hands near enough to repair the pistons — or hold the breach — before full-dark and whatever's already moving in the treeline.

3. The Timer Is Wrong. The hive's higher-ups shorten the gate's daily hours without warning, stranding a caravan — and the crew — outside as the slabs close. Someone uptower wanted them locked out. Finding out who, from the wrong side of a forty-foot wall at nightfall, is the run.

chunks.heading: Cindermarket
chunks.text: *The first market for wasteland goods — and the last honest prices in the Reach*

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

Cindermarket is what a bazaar looks like when no corp takes a cut. It sprawls in the gate's shadow, a chaos of scrap-stalls and tarp-roofed pitches built from the bones of dead cargo-containers, and it sells the things the hive pretends not to want: wasteland salvage, unlicensed grey-tech, foraged jungle reagents, and food that grew in real dirt under real sky. The air is woodsmoke and rust and the strange green tang of things carried in from outside the wall.

There's sky here, filtered through a patchwork of stretched tarps and net, and the light is all firelight and salvaged lumen-strings, warm where the hive is cold. Nobody scans your SIN — half the traders don't have one — and the deals are done face to face, in cash or barter or the sharp-eyed trust of people who all live one wall-breach away from the same death. It is the freest commerce in the Reach and the most dangerous, because everything here came from somewhere it maybe shouldn't have, and someone uptower always wants to know where.

A trader missing two fingers waves you toward a stall of jungle-foraged reagents, grinning like a man who has seen worse than you and lived to mark it up.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**"Two-Finger" Pell** (human) — Cindermarket's unofficial mayor-of-commerce, a wasteland trader who knows the price and provenance of everything that passes through; missing fingers to a jungle reagent that "seemed safe."

**Sesh Marn** (Corran) — a guild-clan fence who moves grey-tech and salvage between Cinderhold and Cassavir's network inside the wall; the market's link to the Flats' economy.

**The Foragers** — a loose brotherhood of wasteland scavengers who go out for the reagents, relics, and salvage the market sells; every one of them has a story about what chased them back.

#### Security

Zone: Cinderhold — self-policed by the traders and the Watch; theft is punished by the market itself, fast and without appeal, because the market only works on trust.

No formal security, but every trader is armed and the Watch patrols the edges. The real deterrent is exile: rob Cindermarket and you're put outside the wall at dusk.

Alert brings the Watch and, for a real threat, Marrow himself — the market is Cinderhold's economy and he protects it as such.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Thin and unreliable, like all of Cinderhold; most deals happen off the Wired entirely, in cash and hand-signal. Public AR shows a stale, corruption-flagged market tag.

Sesh Marn runs a small private mesh linking to Cassavir's network — the one reliable data-thread in the market, and a target for anyone wanting to map the Flats' salvage economy.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
Foraged jungle reagents sometimes carry faint Veil-corruption that fritzes AR near the stalls — a hacker's early warning that a "relic" is more cursed than it looks.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The Provenance Problem. Something in Cindermarket came from a place it shouldn't have — a corp lab, a sealed vault, a Veil-site — and a very serious buyer (or its very serious owner) is coming to collect. Pell wants the problem gone before it burns down his market.

2. The Forager's Map. A scavenger died in the market of jungle-fever, and left a map to where the good salvage is. Everyone wants it. It leads somewhere no one should go.

3. Kestrel's Clean Money. Kestrel Dynamics starts quietly buying up Cindermarket stalls through fronts, paying uptower prices — the soft first move of the Clean Route. Pell smells it and wants the crew to find out who's really behind the generosity.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The Lantern is the heart of Cinderhold — a great low hall of salvaged plate and wasteland timber built right against the gate's shadow, and it is the last place with a roof, a fire, and a door that locks before the wilds begin. Step out its rear door and the hive's ceiling is gone, replaced by the real open dark and, on the horizon, the black wall of primeval jungle where the huge trees stand like the pillars of a drowned cathedral and things move that the Flats has no names for.

Inside, though, it is warm — genuinely, gloriously warm, a real wood-and-scrap fire in a central pit, the smell of roasting meat that walked on its own legs this morning, and light from a hundred hanging lanterns because out here the Wired is thin and a lantern is a thing you can trust. The crowd is unlike any inside the wall: Greenline Rangers off the frontier, wasteland caravaneers, Cinderhold salvagers, hive-exiles who can never go back, and edgerunner crews staging for a job in the green. They drink hard and early, because everyone here knows the odds of the ones who go out the back door.

Behind the bar, a weathered man in a Ranger's old field-coat pours a measure, sets it down, and looks at you the way a man looks at weather coming in.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Ranger-Captain Cael Marrow** (human) — owns the Lantern and pours himself, because it's how he takes the measure of everyone passing his gate. (Full profile at the Marrow Gate.)

**Sister Ona** (Corran) — a Lamp-on-Ninth street-priest who runs a soup-line and vigil-lamp from a corner; Cinderhold's conscience and field-medic.

**"Longtooth" Garrik** (Goliar) — caravan-master and wasteland guide who knows the safe game-trails better than anyone still breathing; hires out to take crews into the near-wilds, on his terms.

**The Ones Who Came Back Wrong** (mixed species, Veil-touched) — survivors of the deep wilds, changed and haunted, whom Marrow shelters and who serve as the settlement's grimmest early warning of what the jungle is doing.

#### Security

Zone: Cinderhold — the settlement's safest room and its command post; held by Marrow's militia.

Marrow's law under his roof: no fighting, and the gate closes at full-dark for everyone. Break either and you're put outside to reconsider.

Alert is the wall alarm; when it sounds every drink hits the table and every hand finds a weapon.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Thin and flickering; Cinderhold runs on lanterns and Marrow's word because the Wired can't be trusted this far out.

Marrow's hardened back-channel to Cassavir lives in a strongbox behind the bar — the most valuable node in town.

A technomancer feels the Wired go strange out here, Veil-corruption whispering in the deep net in a voice that isn't the hive's.

#### Plot Hooks

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
1. The Back Door. Every expedition into the wilds begins here; Longtooth guides, and the question is whether the crew returns through the front door, gets carried in, or not at all.

2. The Wall Alarm. The horn sounds mid-drink, something huge has hit the Outer Wall, Cinderhold is undermanned, and Marrow is looking straight at the crew.

3. The Clean Route. Kestrel arrives at the Lantern with a contract that ends Cinderhold's poverty and its freedom in one signature; Marrow is the fulcrum and the crew's choices decide whether the last unowned ground stays unowned.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

Bolted to the outer face of the wall, higher than anything else in Cinderhold, the Greenline Post is the only structure here that looks built rather than scavenged — a hardened Verdant field-station of green-painted plate and long observation slits, its watch-mast crowned with sensor-dishes and a heavy spotting-scope that never stops sweeping the treeline. This is the Greenline Rangers' forward eye on the wilds, and from its platforms you can see what the gate is really up against: kilometers of poisoned scrub, then the jungle wall, then nothing anyone has mapped and lived to sell.

The sky is fully open here and the wind carries the green rot-and-blossom smell of the wilds straight up into your face. Rangers move with the unhurried economy of people who have learned that panic gets you killed out here; they log every movement in the treeline, every corruption-bloom, every big shape that surfaces and submerges again in the canopy. A Ranger at the scope tracks something you can't see, murmurs a bearing to a logger, and does not look away.

On the wall below the Post, a long tally-board records the things that have come out of the green this season. The numbers are not going down.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Ranger-Lieutenant Vesna Corr** (Elvani) — commands the Post, a Verdant career officer whose corporate poise sits oddly on the frontier; genuinely dedicated to the Rangers' mission even as she navigates Verdant's colder corporate interest in the wilds.

**Scout "Bramble" Teo** (wereraven Changer) — the Post's best long-range eyes, who reads the treeline through a scope from the watch-mast and has named half the apex-things on the tally-board.

**Old Hessing** (human) — the Post's naturalist-of-record, a half-mad former corp xenobiologist who catalogs the wilds' critters and will talk a crew's ear off about the Reach Behemoth if they let him.

#### Security

Zone: Cinderhold — Verdant-held ground, the one corp presence Cinderhold tolerates because the Rangers point their guns at the jungle, not the town.

Hardened and disciplined; the Post is built to survive a wall-breach and coordinate the Watch's defense. It answers to Verdant, but in practice to Marrow when the alarm sounds.

Alert here means a confirmed wilds incursion — the Post is where the wall alarm originates.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The Post runs the only robust Wired presence in Cinderhold — a hardened Verdant sensor-net feeding treeline data back up the wall. Public AR shows Verdant's official corruption-boundary and hazard tags.

The Post's real dataset — mapped incursion patterns, corruption-spread models, and everything Hessing has cataloged about the wilds — is the single best intelligence on what lies beyond the gate, and Verdant guards it.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
A technomancer patched into the Post's net can see the corruption bleeding into the Wired from the jungle in real time — beautiful, and a warning.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The Tally Grows. Incursions are up this season and Corr doesn't know why; she'll hire a deniable crew to escort a Ranger patrol into the near-wilds to find the cause before Verdant sends a "solution" that ends Cinderhold's freedom.

2. Hessing's Specimen. The old naturalist wants a live sample of something from the treeline, and offers the crew a fortune and a map. Bringing it back alive is worse than it sounds.

3. Verdant's Real Orders. Bramble intercepts a coded Verdant directive suggesting the corp's interest in the wilds is not conservation but resource — and that the Rangers, and Cinderhold, are expendable to it. Corr doesn't know. Should she?

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The Caravan Yard is Cinderhold's motor-heart: a wide scrap-paved lot just inside the Outer Wall, hard against the two great gates where the muddy expedition roads punch through and drive off into the jungle. This is where the wasteland haulers muster, refit, and pray before they take those churned-mud arteries out into the green. These are not hive-vehicles — they're armored, up-gunned, jury-welded beasts built to survive a run across the poisoned scrub and back, their hulls scarred by things with claws, their roof-mounts swiveling at every sound. The air is diesel-analog, hot metal, and the ozone bite of overworked shielding.

Under the open sky, crews load cargo and check weapons with the grim focus of people doing math on their own survival. A hauler noses in through the outer-wall gate trailing jungle-vine and a long score down its flank that wasn't there this morning; its crew climbs down one short of the number that left. Nobody comments. In the Caravan Yard, that's just Tuesday, and everyone's already counting whether they'll be the short crew next time.

A rigger with grease to the elbows kicks a tire the size of a person and tells you, without being asked, exactly how your plan to go outside is going to get you killed.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**"Axle" Doreth** (Corran) — the Yard's master rigger and unofficial dispatcher, who refits the haulers and decides, by refusing to work on a doomed rig, who's ready to go outside; her word can scrub a run.

**Convoy-Boss Tam Iker** (human) — runs the biggest caravan operation out of Cinderhold, moving salvage and passengers across the scrub for steep pay; brave, greedy, and running out of luck.

**The Wheelmen** (mixed species) — the drivers and gunners who make the wasteland runs, a superstitious, tight-knit fraternity who know that the difference between a legend and a bone-pile is one bad bearing.

#### Security

Zone: Cinderhold — Watch-patrolled, but mostly self-policed by the crews, who cannot afford sabotage or theft this close to a run.

The Yard is armed to the teeth by nature — every vehicle is a weapon — but violence here is bad for everyone's odds, so it's rare and settled fast.

Alert is the wall alarm; the Yard's guns become part of Cinderhold's defense, and a fueled convoy is both an asset and a bomb.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Thin; the Yard runs on Axle's private rig-mesh for vehicle telemetry and little else. Public AR shows a stale transit tag.

Every hauler carries logged run-data — routes, corruption-readings, where crews died — and Axle's archive of it is a priceless map of the near-wilds for anyone she trusts enough to share it.

Riggers report their vehicle AR going wrong the deeper into the scrub they drive; the telemetry archive is dotted with corruption-glitches that mark the truly bad ground.

#### Plot Hooks

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
1. The Run That Needs a Crew. Tam Iker has a lucrative, dangerous run into the near-wilds and is one crew short after his last trip. The pay is real. So are the odds.

2. Sabotage in the Yard. Someone is quietly damaging rigs bound for a specific destination — someone who doesn't want anyone reaching it. Axle wants it stopped before a doctored hauler kills a crew in the scrub.

3. The Vehicle That Came Back Empty. A hauler rolls in on autopilot, crew gone, cargo intact, and a corruption-scored recording in its logs that no one wants to watch twice. What happened to them is out there still.

chunks.heading: The Outer Wall
chunks.text: *Cinderhold's ring of scavenged iron — the town's own defiance of the green dark*

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

Where the hive has its towering forty-foot rampart, Cinderhold has the Outer Wall — lower, rougher, but no joke: a serious defensive ring welded together from everything the wasteland gives up. Poured-concrete slabs. Shipping-container hulls stacked and filled. Sheet-metal plate, industrial girders, salvaged blast-panels off dead machinery, all lashed and welded into a continuous rampart with a fighting-walk along its top and its own smaller gates where the expedition roads punch through. It is not the hive's monolith, and everyone in Cinderhold knows it: the Outer Wall doesn't always stop what comes out of the green so much as slow it down long enough for the Watch to answer the alarm. It is a wall built of scavenged industry and the understanding that some night it won't be enough.

The sky is fully open along the wall-walk, and the wind off the scrub carries the smell of the jungle — wet green rot, strange blossom, and under it something animal and wrong. Watch-fires burn at intervals along the parapet, and the Watch walk their rounds with eyes fixed outward, on the treeline, always the treeline. In the mud beyond the ditch, you can see the tracks: three-toed, enormous, pressed deep, coming closer to the wall each season than the last.

A Watch-woman hands you a length of pipe without a word and nods toward the dark. Everyone stands a wall-shift in Cinderhold. Even guests. Especially guests.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Watch-Captain Bel Suri** (Goliar) — commands the Outer Wall defense under Marrow, an unflappable veteran who has held the wall through more bad nights than she'll admit and organizes every able body — including guests — into the defense.

**"Ditch" Kova** (Mutant) — the wall's forward scout and trap-layer, Veil-touched from too long in the scrub, who lays the pit-traps and tripline-alarms beyond the wall and reads the tracks better than anyone.

**The Wall-Shift** (everyone) — Cinderhold has no standing army large enough, so every resident and guest stands watch; the Outer Wall is defended by whoever is closest when the horn sounds.

#### Security

Zone: Cinderhold — the town's literal edge; the Outer Wall is the security, backed by the Watch and the Greenline Post's early warning.

Defense is total and communal: the wall alarm turns every citizen into a defender, and Bel Suri's drills mean even a scratch crew knows their station.

Alert is, definitionally, the wall alarm — this is where it's answered, in pipe and gun and fire.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Effectively dead along the outer wall-walk; the Wired fails at the corruption boundary and the Outer Wall sits right on it. Warning-tags flicker and die.

Ditch Kova's tripline-alarm network is the only "tech" that works reliably out here — a low-tech mesh of physical alarms precisely because the Wired can't be trusted.

A technomancer on the wall at night feels the deep-net corruption at its strongest anywhere in the Reach; some who've reached toward it have not come all the way back.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Plot Hooks

1. Wall-Shift. The simplest hook in Cinderhold: the crew stands a watch, the horn sounds, and something out of the Critters chapter comes over the ditch. Survive till dawn.

2. The Weak Point. Ditch Kova has found a stretch of Outer Wall that won't hold another season, and the industrial salvage to shore it up is outside, in the scrub, where the tracks lead. Someone has to go get it.

3. Something Is Testing the Wall. The incursions aren't random — something intelligent is probing the Outer Wall for its weak point, the same stretch each night, learning. Bel Suri needs the crew to find out what, before it finds the gap first.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The Burn-Yard is where Cinderhold's people are made. It's a stark plaza just inside the gate, dominated by a single scarred iron brazier where the newly-arrived burn what's left of their hive identity — the SIN-chips, the corp-IDs, the tracking-tags of a life the wall has ended. To come to Cinderhold is to become SIN-less on purpose, and the Burn-Yard is where that choice gets made real, in fire, in front of witnesses, one identity at a time.

Under the open sky, the brazier throws warm light on a crowd that is always part solemn, part wary: exiles saying goodbye to who they were, Cinderhold-born watching to see who the newcomers really are, and the Watch making quiet note of every face. The smell is scorched polymer and hot metal and the particular acrid tang of a corp-chip dying. Someone is always crying, and someone is always laughing, and in Cinderhold those are frequently the same person.

An old woman tending the brazier holds out a set of tongs and asks you, without judgment, whether you've come to burn something — because everyone who stays here eventually does.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Mother Sabine** (Revenant) — keeper of the Burn-Yard brazier, an embodied-dead woman who has watched a thousand identities die into the fire and treats each with grave dignity; the closest thing Cinderhold has to a priest of its own founding rite.

**"Ledger" Tomas** (human) — a former corp records-clerk who fled with a head full of dangerous data and now helps newcomers scrub their old lives clean; knows exactly how hard the hive looks for the ones who run.

**The Newly-Burned** (any species) — a rotating population of raw exiles, some running from debt, some from crime, some from things worse; each one a potential ally, informant, or complication the crew can adopt.

#### Security

Zone: Cinderhold — Watch-observed, because the Burn-Yard is where the hive's problems walk in and Marrow wants to know which ones will become Cinderhold's problems.

Peaceful by custom — violence at the brazier is taboo — but heavily watched; a burned SIN doesn't stop a determined corp skip-tracer from following someone here.

Alert is rare, but the Burn-Yard is the first place a corp extraction team would strike if they came for a specific exile.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

A strange dead-spot by design: the brazier's proximity and Cinderhold's thin Wired mean burned identities genuinely vanish from the net here, which is the whole point. Public AR shows only Sabine's austere memorial tag.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
The moment of the burn is a small Wired event — a SIN winking out — that a watching hacker (or corp tracer) can catch if they're fast, making the Burn-Yard a paradoxical honeypot for the very people it's meant to hide.

Ledger Tomas runs a quiet scrubbing-service on a private mesh, erasing the digital trails the fire can't reach.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The Tracer at the Brazier. A corp skip-tracer has followed a newcomer to the Burn-Yard and is waiting for the burn to confirm the target before extraction. Sabine won't allow violence at her fire — so the crew has to handle it another way, fast.

2. What Tomas Knows. Ledger Tomas fled with corp data valuable enough to kill for, and the corp has finally located him in Cinderhold. He'll trade everything he knows for protection — and everything he knows is a campaign's worth of leverage.

3. The One Who Won't Burn. A newcomer refuses to burn their SIN, and Marrow won't let them stay armed with a live tracking-chip inside his wall. Their reason for keeping it is either the crew's next job or the reason the corp is already coming.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The Chapel of Ash is the only building in Cinderhold that anyone bothered to make beautiful, and they did it with nothing — a small hall of salvaged glass and wasteland timber, its windows glazed with melted-down bottle-glass so the watch-fires outside throw fractured color across the floor. It's a Lamp-on-Ninth outpost, the frontier edge of the Flats' street-faith, and it exists for a simple reason: people who live one wall-breach from death need somewhere to put their fear.

Under a roof pieced from a hundred salvaged panels, the open sky shows through the gaps like stars, and a single great lamp burns at the altar — never extinguished, tended in shifts, a deliberate defiance of the dark that presses on Cinderhold from every side. The air is candle-smoke, incense improvised from jungle-blossom, and the low murmur of people praying in six tongues to whatever they still believe watches over the last unowned ground. Even the faithless come here; in Cinderhold, the Chapel is where you go to not be alone with what's outside.

A priest in a patched vestment tends the great lamp and, without turning, says you're welcome to sit — the lamp doesn't ask what anyone believes, only that they help keep it lit.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Father Kell** (human) — the Chapel's keeper, a Lamp-on-Ninth street-priest who came to the frontier to tend the faith at its hardest edge; a genuine source of real, costly faith in a place that badly needs it, and Sister Ona's superior in the order.

**The Lamp-Wardens** (mixed species) — volunteers who tend the great lamp in shifts, a cross-section of Cinderhold united by the one job everyone agrees matters; the lamp has not gone out in living memory.

**"The Returned"** (a Veil-touched Mutant) — a survivor of the deep wilds who found faith out there in the green dark and came back changed, now half-oracle, half-warning, whose corruption-tinged visions of the jungle Father Kell isn't sure are madness or prophecy.

#### Security

Zone: Cinderhold — sanctuary by custom; the Chapel is neutral ground where even enemies may sit, and violating it is the deepest taboo in town.

Unarmed and unguarded, protected only by the community's respect — which, in Cinderhold, is stronger than most walls.

Alert almost never touches the Chapel directly; when the wall alarm sounds, it becomes the shelter for those who can't fight and the aid-station for those who did.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Deliberately Wired-dark; Father Kell keeps the Chapel off the net so that what's said here stays here. Public AR shows only a modest lamp-sigil.

A technomancer who reaches into the Wired from the Chapel finds it eerily quiet — a calm pocket in the corruption-frayed edge of the net, which some read as coincidence and some as something more.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
"The Returned" speaks of the Wired and the Veil as one thing out in the jungle, and their corruption-visions occasionally contain data no one in Cinderhold should have — an unexplained, unnerving signal.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The Returned's Vision. The Veil-touched oracle describes, in fevered detail, something coming out of the jungle — and the details are too specific to dismiss. Father Kell asks the crew to find out whether it's prophecy or a fever, before the wall alarm proves which.

2. Sanctuary. Someone the crew is chasing — or protecting — claims sanctuary in the Chapel, and Cinderhold's deepest taboo now stands between the crew and their job. Father Kell will not break it. What will they?

3. Keep the Lamp Lit. The great lamp's fuel is running out, the resupply is trapped outside the wall, and Cinderhold has quietly decided that if the lamp goes dark, the town's nerve goes with it. It's a small errand with the whole settlement's morale riding on it.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The Rustworks never sleeps, because the wall never stops needing repair. It's Cinderhold's foundry and fabrication yard, a clangorous sprawl of salvaged furnaces, jury-rigged presses, and scrap-sorting bays built against the inner face of the Outer Wall, and it turns the wasteland's endless junk into the town's endless needs: wall-plate, weapons, vehicle parts, tools, and the welded girders and blast-panels that are, quite literally, all that stands between Cinderhold and the green. The heat hits you from thirty meters out.

Under a roof of corrugated salvage, forge-light pools orange and fierce, and the open sky glows sullen through the smoke-vents above. The sound is a physical thing — hammer on plate, the shriek of cutting, the roar of the furnaces — layered over the sub-bass thrum of the great presses. Sparks fountain. Workers in scorched leathers move with the wary economy of people who handle molten metal for a living and have no attention to spare for yours. Everything here is being turned into something the wall will need before dawn.

A soot-black smith looks up from a length of glowing rebar, sizes up your gear in one glance, and asks if you're here to fix something or break something — because the Rustworks does a brisk trade in both.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Foreman Grud** (Goliar) — runs the Rustworks with a bellow and an unerring eye for metal, prioritizing wall-repair above all else; the person who decides whether the crew's job gets fabrication time or waits behind the Outer Wall's endless needs.

**"Spark" Ivane** (Corran) — the Works' master weaponsmith and grey-tech tinkerer, who builds and modifies the guns that hold the wall and will craft or repair a crew's gear for the right price or the right favor.

**The Salvage Crews** (mixed species) — the sorters and scrappers who feed the furnaces, who see everything that comes in from the wasteland first and know which "junk" is actually something dangerous, valuable, or cursed.

#### Security

Zone: Cinderhold — Watch-linked, because the Rustworks makes the wall's weapons and its loss would doom the town; guarded accordingly.

The Works is dangerous by nature — molten metal, presses, furnaces — and self-policed by workers who know a moment's carelessness kills; deliberate trouble is dealt with by Grud personally.

Alert means the Works shifts instantly to war-production and its furnaces become part of the wall's last-ditch defense.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Thin, and drowned in electromagnetic noise from the furnaces and presses; the Wired barely functions inside the Works. Public AR shows a stale industrial tag.

Spark Ivane keeps a private fabrication-mesh with schematics for every weapon and wall-component Cinderhold uses — a small but critical dataset for anyone wanting to arm, or disarm, the town.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
The salvage crews sometimes feed Veil-corrupted metal into the furnaces by accident, producing brief, alarming Wired-glitches that Spark has learned to recognize as a warning to pull the batch.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Behind the Wall's Needs. The crew needs something fabricated — a part, a weapon, a tool for the job — but Grud won't bump wall-repair for anyone. Getting to the front of the line means solving one of the Works' problems first.

2. Spark's Special Order. Someone commissioned a weapon from Spark that shouldn't exist in Cinderhold — something meant for people, not critters. She's uneasy about the buyer and wants the crew to find out what it's really for.

3. The Cursed Batch. A shipment of "clean" salvage turns out to be Veil-corrupted, and it's already in the furnace-cycle; if it goes into the wall-plate, the corruption goes into the Outer Wall itself. The Works needs it found and pulled before it becomes part of the wall.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The Overlook is the highest point in Cinderhold that isn't the gate itself — a salvaged watch-platform bolted to the tallest surviving section of old wall, reached by a switchback of welded ladders, and it exists for one purpose: to look out. From up here the whole grim geography lays itself bare. Directly below, Cinderhold's scrap-roofs huddle against the Outer Wall. Beyond the wall, the poisoned scrubland runs gray and dead to the horizon. And past that, filling half the world, the primeval jungle — huge trees like green thunderheads, mist pooling in the ravines, and the winding black thread of a river that no one in Cinderhold has followed to its end and returned.

The sky is enormous here, and empty of the hive's comforting ceiling, and the wind never stops. In the far distance, when the mist parts, you can sometimes see them: shapes moving above the canopy, or the slow bulk of something vast pushing through the trees, throwing up a wake of startled birds. The Overlook is where Cinderhold reckons with its future, because everyone who climbs up here understands the same thing at the same moment — the Wild Lands are huge, and the town is very, very small.

A lone watcher shares the platform, spotting-scope trained on the treeline, and doesn't lower it as they say: "First time seeing it? Everybody's quiet, the first time."

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**The Watcher** (rotating, any species) — whoever holds the Overlook shift, a quiet, thousand-yard-stare posting that Cinderhold treats as half-duty, half-meditation; the Watchers are the town's dreamers, mystics, and the ones who've decided to face the future head-on.

**Cartographer Nyle** (Elvani) — a Verdant-trained mapmaker who defected to Cinderhold and now works to chart the near-wilds from observation and caravan-data, building the first real map of the Wild Lands to come; brilliant, obsessive, and short on data he can only get by going out.

**"Skyeye" Bram** (wereraven Changer) — a Changer scout who flies short reconnaissance loops beyond the wall in raven-form, the only Cinderholder who regularly sees the near-jungle from above and comes back; his sightings feed both the Rangers and Nyle's map.

#### Security

Zone: Cinderhold — lightly held; the Overlook's value is observation, not defense, though it feeds the wall alarm alongside the Greenline Post.

Exposed and high, the Overlook is safe from ground threats but vulnerable to anything that flies — and some things out there do; watchers keep one eye on the sky as well as the treeline.

Alert originates here as often as at the Post; the Overlook is frequently first to see a big incursion cross the scrub.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The Wired is nearly gone at this altitude and this close to the boundary; the Overlook runs on optics and Skyeye's own eyes precisely because the net can't be trusted here.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
Nyle's growing map — part data, part observation, part educated guess — is the single most valuable document about the Wild Lands in existence, and the seed of the eventual Wild Lands expansion; every faction that wants the wilds wants a copy.

A technomancer who reaches out from the Overlook toward the jungle touches the rawest edge of the Veil-corruption in the Wired — and more than one has reported the deep net seeming to look back.

#### Plot Hooks

1. Nyle's Map. The cartographer will pay well for firsthand data from specific points in the near-wilds — a river-bend, a ruin, a corruption-bloom — turning the crew into the surveyors of the Wild Lands to come. Each expedition fills in one more terrifying blank.

2. What Skyeye Saw. The Changer scout returns from a recon loop shaken, describing something new beyond the treeline — a structure, a migration, a threat — that changes what Cinderhold thought it knew about the wilds. Confirming it means going out.

3. The Long View. From the Overlook, an observant crew can see the shape of the whole campaign's future — the routes into the wilds, the corruption spreading, the corps circling Cinderhold. This is the POI that plants the Wild Lands hook and lets a Director foreshadow everything to come.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

You don't so much find the Dead Line as let the Switchboard's crowd deposit you at its door. It's built into the shell of a decommissioned signal-relay station not forty meters off Cassavir's booth — close enough that the old woman's runners use it as a waiting room, close enough that when a deal goes live you can be at her switchgear before the message stops blinking. The sign is a length of genuine dead phone-line, coiled into a noose and strung with amber lumen-wire, humming that one warm note over the door.

Inside, there is no sky — there never is, this low — only the relay station's old cable-vaulted ceiling, close and black, sweating the warm chemical rain down the dead conduit-runs so the whole bar shines faintly wet. But it's warm here, and quiet in the way the Flats almost never lets you have: the sound-wall of the concourse drops to a murmur the moment the door seals, swallowed by decades of acoustic dead-panelling the relay techs bolted up a thousand years ago. Salvaged booth-lights pool amber and low. A wall of dead switchboard jacks behind the bar has been rewired into taps. Courier-drones can't come inside — house rule, enforced — so for once nothing is watching you from the ceiling.

The barkeep is a broad Corran woman with forearms like cable-bundles and a memory like a ledger, and she has already set down the drink you didn't order yet, because you look like the last three crews who came in off a hard run and she was right about all of them.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Ferra Vantoll** (Corran) — the barkeep and owner, a former guild-clan foreman who took the relay-shell as payment for a debt no one will name. She is Cassavir's in the way water is the river's: not employed, but aligned. She keeps the peace, keeps the tabs, and keeps her mouth shut, and she has thrown out corp-scouts twice her size for asking the wrong question.

**"Splice" Odarum** (wererat Changer) — a twitchy off-books decker who holds the back booth as an office, sells burner-SINs and clean comm-lines, and functions as the bar's unofficial fixer-below-the-fixer for jobs too small to bother Cassavir with.

**Tover "Two-Line" Vask** (Corran) — Cassavir's floor-runner (see the Switchboard) drinks here between errands; if the crew is owed a message, it arrives through him, at this bar, over a drink.

**The Regulars** — a rotating table of burned-out edgerunners who will trade a war-story for a round and, occasionally, a genuinely useful warning about who's hiring and who's a trap.

#### The Menu (What Nuyen Buys at the Bar)

**"Dead Air"** — house rotgut cut with synth-citrus; ¥4. The drink Ferra sets down unbidden.

**Relay Black** — real (allegedly) coffee, thick enough to stand a spoon in; ¥6. Standard for a crew about to run.

**Corran Ferment** — a sour guild-clan grain-beer, warm, communal; ¥5 the jug.

**The Long-Distance** — top-shelf smuggled Spire liquor, poured only for crews who just got paid; ¥40.

**Ferra's Plate** — whatever the kitchen has: usually cargo-noodle, grey-protein skewers, real onion if you're lucky; ¥8.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
**Booth rental (back room, sound-dead, drone-proof)** — ¥50 the hour, ¥30 more if you want Ferra to forget you were there.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — under Cassavir's peace by extension. No gang claims it because everyone's deals route through here and no one wants to be the crew that soured Ferra.

No visible guns; Ferra's rule is the rule. Drawing steel in the Dead Line gets you barred from the Switchboard itself — a social death sentence in the Flats — before it gets you shot. Two of the Regulars are Ironclad-trained and slow to move, exactly like Cassavir's porters.

Alert here is social and instant: the room goes silent, Ferra makes one call, and the concourse outside closes to you.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The bar sits in a genuine **dead-air pocket** — the old relay's shielding kills most AR and comms inside, which is precisely why runners love it and corp-scouts hate it. Public overlay shows only a faded "DECOMMISSIONED — MERIDIAN SIGNAL" tag.

Splice runs a tiny private mesh from the back booth for those who know the handshake; a hacker who digs finds it, and finds it politely booby-trapped.

Cassavir's deal-threads terminate a node here — this is one of the three places in the Flats where a message from the old woman can physically reach you when the Wired can't.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The Waiting Room. The crew is nursing drinks when Two-Line Vask slides in: Cassavir has a job, right now, and it starts the moment they walk out the door. The Dead Line is where most sessions can begin.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
2. Splice's Small Problem. Splice sold a burner-SIN to the wrong buyer and now a Sanctum skip-tracer is sitting three stools down pretending to drink. He'll pay the crew in clean comm-lines to make the problem leave without a scene Ferra would blame him for.

3. Ferra's Debt. The unnamed debt that bought Ferra the relay-shell comes calling — a Nyx lieutenant wants the dead-air pocket as a drop-node and won't take no. If Ferra loses the bar, the crew loses their waiting room, and Cassavir loses a terminal. She won't ask for help. She shouldn't have to.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

The line starts three lanes out, and it is the best-dressed crowd you will ever see this deep. The Velvet Stair is Obsidian's flag planted in the Flats — a genuine uptower pleasure-house dropped into the underlevels like a jewel into mud, and it wants you to feel the difference. The rain still falls here, because there is no sky here either, but Obsidian has strung a canopy of warm gold heat-lamps over the entrance so the chemical drizzle turns to steam before it touches the clientele, and the effect is deliberate: even the weather is better on Obsidian's threshold.

Above, the traffic is corp-grade — a sleek private hovercab settles onto a reserved cradle, disgorging Grid-dwellers slumming for the night, while the district's usual courier-drone chaos is held back by a soft-glowing exclusion-boundary Obsidian pays Meridian to enforce. Inside the doors, the sound-wall doesn't stop so much as transform: the concourse roar becomes a low, engineered warmth of music tuned just beneath the pulse, and the light goes from neon-riot to a single seductive obsidian-and-violet glow that makes everyone look like the best version of themselves.

A hostess who is too beautiful to be an accident — Elvani, of course, they always are — reads your Lifestyle off your clothes in half a second and decides, with a smile that costs Obsidian money to train, exactly how much of the Stair you are going to be allowed to see tonight.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Madame Sévrine Cael** (Elvani) — the Stair's manager, an Obsidian company officer with three centuries' patience compressed into flawless hospitality. She remembers every face, every tab, every weakness, and files all three. She sells pleasure and buys secrets, and the second trade is the real business.

**Doss** (Goliar) — the door. Seven feet of engineered muscle in a tailored coat, unfailingly polite until the exact instant he isn't. He has never had to hit anyone twice.

**"Kitten"** (human, chromed) — a simsense dream-hostess and one of Sévrine's best listeners; every pillow-side confession she hears becomes a line in Obsidian's ledger. She'd like to stop. She can't afford to.

**The Dreamers** — the high-end simsense clientele in the upper booths, chasing tailored experiences most of the Flats will never afford; some are Grid tourists, some are addicts, one of them is always someone important pretending not to be.

#### The Menu (What Nuyen Buys — Obsidian Takes Chip Only, Never Cash)

**The House Pour** — engineered cocktails keyed to your mood-read; ¥25 and up.

**A Clean Dream** — licensed simsense, an hour of curated experience, safe and legal-ish; ¥120.

**The Velvet Hour** — private dream-booth, hostess-guided, discretion included; ¥400.

**Designer Highs** — Obsidian's own tailored intoxicants, the safest illegal thing you can put in your body; ¥60 the dose.

**The Back Menu** (invitation only) — BTL, deep-immersion illicit simsense, and appetites the front room doesn't list; priced in favors as often as nuyen.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
**A Conversation With Sévrine** — free. It is never free.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — but a corporate island. Obsidian holds the Stair and two lanes around it as effective extraterritorial ground; the district's usual rules stop at the heat-lamp canopy.

Response is layered and quiet: Doss at the door, unseen Ironclad contractors on retainer, and Obsidian's real deterrent — the threat of being cut off, blacklisted from the one clean pleasure in the Flats. Physical violence is answered fast and professionally, but the Stair prefers you never see it.

Alert brings Obsidian corporate security, not street muscle — a serious escalation most crews can't afford to provoke.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The public layer is gorgeous and total — Obsidian floods the entrance with the richest, most seductive AR in the district, all of it advertising, all of it tracking. Every guest is logged, scored, and filed the moment they cross the boundary.

Beneath it, a hacker finds Obsidian's true product: the **confession-vault**, an encrypted archive of everything every hostess has ever heard. It is one of the most valuable and most dangerous datasets in the Flats, and breaking it is a campaign-defining score.

The dream-booths run on a closed simsense-net; a technomancer who slips into it can ride a client's tailored dream — or trap them in one.

#### Plot Hooks

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
1. The Confession-Vault. Someone — a rival corp, a blackmailed official, a jilted lover — will pay enormously to steal, copy, or erase a specific entry in Sévrine's vault. Getting in means getting close to Sévrine, who is nobody's fool.

2. The Dreamer Who Won't Wake. A high-value client has been in a Velvet Hour booth for two days and Obsidian can't rouse him without admitting the booth did it. Sévrine hires the crew, quietly, to extract him — and the reason he won't wake is worse than an overdose.

3. Cut Off. A crew member runs up a debt they can't pay and Obsidian offers the classic bargain: work off the tab, in favors, forever. The Stair is how Obsidian turns edgerunners into assets, one clean dream at a time.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

Every district has a bar like the Grind, and pretending otherwise is how tourists get rolled. It's a low, wide, smoke-yellow room wedged under a load-bearing pylon where three lanes of the Flats bleed together, and it has exactly one virtue: it does not care who you are. No SIN-reader at the door. No dress code but "conscious." No music but whatever the ancient wall-speaker is mangling tonight and the low grind of the pylon's stress-bearings overhead, which is where the place got its name.

There is no sky, only the pylon's vast underside dripping rust-brown rain into buckets the staff never empty, and the light is the color of a dying battery — sodium-yellow, flickering, merciful, because at this wattage you can't see the state of the floor or the state of the other patrons. Overhead traffic doesn't bother with the Grind; the drones don't fly this low under the pylon and the cabs won't stop here, which is exactly the point. The only things that come to the Grind are the things that walk in.

The bartender is a Revenant — grey-skinned, patient, unbothered by time — and he has been pouring here longer than anyone can remember, which in a place this rough is its own kind of reference. He pours, he listens, and he says nothing, ever, and that silence is the most valuable thing on the menu.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Grale** (Revenant) — the bartender and closest thing the Grind has to law. The embodied dead unsettle the tidy uptower world, but down here Grale's changelessness is a comfort: he has seen every kind of trouble walk in and walk out or get carried out, and he keeps no side but the bar's.

**"Cinder" Mok** (Mutant) — a wasteland-scarred information-seller who works the Grind's corner table, trading rumors out of Cinderhold and the outer gate; the only person here who's been outside the wall and come back, and he'll remind you of it for a drink.

**Vess Karr** (human) — a washed-out ex-Ironclad who drinks alone and will, three drinks in, either sell you the best combat advice in the district or start the fight that gets everyone barred.

**The Barred Table** — a corner where crews the rest of the Flats won't touch drink together in wary truce; if the crew needs muscle nobody else will hire, it's sitting right there, dangerous and cheap.

#### The Menu (Cash Only; the Chip-Reader "Broke" Years Ago)

**The Grind** — whatever's in the tank, poured until you stop asking what it is; ¥2.

**Battery Acid** — the Grind, but they charge it and add a slice of something citrus-adjacent; ¥3.

**Wasteland Brew** — Cinder's own import, fermented outside the wall, tastes like green corruption and courage; ¥5, and Grale won't vouch for it.

**The Quiet** — a booth in the back and Grale's guaranteed silence; ¥10, no questions, no memory.

**Food** — there is a pot. It is always the same pot. It is ¥3 and it has never once made anyone sick, which is a miracle nobody examines.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Security

Zone: Flats — genuinely lawless, self-policed by Grale's presence and the mutual understanding that the Grind only works if it stays neutral ground.

No guns drawn is the only rule, and it's enforced by consensus: pull steel in the Grind and every hard case in the room, including the Barred Table, has reason to end you before you become their problem. Grale keeps a shotgun no one has ever seen him reach for.

No Alert response of any kind — nobody's coming. That's the danger and the appeal. What happens in the Grind gets settled in the Grind.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

Near-total dead-air, and not by design — the Grind is just too far under the pylon and too poor to matter, so the Wired barely renders it. Public AR shows a decades-stale tag and nothing else.

This makes the Grind a natural low-tech meeting ground: no logging, no tracking, no ad-noise. A hacker finds almost nothing, because there's almost nothing here to find, which is itself a kind of privacy money can't buy uptower.

Cinder Mok sells the one valuable data-stream in the room: word-of-mouth intelligence from outside the wall, unlogged and unverifiable, worth everything or nothing.

#### Plot Hooks

1. The Man From Outside. Cinder Mok has seen something in the wilds beyond Cinderhold that has him too scared to go back — and too broke to stay. He'll sell the crew the location for a fortune, and the location is where the campaign's next act lives.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
2. Vess's Last Fight. The ex-Ironclad has a name, a grudge, and a corp bounty on the man who burned his old unit. He wants a crew. He is either the best lead the crew will get this month or the fastest way to die, and telling the difference is the job.

3. Neutral Ground No More. A gang decides the Grind's dead-air pocket is too useful to leave neutral and moves to claim it. If they succeed, the Flats loses its one truly open table — and every crew that ever needed the Grind now owes the wrong people.

chunks.heading: The Choir Room
chunks.text: *The night-market's underground pulse — where the Flats dances so it doesn't scream*

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

You feel it in the floor before you find the door — a sub-bass pulse coming up through the soles of your boots, threading through the Neon Shambles' medieval tangle of market-lanes until you follow it down a stairwell that shouldn't lead anywhere and it opens into sound. The Choir Room is a converted cistern, a vast domed drum of a space three levels below the night-market, and the entire Flats' worth of people who can't afford the Velvet Stair come here to lose themselves instead.

There is no sky — there is the cistern's great curved ceiling, streaming condensation and reclaimed rain down the old overflow-channels so the walls themselves seem to weep in time with the music, every drop lit by a storm of salvaged holo-projectors throwing pink and cyan and gold across a thousand moving bodies. No air-traffic reaches this deep; the only things in the air are the light, the heat, and the smell of a crowd that has been dancing since the last shift ended. The music is not tuned beneath the pulse like Obsidian's — it is the pulse, a live technomancer-driven set that reads the room's mood off the Wired and answers it, so the whole crowd moves as one enormous animal.

Somewhere on a scaffold-stage above the churn, a figure with wires running from their temples to the sound-rig lifts a hand, and the entire cistern inhales with them.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Mira "The Choir" Sen** (Technomancer, human) — the resident set-runner, who mixes live by riding the crowd's emotional signature off the Wired and feeding it back as sound. She is a genuine folk-hero of the Flats' night-culture and, quietly, one of the best informal read-the-room intelligence assets alive — she can feel when a room turns.

**Bexx** (wereraven Changer) — the door and the lookout, perched literally above the entrance stair, who reads every face coming down and caws a coded warning to the floor if it's the wrong one.

**The Dust Brothers** (two Corran cousins) — the dealers who work the edges, selling club-grade designer highs cut cheaper and rougher than Obsidian's; tolerated because they keep the doses survivable and the overdoses out of the Choir Room's reputation.

**Sanctum's Eyes** — somewhere in the crowd, always, at least one insurance-actuarial watcher counting bodies and calculating the room's illegal occupancy against the day they decide to raid it.

#### The Menu (Chip or Cash; the Bar Is a Converted Overflow-Pipe)

**Cistern Water** — the house drink, luminous and cheap, glows under the holos; ¥3.

**The Drop** — a stronger pour timed to the set's big moments; ¥6.

**Dust** (from the Brothers, off-menu) — club-grade designer high, ¥15 the dose, "survivable, mostly."

**A Word With The Choir** — access to Mira between sets, worth more than any drink; priced in favors, information, or genuine loyalty, never nuyen.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
**The Cool-Down Loft** — a quieter mezzanine above the churn for deals, recovery, or a private conversation; ¥20 the seat.

#### Security

Zone: Flats — Neon Shambles turf, unclaimed by any single gang because the Choir Room belongs to the scene, and the scene protects itself. Bexx's warning-network is the first line; the crowd is the second.

No hard security and no guns tolerated — the danger here is the crush itself and the occasional bad dose. A drawn weapon empties the room in seconds, and the crowd will not protect whoever drew it.

Alert means Sanctum finally moves — an occupancy raid, a shutdown order, a checkpoint at the top of the stair. It's the sword hanging over the whole venue.

#### The Overlay (What the Wired Shows Here)

The Choir Room is an overlay phenomenon — Mira's set floods the local Wired with the crowd's live emotional signature, making it one of the richest, strangest AR-spaces in the Flats. A technomancer who drops in feels the whole room's mood as a tangible thing.

Public AR shows nothing; the venue is unlisted, passed hand to hand. Finding it the first time is a small rite of passage.

Beneath Mira's set, a hacker can find the raw crowd-read data — a real-time map of a thousand people's feelings, which is either the most beautiful thing in the district or, in the wrong hands, a targeting solution.

#### Plot Hooks

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
1. Read The Room. Mira felt the crowd turn wrong three nights running before three separate crews vanished, and she's convinced someone is using the Choir Room as a hunting ground. She'll trade the crew everything she knows for someone willing to be bait.

2. The Raid. Sanctum finally moves on the Choir Room, and the crew is inside when the checkpoint seals the top of the stair. Getting a thousand panicking dancers — and themselves — out through the overflow-channels is the run.

3. The Choir's Price. Mira's read-the-room gift is drawing corporate attention; Meridian wants to hire or acquire her, and Obsidian wants her set silenced so the Velvet Stair has no rival. She needs a crew to keep her free, and neither corp intends to lose gracefully.

chunks.heading: Player Description
chunks.text:
*(read aloud as the crew arrives)*

This is the only entry in the Roster that sits outside the wall. Marrow's Lantern is the heart of Cinderhold, a great low hall of salvaged plate and wasteland timber built right against the outer gate's shadow, and it is the last place with a roof, a fire, and a door that locks before the wilds begin. Where every other venue in the Flats has no sky, the Lantern has too much of one — step out its rear door and the hive's ceiling is gone, replaced by the real, terrible open dark and, on the horizon, the black wall of primeval jungle where the huge trees stand like the pillars of a drowned cathedral and things move that the Flats has no names for.

Inside, though, it is warm — genuinely, gloriously warm, a real wood-and-scrap fire in a central pit, the smell of roasting meat that walked on its own legs this morning, and light from a hundred hanging lanterns because out here the Wired is thin and a lantern is a thing you can trust. The crowd is unlike any inside the wall: Greenline Rangers off the frontier, wasteland caravaneers, Cinderhold salvagers, hive-exiles who can never go back, and the occasional edgerunner crew staging for a job in the green. They drink hard and they drink early, because everyone here knows the odds of the ones who go out the back door.

Behind the bar, a weathered man with a Ranger's old field-coat and a gatekeeper's hard eyes pours a measure, sets it down, and looks at you the way a man looks at weather coming in.

chunks.heading: Director's Section
chunks.text:
#### Key NPCs

**Ranger-Captain Cael Marrow** (human), "the Gate" — Cinderhold's protector and the Lantern's owner, a former Greenline Ranger who holds the settlement by being harder, fairer, and more feared than anyone who'd take it. He keeps a cold professional back-channel to Mama Cassavir inside the wall; the two of them are the twin switchboards of the hive's edge. He pours drinks himself because it's how he takes the measure of everyone who passes through his gate.

**Sister Ona** (Corran) — a Lamp-on-Ninth street-priest who came out to Cinderhold and stayed, running a soup-line and a vigil-lamp from a corner of the Lantern; the settlement's conscience and its field-medic both.

**"Longtooth" Garr** (Goliar) — a caravan-master and wasteland guide who knows the safe game-trails through the near-jungle better than anyone still breathing; he'll guide a crew outward for a steep price and a signed understanding of the risk.

**The Ones Who Came Back Wrong** — a quiet table of survivors who went into the deep wilds and returned changed — Veil-touched, haunted, marked.
